events.text: Prayers addressed to {b3_house} arrive at its head's door in bundles, tied with reed, since the day you took the seat. Most are for the Line itself: for crops, for births, for safe roads. A few are for you by name. One, in a child's hand, simply asks that you be happy. It has no offering.

choices.text: Keep that prayer on the Lineage altar

effects.log: You keep it. Every year, on the same day, the altar-flame leans toward it, and the Lineage acquires a reputation for a kind of gentle luck.

choices.text: Answer it, in a dream, with a single word

effects.log: You answer. The child, waking, tells the household that the Line said "yes", and the household, hearing, leaves out a second bowl of milk.

events.text: The Offering Hall of {b3_house} has fallen behind its quota of worship for the first time in memory. The Officers present charts. The charts blame the other Lineages, who are said to have been "stealing" prayers by being slightly more vivid. The Officers want a campaign of vividness.

choices.text: Authorise a festival of the Line's oldest stories

effects.log: You authorise it. The Line's stories are told in a hundred villages below, and the offerings recover, and the Officers are insufferable about it for a century.

choices.text: Refuse, and send a gift to the Lineages who are "stealing"

effects.log: You send gifts. The Lineages are baffled, and the Officers appalled, and the quota recovers anyway, by what seems pure spite.

events.text: Your cousin of {b3_house} has made a mortal river-spirit a minor patron of the Line, without telling anyone. The spirit is a small, greedy, adorable thing that eats offerings of fish. The Officers say it is an irregularity. The cousin says it is a friend. The spirit says nothing, and ate the minutes of the meeting.

choices.text: Enrol the spirit in the Lineage as a "guest"

effects.log: You enrol it. It is the first guest in the history of the Line, and the Book of the Line, which has never had a smudge, acquires one on page nine.

choices.text: Ask the cousin to quietly return the spirit to its river

effects.log: The cousin does, in tears, and the river that year floods exactly once, gently, in the Line's favour.

events.text: A prayer to {b3_house} reaches your hall, so urgent that it arrives with a smell of smoke. It is a village on fire, far below, and a mother calling the Line's name over and over. The Lineage rule is that the head may not meddle with the mortal weather. The prayer goes on.

choices.text: Break the rule, and send a rain

effects.log: You send it. The fire is out in a minute, and the Book of the Line, which records your breach, records it in gold, and the Officers cannot decide whether to praise or censure.

choices.text: Obey the rule, and send a dream of the well

effects.log: You send a dream. The mother wakes, runs to the well, and the village is saved by a bucket brigade, and the Line is thanked by name.

events.text: It is the Feast of Names for {b3_house}. Each of the Line is called aloud in the hall, three thousand names. The herald stumbles on the two thousandth and falls silent. The hall waits. The name is unfamiliar. A child has put it into the register in the night, in a hand nobody knows.

choices.text: Say the name yourself, aloud

effects.log: You say it. The hall echoes it, and from the roof there is a small silvery sound, like a bell struck with a feather, and the name is the Line's from that night.

choices.text: Strike the name and call the next

effects.log: You strike it. The hall breathes out. The child comes to you in the morning, in tears, and you are obliged to explain the Line's limits to a very small god.

events.text: The Book of the Line of {b3_house} has a page that is blank except for a single smear of ink. It has been blank since the founding. A young scribe, hired to copy the Book, is the first to ask what it is for. The head scribe says: for the thing that must be written and has not yet been done. The young scribe asks you what that might be.

choices.text: Say you do not yet know, and leave the page blank

effects.log: You say so. The scribe, delighted, copies the blank page with painstaking care, and the Line is somewhat more thoughtful for a hundred years.

choices.text: Write one word on the page: "mercy"

effects.log: You write it. It dries gold, and the Officers argue over it for a century, and the Line, quietly, becomes kinder.

events.text: The sky over {b3_house} goes strange at noon: a lightless circle where the sun should be, a hush, and all the offerings in the hall begin to rise gently from their bowls. The Officers freeze. The old Reader of Omens announces that this is either the end of all things or a very rare form of hospitality.

choices.text: Greet the visitor with a libation

effects.log: You pour a libation to the empty sky. The circle dwindles, and a great and mild voice thanks the Line, and the offerings settle, and the Reader of Omens is promoted.

choices.text: Close the hall and wait it out

effects.log: You close it. When the doors reopen, the sun is back, and every offering has been replaced with a different offering of the same weight, and nobody can say whose.

events.text: A younger Lineage petitions {b3_house} for protection against the older ones. Their head is an anxious, bright-eyed god of mountains, seated in the hall with a bundle of small gifts. Their Line is barely three thousand years old. Your own Officers say the Line is trouble, and cheap.

choices.text: Take them under the Line's wing

effects.log: You take them. They are loud, grateful, and demanding, and in two thousand years are the most loyal of your allies, and the most exhausting.

choices.text: Give them a letter of introduction to the Thrones and send them on

effects.log: You give it. They go, hopeful, and are well received, and send a basket of mountain flowers every spring.

events.text: The seat of the Line's Herald has been empty for a century. The two candidates are both loyal, both capable, and both utterly sure the other is a fool. They have each written you a letter. The letters are the same length and in the same ink and say the same thing about each other.

choices.text: Appoint both, as Herald of the Dawn and Herald of the Dusk

effects.log: You appoint both. They spend the first century at war, the second in a grudging alliance, and the third in a friendship so deep it surprises them.

choices.text: Appoint neither, and let the post stand empty a little longer

effects.log: You leave it. The Line, a century later, discovers it has been doing perfectly well without a Herald, and the two candidates settle into a happy retirement.

events.text: An old rival god of {b3_house} dies, and his Line asks yours to take in his shrine. It is dusty, plain, and defended by a single stone dog. The Officers are against. The dead god was your enemy for six thousand years. The dog, you notice, has been polished, recently, by someone who loved it.

choices.text: Take in the shrine and the dog

effects.log: You take them. The dog is placed at the gate of your own hall, where it sits for a long time, and one winter it lifts its head and howls once, and the Line understands.

choices.text: Offer a place for the shrine on a neutral mountain

effects.log: You offer one. It is accepted. Years later a pilgrim brings you a flower from the dog's head, and tells you it is from the old god.

events.text: Ossel, Keeper of the Offerings of {b3_clan}, has been setting aside one bowl of incense-rice in nine. The Officers call it theft. The bowl goes, every dawn, to a shrine on a far ridge where a god who died before the pantheons had names is still, faintly, remembered by one goat-herd.

choices.text: Let Ossel keep the bowl, and say so in the Book

effects.log: You write it into the Book of the Line as a standing offering. Ossel weeps into the rice, and the Officers go quiet, which is its own kind of applause.

choices.text: Ask Ossel why, and listen to all of it

effects.log: The answer takes an afternoon and involves a debt of four thousand years. You leave knowing a good deal about the Line you did not, and Ossel keeps the bowl anyway.

choices.text: End it; the Line feeds its own

effects.log: You end it. Ossel obeys without a word and for a year the rice smells faintly of reproach.

events.text: The goat-herd from the far ridge climbs the stair of dawn to the gate of {b3_clan}, leading one goat. The herd-boy has come to thank the Line for the bowl. The Warden of the Domain Gate does not know what to do with a thanker, and sends for Ossel, who is already running.

choices.text: Receive the herd-boy in the Hall of Names

effects.log: You receive the boy in the Hall of Names, goat and all. The goat eats a garland, and the Hall of Names is, afterward, a more honest room.

choices.text: Let Ossel host the boy, and watch from the gallery

effects.log: Ossel hosts. You watch an old keeper be thanked for the first time in four thousand years, and you look away to give them the privacy.

events.text: Years on, a thin god steps out of a rock on the far ridge and walks to the gate of {b3_clan}. It is the dead god of the bowl, assembled out of one goat-herd's memory and nine hundred bowls of rice. They say they are not here to claim anything. They would like to sit by a fire.

choices.text: Give the old god a seat at the vigil flames

effects.log: You give them a seat. The old god warms their hands and tells stories of the world before the first fire, and by morning the Hall of Names has a new corner.

choices.text: Offer the old god a place in the Line, as an Elder of the Bowl

effects.log: You enrol them. The Line gains a patient presence and a ridge, and the old god gains, in the Book, a name in your handwriting.

events.text: A name on the name-pillars of {b3_clan} has gone faint. Nobody has spoken it in three thousand years. A name unspoken is a god half-unmade. The Herald of the Line says the Officers have no record of who it belonged to, only that the stone seems to want it back.

choices.text: Have the Herald speak the name at every dawn

effects.log: You order it spoken at every dawn. In a year the stone darkens and the Officers note, with a certain uneasiness, that something has heard it.

choices.text: Search the old records for whose it was

effects.log: You send the scribes into the lower stacks. They come out, after eleven years, with a cough, a name, and a story that the Line would rather had stayed in the stacks.

choices.text: Let it fade; not every name is owed forever

effects.log: You let it fade. The stone goes smooth, and for a century a small cold spot lingers in the hall, which the servants step around.

events.text: The faint name on the pillar of {b3_clan} has answered. A guest stands in the Hall of Names who is not quite there: a god, you think, or the shape of one, in a coat of a style the Line gave up before writing. They say the name was theirs. They say they have been waiting politely to be asked in.

choices.text: Ask them in, and ask what the Line did to them

effects.log: You ask. The answer is that the Line did nothing, which is the injury, and you write it down.

choices.text: Ask them in, and ask nothing at all tonight

effects.log: You pour a libation and ask nothing. The guest drinks it, enormously relieved, and sleeps in the hall like a cat.

events.text: The guest of {b3_clan} turns out to be a god of a small thing, the hush between a prayer being said and a prayer being heard. The Line forgot them because it never noticed the hush. They offer to teach it. The Officers are divided on whether a hush can be taught.

choices.text: Take the god as a Lineage tutor in the hush

effects.log: You take them. For a decade the prayers arriving at the Line come a little slower and are, somehow, better answered.

choices.text: Honour them with a pillar of their own

effects.log: You carve a pillar. It stands apart from the others, and the god sits at its foot and is, by every sign, content.

events.text: The prayer bell of {b3_clan} rings by itself at noon, one stroke, and again at dusk. The Officers trace it: a single mortal village, far below, has begun to pray to the Line by name, though no one there has ever been taught the name. {b3_peer} says it is a mistake. The bell does not.

choices.text: Send a small sign: a good rain on the village

effects.log: You send rain. The bell goes silent for a week, and then rings again, once, as if to say thank you.

choices.text: Send a herald in the shape of a pedlar

effects.log: The herald goes down as a pedlar of needles and returns with the village's whole history in a story told wrong on purpose.

choices.text: Leave the bell unanswered; a Line does not chase

effects.log: You leave it. The bell rings at noon and dusk for a year, and the Officers learn to stop looking up.

events.text: The village that prays to {b3_clan} has built a shrine: a roof, a bowl, a stone with the Line's name cut into it wrong. The mason knew only the sound. The prayers are plain and astonishingly detailed. {b3_elder} says the first offerings from the village have reached the Hall like a warm draught.

choices.text: Correct the name in a dream to the mason

effects.log: You correct it. The mason wakes, weeps, and recuts the stone, and the village is thereafter very sure of itself.

choices.text: Let the wrong name stand; it is theirs now

effects.log: You let it stand. The Line becomes, in one village, a god with a slightly different name, which pleases the village and troubles the Officers.

events.text: A generation later the village shrine of {b3_clan} has a school, a market, a feast-day, and a quarrel. Two half-villages disagree about how the Line likes its rice. Each sends a delegate up the prayer-road. Both have prepared a speech. Neither speech mentions rice.

choices.text: Hear both delegates in the Hall, together

effects.log: You hear them together. By the second speech both delegates are laughing at their own, and the quarrel is settled over a joint offering.

choices.text: Send a dream to each, telling the other's side

effects.log: You send the dreams. Each delegate wakes knowing the other's whole case, and the quarrel ends in an awkward silence and a marriage.

events.text: Pim, the youngest god of {b3_clan}, three hundred years old and very proud, has been answering prayers on their own. Every answer is granted exactly as asked and goes wrong in some small way. A man asked for a bigger harvest, and has been harvesting, in his sleep, for a month.

choices.text: Take Pim's authority away until they have learned

effects.log: You take it. Pim is mortified, and the Officers are relieved, and the sleeping man is woken with an apology and a basket of pears.

choices.text: Sit with Pim and read every answer aloud

effects.log: You read them aloud. Pim, red to the ears, finds the pattern of the mistakes in an hour, which is more than three Officers managed in a year.

events.text: Pim of {b3_clan} returns to the prayer-desk, shaking, and answers one prayer. It is a plain request for a safe road, and the answer is a safe road and nothing else, no extra, no flourish. The petitioner never knows. Pim looks at you across the Hall as though they had climbed a mountain.

choices.text: Nod once, and say nothing

effects.log: You nod once. Pim goes pink and bends back to the desk, and the Hall hears a very young god trying not to hum.

choices.text: Give Pim a vigil flame of their own

effects.log: You light one in their name. Pim keeps it, in a bowl, for ten thousand years, and tells it things.

events.text: Three thousand years on, Pim is the best Reader of Prayers {b3_clan} has had, and the youngest in the stacks calls them master. A prayer arrives from a mortal who writes: "I know you are not listening, but." Pim holds it a long time, then walks to your door with the ink still wet.

choices.text: Read the prayer with Pim, and decide together

effects.log: You read it together. The answer you choose is not the one either of you expected, and it is correct.

choices.text: Tell Pim the choice is theirs, and leave the room

effects.log: You leave. Pim answers the prayer alone, and the Line is thereafter a little more Pim than it was.

events.text: An envoy of the Lineage of Ash and Morning arrives at {b3_clan} and, before greeting anyone, corrects the angle at which the first fire is depicted in the lintel. They were there. They say so, kindly, and then for an hour, less kindly. The Officers write it all down.

choices.text: Have the lintel recarved to the envoy's account

effects.log: You recarve it. The fire is smaller than the Line had imagined, and wilder, and the Officers admit it looks truer.

choices.text: Thank the envoy and keep the Line's own account

effects.log: You thank them and keep it. The envoy leaves with a very small bow, which, from Ash and Morning, is a considerable concession.

events.text: A Long Tide matchmaker comes to {b3_clan} with a tray of pearl-shell tokens, one for each unmarried god of the Line. The Lineage of the Long Tide marries into every pantheon and belongs to none, and the matchmaker is honestly pleased to discover it has no preference.

choices.text: Accept the tokens and open the Line to the sea

effects.log: You accept. A tide of sea-gods' cousins comes in over the next century, with salt in their hems and gossip in their pockets.

choices.text: Send them back with thanks and a counter-gift of lamps

effects.log: You send lamps. The matchmaker shrugs the shrug of a person who has been refused by greater gods and will be back in a century.

events.text: A scribe of the Lineage of the Unlit Lamp calls at {b3_clan} at midnight and asks to consult one document. It is a seating plan from nine thousand years ago. The scribe will explain nothing and copy nothing. The scribe will merely look at it, with a lamp unlit, in the dark, for an hour.

choices.text: Allow it, and leave the scribe alone in the archive

effects.log: You allow it. The scribe leaves at dawn without a word and, a week later, a locked box of records arrives in exchange, unlabelled.

choices.text: Allow it, and ask what the plan will tell the scribe

effects.log: The scribe says it will tell them where to dig. Then, as if reconsidering, where not to. You never learn which, and the Unlit Lamp remembers that you asked politely.

events.text: The Lineage of the Root is owed a great deal by {b3_clan}: grain-seasons, three floods, and a mountain. They have never mentioned it. Today a very patient old goddess of the deep earth arrives and mentions it, once, and then sits on the floor of the Hall and admires the grain of the wood.

choices.text: Settle the oldest debt in full, in front of the Line

effects.log: You settle it, in grain and in word. The old goddess accepts it as one accepts rain, and thereafter the Root treats your Line as family.

choices.text: Ask what the Root would most like in return

effects.log: She says: "a pillar in the sun." You carve it. She sits against it for a decade and the Line is much calmer.

events.text: A star that has been hidden for nine thousand years chooses the sky over {b3_clan} to be seen in. The Lineage of the Hidden Star sends a note saying only: "sorry about the light." The Officers are in a flurry; the Reader of Omens says it means a great many things, all of them embarrassing.

choices.text: Hold a vigil under the star

effects.log: You hold it. The star seems to attend, politely, and in the morning is gone, leaving a faint warmth on the pillars.

choices.text: Ask the Hidden Star's Lineage why now

effects.log: The answer arrives in a month. They do not know. They hoped you might.

events.text: The Lineage of the Nine Wells has sent {b3_clan} a gift: a jar of water from the seventh well, which they say tastes of the thing you most regret. The Officers decline to taste it. {b3_peer} tastes it and walks away very quietly, and returns in the morning to say it tastes of lemons.

choices.text: Drink a cup, and say what it tasted of

effects.log: You drink. You say nothing, and the Hall does not ask, and you think of a particular morning for most of a month.

choices.text: Pour it into the Line's own well, unopened

effects.log: You pour it in. The well tastes the same, but the Line, over the next century, becomes slightly less embarrassed by itself.

events.text: A drummer of the Lineage of the Silent Drum comes to the gate of {b3_clan} and beats a drum without a skin. The Hall holds its breath. The drum makes no sound, and the silence is somehow enormous, and every flame in the Hall leans toward the drummer and then, together, away.

choices.text: Ask the drummer what the drum has said

effects.log: The drummer writes one word on the floor in rice: "listen." Then eats the rice. The Hall is very quiet for a month.

choices.text: Answer with the Line's own bell, once

effects.log: You ring the prayer bell once. The drummer inclines their head, accepting the trade, and goes without a word.

events.text: The Laughing River has changed its course by a mile to flow past the gate of {b3_clan}, and every god of the Line stands in the water laughing. The Lineage of the Laughing River do this at weddings, funerals and treaties, and have never explained how to tell the three apart.

choices.text: Laugh with them, ankle-deep, and see what it was

effects.log: You wade in. It was a wedding, and you were the best guest they could find, and for a century the river is on your side.

choices.text: Send the Warden of the Domain Gate to stay dry and watch

effects.log: The Warden watches with a face like a closed door. By evening it is clear it was a treaty, and the Warden has mis-signed it, and you are suddenly in an alliance.

events.text: The Herald of the Line, Maunt, has lost their voice. They say it is a cold. The Officers know better: a Herald calls the names of the Line, and tens of thousands of years of names wear a throat. A deputy of eighteen nervously volunteers. Maunt gestures that it is a terrible idea and also the only one.

choices.text: Let the young deputy call the names, with Maunt at their elbow

effects.log: The deputy calls them, cracking on every third. Maunt mouths every one. It is the most moving Feast of Names in a thousand years.

choices.text: Postpone the calling until Maunt's voice returns

effects.log: You postpone it. It returns in a year, lower, and the names are called with a roughness the Line decides it likes.

events.text: A mortal has climbed the stair of dawn to the gate of {b3_clan}, on their knees, over eleven years. They arrive at the top with raw palms and ask nothing. The Warden of the Domain Gate, who has seen it a thousand times, looks at you in a way that says: this one is different, and I cannot say why.

choices.text: Raise the pilgrim and grant them a plain wish

effects.log: You raise them. They ask for a quiet field and a well. You give both, and the pilgrim, to your surprise, is not content, and tells you what they actually wanted.

choices.text: Honour the climb itself with a name on the pillars

effects.log: You carve their name. They weep, not for joy, and the Warden stands a little straighter all week.

events.text: The Oracle Pool of {b3_clan} has gone cloudy. The Reader of Omens says it happens when the Line is about to be asked a question it does not want to answer. {b3_elder} says it is silt. The pool, when you lean over it, shows your own face, ten thousand years older, looking nervous.

choices.text: Ask the pool the question it is clouded about

effects.log: The pool clears. You are told something exact and unwelcome, and the Line changes a custom within the year.

choices.text: Let the pool settle; some questions can wait

effects.log: It settles over a decade. What was asked is never asked, and the Line is, you suspect, a little weaker for the courtesy.

events.text: The vigil flames of {b3_clan} must never go out. A flame goes out. The god on duty, a sleepy young cousin, swears it was fine a moment ago. The flame's ash is still warm. The Officers want the cousin sent to the Root for a century of penance. The cousin is crying.

choices.text: Relight it yourself, and say the cousin held it all night

effects.log: You relight it with a breath. The cousin never forgets the lie, and the flame, at the very least, burns a trifle warmer.

choices.text: Let the cousin relight it, with the Officers watching

effects.log: The cousin relights it, trembling. It catches. The Hall exhales, and the Officers drop the penance to a month of keeping the lamps.

events.text: Midway through the night-rite at {b3_clan}, the Gate of Incense swings open on its own and the smoke pours out in the shape of a procession: a hundred small figures, all carrying lamps, all walking in step toward the east. The Reader of Omens has never seen it. {b3_peer} says to follow.

choices.text: Follow the smoke procession to wherever it goes

effects.log: You follow. They walk the whole night and vanish at a pond on the eastern boundary, where the water is, in the morning, faintly sweet.

choices.text: Close the Gate of Incense and ask what it meant

effects.log: You close it. The smoke recoils and returns to the censers. The meaning arrives in a dream a month later and is mostly an apology.

events.text: A younger god of {b3_clan} has fallen in love with a Lineage the Officers dislike, and has sworn to marry in the Silent Hall without asking. They come to you with the oath ready and half their courage gone. {b3_elder} says the marriage will split the Line. The younger god says the Line is split already.

choices.text: Bless the match openly, in the Hall of Names

effects.log: You bless it. The Line splits a little further and heals a little more, and the younger god's house becomes a bridge.

choices.text: Insist on the full Covenant, with all the Lineages invited

effects.log: You insist. It takes sixty years and the wedding is magnificent, and the guests spend it settling old scores in whispers.

events.text: The offering stores of {b3_clan} are overfull. A great harvest of prayers has come in and nobody asked the Line to answer them all at once. The stores smell of cut grass, cedar and hope. The Keeper of the Offerings, in a flap, asks whether it is permitted to simply give some away.

choices.text: Open the stores to the lesser shrines of the district

effects.log: You open them. The small shrines for a hundred miles hold feasts, and the Line is, for a generation, spoken of in every kitchen.

choices.text: Burn the surplus as a great offering to the sky

effects.log: You burn it. The smoke stands over the domain for a week, and the Line is admired by those who like a spectacle and resented by those who like rice.

events.text: The Warden of the Domain Gate of {b3_clan}, Tirk, has turned away the same god nineteen times. Today the god returns with a petition signed by all the Elder Lineages, and a face like a thundercloud. Tirk says the rule is the rule. The petition says the rule is old, which it is, and bad, which Tirk will not say.

choices.text: Overrule the Warden and admit the petitioner

effects.log: You admit them. Tirk takes it with the dignity of a person whose life's work has been undone in a sentence, and offers to resign. You refuse, with effort.

choices.text: Back the Warden, and hear the god in the Hall instead

effects.log: You back Tirk and hear the god at length. The god leaves unsatisfied but heard, which is, you learn, about eighty percent of what they wanted.

events.text: The domain beneath {b3_clan} has gone quiet. Not dead, not hostile: quiet. Prayers continue; the weather is mild. But the Officers say a domain that is never surprised is a domain that has stopped being looked at, and a god who is not surprised for a century becomes a god nobody asks anything of.

choices.text: Walk the domain in person, unannounced

effects.log: You walk it. The mortals do not know you and are not meant to, and you return with three small, specific worries the Officers had missed.

choices.text: Send a storm, a small one, to wake it

effects.log: You send a storm. The domain wakes, furious and grateful, and prayers pour in, many of them rude.

events.text: A scholar of the Hall of Names catalogues the epithets of {b3_clan}, and finds that the Line has acquired, over ten thousand years, one hundred and nine titles, eleven of which contradict each other. "The Gentle," "The Terror of Rivers." The scholar asks, quite seriously, which the Line wishes to be.

choices.text: Keep all of them, and have them recited at the Feast

effects.log: You keep all. The recitation takes an hour, and the Line is moved by its own contradictions and a bit proud of them.

choices.text: Choose three, and let the rest fade

effects.log: You choose three. The Line reads them aloud, and is quiet, and recognises itself in precisely none of them.

events.text: Your cousin Veyl of {b3_clan} has laid down a divinity and gone down to live as a fisherman on a mortal coast. The Officers call it a scandal. The Book of the Line calls it "an absence." Veyl sends one letter: a smear of fish-scale, a drawing of a boat, and the words "come and see."

choices.text: Go down in disguise and see for yourself

effects.log: You go down as a net-mender. Veyl hauls you out of a squall by the collar, laughing, and you spend a week eating what you are given and being no one.

choices.text: Send a herald with a gift and a polite question

effects.log: The herald returns sunburned and strangely cheerful, with a salted fish for you and no answer at all.

choices.text: Strike Veyl's name from the pillars

effects.log: You strike it. Veyl will not know for a century, and the Officers sigh with relief, and the pillars have a new gap.

events.text: Veyl's fishing village prays to the Line now, because Veyl taught them how, in a whisper, over a cooking-pot. The prayers are in the broken dialect of the coast and hit the Hall of Names like a cold wave. {b3_elder} hardly knows whether to be offended or moved. The Keeper of the Offerings is both.

choices.text: Answer the village in Veyl's own idiom, in dreams

effects.log: You learn the idiom and answer. The village is astounded that the Line talks like a neighbour, and the Hall gets a new, rougher grace.

choices.text: Keep the village at a formal distance

effects.log: You answer in the formal tongue. The village is respectful and a little frightened, and the offerings dwindle to a polite trickle.

events.text: Veyl is dying, as mortals do, in a cottage that smells of tar. The village has gathered. Veyl's divinity is still where it was laid down, in a box under the bed. They ask only one thing of you: to decide, since Veyl cannot, whether the box is taken back into the Line or buried with the body.

choices.text: Take it back into the Line, with honours

effects.log: You carry the box home and set it on a pillar by itself. The Line learns that a god can step down and still be of it.

choices.text: Bury it with Veyl, at the village

effects.log: You bury it. The village raises a mound, and the Line, from that day, answers the coast with a tenderness it never had.

events.text: A mortal sect far below has begun to pray to the cook of {b3_clan}. A real cook, the third in a line of cooks, a small gruff god of the hearth who has never been prayed to in his life. The sect leaves bread. The cook is appalled, and eats it, and says nothing.

choices.text: Make the cook a minor god of the hearth, officially

effects.log: You make it official. The cook is horrified and then, to their own astonishment, rather good at it, and the bread becomes a daily offering.

choices.text: Tell the sect, in a dream, that the cook is only a cook

effects.log: You send the dream. The sect nods gravely and begins to pray to the dream instead.

choices.text: Ask the cook what they want done

effects.log: The cook says: "they could stop leaving the crusts." You pass this on, and the crusts stop, and the cook is quietly bereft.

events.text: The hearth-sect of {b3_clan}'s cook sends a delegation up the prayer-road: nine mortals in clean aprons, carrying a loaf the length of a man. They want the cook to bless it. The Warden of the Domain Gate lets them in because he cannot find a rule against aprons. The cook is hiding in the larder.

choices.text: Coax the cook out to bless the loaf

effects.log: The cook comes out, red to the ears, and blesses it in four words. The delegation weeps. The loaf is the best bread of your life.

choices.text: Bless the loaf yourself, in the cook's name

effects.log: You bless it. The delegation accepts it with dignity, and the cook finds you afterward and says, gruffly, "owed you one."

events.text: A thousand years on, the hearth-sect has spread to a hundred kitchens. The cook of {b3_clan} is, by head-count of believers, the most prayed-to god of the whole Line. The Officers are quietly uneasy. The cook is not. The cook has a request: a bigger stove, and a day off.

choices.text: Build the stove and grant the day off, in writing

effects.log: You build the stove and write the holiday into the Book. The cook is thereafter the most loyal god in the Line.

choices.text: Build the stove, but keep the cook on duty

effects.log: You keep the cook at the fire. The stove is magnificent and the bread improves, and the Hall begins to detect a note of exhaustion in the soup.

events.text: A young archivist of {b3_clan} brings you a fragment of the founding scroll with a worm-hole through the divine title. Without the hole, the first line reads: "The woman who carried the fire." Not the god. The woman. The archivist has not slept. The Officers have not been told.

choices.text: Tell no one; read the rest of the scroll with the archivist

effects.log: You read it together over a week. The founder was a mortal who stole a coal and was made a god by the people she lit. The Line is built on a theft, and on gratitude.

choices.text: Burn the fragment; the Line stands on its title

effects.log: You burn it. The archivist watches with a face you will remember for a long time, and the Line stands, slightly more brittle.

choices.text: Put it before the Officers at once

effects.log: The Officers are silent for an hour. Then {b3_elder} says the Line has always known, and nobody had the courage to write it down.

events.text: The truth about the founder of {b3_clan} has leaked among the Officers. Half want it carved in the Hall. Half want the archivist sent to the Lineage of the Unlit Lamp, to be kept, with the scroll, in the dark. The archivist sits in the corner, small and defiant, with the scroll held to their chest.

choices.text: Carve the truth in the Hall of Names

effects.log: You carve it. The Line is shaken and, in a century, prouder than it has ever been.

choices.text: Seal the scroll in the Hall and say nothing yet

effects.log: You seal it behind a pillar. The truth rests there, patient, until a head of the Line is ready, and you choose to be that head later.

events.text: Pilgrims have begun to arrive at {b3_clan} asking to see "the Woman Who Carried the Fire." The carving has reached them through other Lineages. The Line now has a great many visitors, most of them mortals, many of them women, all of them looking at the pillar with an unfamiliar expression.

choices.text: Open a shrine to the founder at the gate

effects.log: You open one. A line of mortals comes every day, and the Line learns a new custom: being looked at by those it once only watched.

choices.text: Keep the pilgrims to a single day each year

effects.log: You set a day. The Line keeps its dignity, and the pilgrims keep, in their villages, a feast of coals.

events.text: The Reader of Prayers of {b3_clan} reports that for the first time in memory the Line has more prayers asking for it to be quiet than for it to speak. Mortals below are tired of omens. The Reader suggests, nervously, a year of doing nothing at all.

choices.text: Declare a year of Quiet in the domain

effects.log: You declare it. The mortals wake from a year of unremarked days astonished at how much they had been listening for you, and the prayers return richer.

choices.text: Refuse; a Line that goes quiet is forgotten

effects.log: You refuse. The omens continue, and the prayers for quiet get louder, which is, one of the Officers observes, a kind of irony.

events.text: A moth has settled in the scroll-stacks of {b3_clan} and is eating, with great precision, only the vowels of the Line's oldest prayers. The Archivist holds a sheet up to the light and it is lace. The moth is, by the shape of its wings, a minor god of attrition, and quite pleased with itself.

choices.text: Make an offering to the moth and ask it to stop

effects.log: You offer it a clean parchment. It eats that too, but takes the next prayer more slowly, and the vowels survive.

choices.text: Have the stacks copied in full before the moth finishes

effects.log: You set fifty scribes to it. The copy costs a century of ink and is, uniquely, a better text than the original.

events.text: On the Day of the Lost War, {b3_clan} keeps a silence. It is the Line's great shame: a battle fought ten thousand years ago against an enemy that turned out to be a misunderstanding. This year a young god breaks the silence, aloud, to ask whether the shame has not lasted long enough.

choices.text: Let the young god speak, and listen to the Hall

effects.log: You let them. The Hall is angry for a minute and quiet for an hour, and by the end of it the silence is shorter by half.

choices.text: Keep the silence whole and speak with the young god alone

effects.log: You keep it. Afterward you speak with the young god for a long time, and the Line's shame is, quietly, set down.

events.text: Twin gods of {b3_clan}, born in the same breath of the same dawn, have been sharing a domain, the sunrise, by alternating days. This week they have stopped speaking. The sun has risen twice at once and once not at all. Mortals below are putting it down to the weather.

choices.text: Sit them down and split the morning by the hour

effects.log: You split it. The sun rises on schedule again, and the twins sulk beautifully for fifty years.

choices.text: Let them fight it out, but away from the sky

effects.log: You send them to a quarrelling mountain. They return a month later arm in arm, and the sun rises, a little crooked, every day after.

events.text: A mortal king of the lands under {b3_clan} has announced that he descends from the Line. He has drawn a genealogy. It is entirely plausible and entirely invented. His people believe it. The Officers hold that the Line cannot allow a false descent, and cannot, either, admit that a mortal can be so convincing.

choices.text: Confirm the descent, with a condition or two

effects.log: You confirm it, in a dream. The king is thereafter careful, and the realm is gentler, and the Line gains a very useful cousin.

choices.text: Send a dream to the king: you are not of us, but you may be loved

effects.log: The king wakes, stricken, and then, after a month, rather relieved. He rules better for being loved than for being related.

events.text: The cloud-chariot of the head of {b3_clan} has been stolen, again, by the same cousin, for the sixth time. It is found parked on a mountaintop with a picnic laid out. The cousin says it was a lovely day. The Officers recommend a harsh penalty. The chariot, notably, is spotless.

choices.text: Forgive the cousin; and ask to be invited next time

effects.log: You forgive. The next picnic is in a high green valley, and the chariot is, you note, more comfortable with company.

choices.text: Assign the cousin the post of Chariot-Keeper

effects.log: You make it a post. The cousin keeps the chariot meticulously, and takes it nowhere, and is visibly pining.

events.text: The Book of the Line of {b3_clan} has a footnote war. Two scribes, a century apart, have added contradictory notes to the same page, each with a more elaborate source. The margin is full. The Archivist, grim, asks whether the Book is a record or an argument.

choices.text: Declare it an argument and begin a new volume of Disputes

effects.log: You open a volume of Disputes. The Line, with relief, begins to argue on the page rather than in the hall.

choices.text: Rule on the page, once, and lock the margin

effects.log: You rule. One scribe is vindicated, one is crushed, and the margin is clean and joyless.

events.text: A drought lies on the domain beneath {b3_clan}. The mortals blame the Line. A delegation arrives with offerings, in the manner of people who are trying to make a threat look like a gift. The Officers wish to be offended. The rain-god of the Line has, in fact, gone on holiday.

choices.text: Recall the rain-god and send the rain, with an apology

effects.log: You recall them. The rain returns on a Tuesday, and the delegation weeps into its offering.

choices.text: Send the rain, and say nothing about the holiday

effects.log: You send the rain and say nothing. The mortals never know, the rain-god never forgets, and the Line takes a quiet vow to give notice next time.

events.text: An old god of {b3_clan}, three-fifths faded, refuses to be retired and sits at the Gate of Incense every day demanding that prayers be addressed to them by name. No one prays to them. The Warden of the Domain Gate, who is fond of them, brings them tea and says nothing, and so does everyone.

choices.text: Pray to the old god yourself, once a day, in private

effects.log: You pray. The old god, who knows exactly what you are doing, accepts it with a nod, and sits straighter for a century.

choices.text: Give the old god the post of Gate Keeper of the Memory

effects.log: You give them the post. They stand at the Gate and tell every visitor the Line's history, wrong in places, and everyone loves it.

events.text: The accounts of belief for {b3_clan}, tallied every thousand years, show a decline of three percent in faith. The Keeper of the Offerings is grey with worry. The Reader of Omens says the numbers are fine if you squint. The Archivist says that three percent is, historically, how every great Line began to die.

choices.text: Fund a great rite of renewal at the Gate of Incense

effects.log: You fund it. Faith rises four percent over a century, and the Officers conclude, a bit sourly, that spectacle works.

choices.text: Do nothing for fifty years and watch the numbers

effects.log: You watch. The decline reverses on its own, as declines do, and you take the credit anyway.

events.text: A saint of the Silent Hall has come to {b3_clan} to dine, which is a distinction. The saint speaks only in proverbs. All dinner the Officers try to interpret them. The saint eats the first course, praises the second, and leaves behind the third, with the words: "the salt is the sermon."

choices.text: Take the proverb as a standing rule of the Line

effects.log: You make it a rule. The salt is thereafter set before the first dish, and the kitchen is furious, and the Hall oddly steadier.

choices.text: Ask the saint what the proverb means

effects.log: The saint says it means salt. The Hall is silent. Then {b3_peer} laughs, and the saint, almost invisibly, smiles.

events.text: A Reader of Omens at {b3_clan} announces that the Line will end in nine thousand years, to the day, with a flood. It is a very exact prophecy. Several junior gods are already making retirement plans. {b3_elder} asks, coolly, if the Reader would care to specify which flood.

choices.text: Build a great ark-temple on the high ground, as a precaution

effects.log: You build it. The Line has a magnificent folly and a magnificent refuge, and nine thousand years pass without incident.

choices.text: Rule that prophecies of the Line's end are not to be taken as dates

effects.log: You rule so. The Reader grumbles for a century; the junior gods unpack; the flood, in the end, is a small one.

events.text: A dry-eyed little god of grief, newly arrived in the Line, has been sitting in the Hall of Names every night for a month, reading the names aloud to the dead. The Officers are uncomfortable. The god says they are only keeping the names warm. {b3_peer} confesses to sitting with them on Tuesdays.

choices.text: Sit with them yourself, on one of the nights

effects.log: You sit through the names. It is slower and more tender than you had thought, and in the morning the Hall seems to have been dusted by hand.

choices.text: Give the little god a corner and a proper title

effects.log: You make them the Keeper of Warm Names. They are astonished to have a title for the thing they were already doing.

events.text: A god of thieves, unasked, has taken to leaving small offerings at {b3_clan}: a coin, a ring, a spoon. All of them are stolen from other Lineages. The offerings are quite lovely. The Officers want them returned. The Lineage of the Laughing River wants them returned with a joke.

choices.text: Return each one with a note, and a joke of your own

effects.log: You return them with notes. The Laughing River sends back, a month later, a note which is funnier than yours, and the matter ends in a draw.

choices.text: Keep the spoon, and send the rest back

effects.log: You keep the spoon. It is a very good spoon. The thief-god nods, as at an understanding reached, and leaves nothing more.

events.text: The Gate of Incense of {b3_clan} burned out its brazier last night: a fire that has not gone cold in nine thousand years. The Warden stands over it, appalled. The ash is a perfect circle. A mortal child has been seen near the gate in the small hours, standing silent. The child leaves a daisy.

choices.text: Relight the brazier from your own flame

effects.log: You relight it from your own hand. The Line is warmer, for a while, in a way the Officers cannot quite prove.

choices.text: Ask the child what they saw

effects.log: The child says the fire was tired and wanted to sleep. You light a smaller one, and the Gate burns gently, and the daisy is pressed into the Book.

events.text: Two members of the Line have fallen out over how many times a prayer should be repeated before it is answered. One says once. The other, seven. Both have a century of precedent. They come to you with notebooks. The mortals below are meanwhile left in limbo, in a sort of divine rest.

choices.text: Rule three, and write the reason in the Book

effects.log: You rule three. Both are insulted, and both comply, and the mortals below notice that their answers come faster.

choices.text: Let each follow their own count and publish the results

effects.log: You let them. Within a century the data are in, and the middle count wins, and both gods are pleased to have been proven partly right.

events.text: A scullery child of {b3_clan} named Wren has been found asleep under the Oracle Pool, and the water above the child is full of stars. The Reader of Omens turns pale. The Lineage of the Hidden Star lost an heir ten thousand years ago, and has never said how. The child only wants breakfast.

choices.text: Keep the child in the kitchens and tell no one

effects.log: You keep Wren in the kitchens. The child sweeps, is fed, is happy, and the Oracle Pool is a degree clearer every morning.

choices.text: Send word quietly to the Hidden Star

effects.log: You send word. The reply, a month later, is a single sentence: "do nothing until we come." You do nothing, feeling the weight of it.

choices.text: Raise the child as a ward of the Line, openly

effects.log: You name Wren a ward of the Line before the Hall. The Officers murmur, and the child, who has never been looked at by so many, hides in your sleeve.

events.text: Wren of {b3_clan} has grown tall in the kitchens, and has begun, unintentionally, to be seen: stars appear on the ceiling of the larder when the child is happy, and go out when sad. The cooks have learned to tell the weather in the Line by the larder roof. Wren has learned the same, and is mortified.

choices.text: Teach Wren to keep the stars quiet

effects.log: You teach Wren a small breath-rite. The larder ceiling is dull again, and Wren, relieved, is a bit less themself.

choices.text: Let the stars shine and tell the cooks to enjoy it

effects.log: The cooks do. The larder becomes the most beloved room of the Line, and Wren, in it, is fully themself at last.

events.text: Envoys of the Lineage of the Hidden Star have come for Wren at last, silvery and travel-worn, with a letter in no language you know and a gentleness you did not expect. They say the child may choose. Wren is standing between you and the envoys with a ladle held like a spear.

choices.text: Tell Wren the choice is theirs, and step aside

effects.log: You step aside. Wren puts down the ladle, and goes with the envoys, and returns every spring with the larder's stars on their shoulders.

choices.text: Offer the envoys a seat, and the child time

effects.log: You give them a feast, and the child time. It takes nine years, and Wren chooses both: a half-year in each house.

events.text: A mortal poet named Isande, in a hill town below, has written a hymn to {b3_clan} that is simply better than the Line's own. It has been sung in a hundred villages. It is cleverer, warmer and shorter. The Herald of the Line, in the Hall, sings the old hymn through gritted teeth and checks the new.

choices.text: Adopt the poet's hymn at the Feast of Names

effects.log: You adopt it. The Herald sings it in a voice that cracks, and the Hall rises, and Isande, below, hears a god sing her words.

choices.text: Send the poet a dream of praise and leave the Feast alone

effects.log: Isande wakes in tears and writes a hundred more. The old hymn is sung at the Feast, and the new in every kitchen.

choices.text: Forbid the hymn in the Line's halls

effects.log: You forbid it. The halls are quiet, the villages loud, and the Herald hums it in the corridors.

events.text: Isande, the poet who wrote the best hymn to {b3_clan}, is old, and dying in a hill town where a shrine already carries her name by accident. The Herald of the Line, who never forgave her for being right, asks to go down and sing the old hymn at her bedside. As an apology. In the old words.

choices.text: Let the Herald go, with the poet's hymn in their pocket

effects.log: The Herald goes, sings the old words, and then, trembling, the new. Isande hears both, and sleeps.

choices.text: Go down yourself, hooded, and sit beside the bed

effects.log: You sit. Isande knows you at once, and says only, "you took your time." She is dead by morning, and her shrine is, from then on, truer.

events.text: A thousand years on, Isande's hymn is the oldest song of {b3_clan}, and nobody knows she wrote it. A scholar proves it, in a tidy argument, and the Hall splits: half want her name restored on the pillars, half want the hymn to remain the Line's. The Herald, ancient, says it can be both.

choices.text: Cut her name into the pillars beside the Line's own

effects.log: You cut it. A mortal on the pillars of a Lineage is unheard of, and the Hall, once the dust settles, is rather proud.

choices.text: Keep it in the Book, in the Herald's hand, not on the stone

effects.log: You keep it in the Book. Her name is read once a year, softly, at the end of the Feast of Names.

events.text: A prayer has come to the Hall of Names of {b3_clan} addressed only "to whoever is in charge." Three gods of the Line instantly lay claim to it. The prayer is from a woman in a flooded cellar and is, in fact, extremely specific about the cellar. The three are now arguing about jurisdiction at the stair.

choices.text: Take the prayer yourself and drain the cellar

effects.log: You drain it. The woman never knows who, and the three gods sulk, correctly, because the prayer was theirs.

choices.text: Give it to whichever of the three is quietest

effects.log: The quietest, a young god of damp, answers it with unexpected competence, and the other two forgive nobody.

events.text: The cedar forests that supply the incense of {b3_clan} have been felled by mortals in a hurry to build. The Gate of Incense burns a thin sour smoke. The Keeper of the Offerings is beside himself. A delegation of forest-spirits is waiting at the gate with a petition and, notably, no hats.

choices.text: Hear the forest-spirits and set a limit to the felling

effects.log: You hear them, and a quiet word in a king's dream sets a limit. The forest grows back slowly, and the incense with it.

choices.text: Move the Line's incense to a distant mountain grove

effects.log: You move it. The mortals keep their timber, the spirits their sulk, and the Gate burns sweet again.

events.text: The Oracle Pool of {b3_clan} has shown a cousin's secret to the whole Hall. The cousin is a god of harvests who has been secretly writing love poems to a mountain. The poems are quite good. The cousin is crimson. The Officers do not know whether to be scandalised or to ask for copies.

choices.text: Ask the cousin to read one aloud, in the Hall

effects.log: The cousin reads. The Hall goes quiet, and then the mountain, far off, rumbles in what is plainly a reply.

choices.text: Close the Pool for a season, and give the cousin back their privacy

effects.log: You close it. The cousin is grateful beyond words, and the poems, thereafter, are even better.

events.text: A dying star has asked, by the old treaty, for a god of the Line to hold its hand through the last century. The treaty is plain and nobody has had to do it in nine thousand years. The Officers draw lots. The loser is the youngest god of the Line, and she is white to the lips.

choices.text: Go yourself, in the youngest's place

effects.log: You go. A century at a dying star's side is slow and bright and strangely restful, and you come back with a new silence in you.

choices.text: Go with the youngest, and hold her hand while she holds the star's

effects.log: You go together. The star dies gently, and the young god is changed, steadier, and calls you a friend for ten thousand years.

events.text: At the Feast of Names of {b3_clan}, two gods stand and claim the same name. Both have a witness. Both have a document. Both are so civil about it that the Hall is chilled. It is an ancient and venerable name, borne by a hero of the Line, and each is sure it is theirs by right of descent.

choices.text: Give each half the name, and a new title to join them

effects.log: You split it. The two gods are appalled and, in fifty years, inseparable, and the Line has two heroes where it had one.

choices.text: Check the pillars; the stone remembers who was meant

effects.log: You consult the stone. It had remembered neither, but a third, forgotten cousin, who is summoned from the stacks, bewildered and delighted.

events.text: A temple-keeper of the mortals below has written a letter of complaint to {b3_clan}, forty pages long. It concerns, in sorrowful detail, a decade of prayers that went unanswered and a leaking roof. The letter is polite. The tone is that of a person who has run out of other places to send it.

choices.text: Answer the letter in person, in a dream, and mend the roof

effects.log: You appear, hat in hand, and mend the roof. The keeper wakes with a dry shrine and a long, strange conviction that gods have manners.

choices.text: Have the Reader of Prayers draft a considered reply

effects.log: The reply is magnificent and takes two years to arrive. The keeper reads it, nods, and frames it over the leak.

events.text: A god of {b3_clan} has been caught taking commissions on answered prayers: a little extra in offerings, kept for themselves. The Keeper of the Offerings is incandescent. The god is unrepentant: the Line has never paid them, and they have been working for nine thousand years.

choices.text: Pay the god a proper stipend from the stores, and end the commissions

effects.log: You set a stipend. The god is humbled and slightly terrified of being rich, and the commissions stop.

choices.text: Strip the god of the post and reassign it

effects.log: You strip it. The god leaves without a sound, and the Line has a hole in its prayer-desk and a conscience in its neck.

events.text: A beloved cousin of {b3_clan} has faded out of the world, quietly, in a chair by a window. The Line keeps nine days of silence. On the ninth, the Hall is asked to say one thing the cousin liked. A young god says: "the way they hummed off-key." Everyone laughs, and cries, and the Hall is warm.

choices.text: Hum it, off-key, at the Gate of Incense, at dawn

effects.log: You hum it. The Gate smokes in a gentle spiral, and for a year the Line hums off-key in the corridors.

choices.text: Carve the humming into the pillar beside the name

effects.log: You carve a small wavering line beside the name. It is the only pillar in the Hall that moves with the light.

events.text: A caravan of lesser deities has arrived at the Gate of {b3_clan}: gods of crossroads, of spoons, of the sound of a door closing, of third-born sons. Each carries a trunk of tiny offerings and a petition. The Warden of the Domain Gate, who has never seen so many small gods at once, just opens the gate and steps back.

choices.text: Host them all for a night, with the Hall at their service

effects.log: You host them. The Hall is for one night a chattering fair, and the small gods leave overjoyed, with the Line's name on their trunks.

choices.text: Receive their petitions at the gate, one by one

effects.log: You hear every petition at the gate, over a month. The small gods are a surprisingly good source of news.

events.text: A crack has run down the third name-pillar of {b3_clan}, from the title to the base, and a faint breath of old air is coming out of it. The Officers argue about whether to seal it or to open it. The Reader of Omens says pillars crack where a name is about to be spoken that has been silent.

choices.text: Open the pillar a little, carefully

effects.log: You open it. Inside is a hollow, a sleeping seed and a scrap of vellum with a single name, which you speak.

choices.text: Bind the pillar with a ring of cedar and wait

effects.log: You bind it. The crack closes over a decade, and the breath of air lingers in the Hall like a rumour.

events.text: The guardian tortoise of {b3_clan}, a creature of four thousand years that has not moved in three, has laid an egg. The Officers are thrilled. The egg is the size of a hall-bell. The tortoise looks at it, then at you, then, with great effort, away. Nobody knows what the egg wants.

choices.text: Make a nest for the egg in the warm lee of the Gate of Incense

effects.log: You make the nest. The egg hums for two hundred years, and then hatches a very small, very grave tortoise who sits on your foot.

choices.text: Ask the Lineage of the Root to foster the egg in the deep earth

effects.log: The Root takes the egg with tenderness and a good deal of mud. In a thousand years it returns, huge and affectionate.

events.text: A god of dreams has been visiting the sleeping Officers of {b3_clan} and leaving them small improving thoughts. The Officers wake brighter, with an inexplicable urge to file. The god says it is a favour. The Warden of the Domain Gate says it is a trespass, and has stopped sleeping.

choices.text: Thank the dream-god and ask for a lesson

effects.log: You ask for one. The god teaches you how to leave a thought behind like a coin in a coat, and the Line is, thereafter, a little more diplomatic.

choices.text: Post a vigil flame at the dormitory door against uninvited dreams

effects.log: You post one. The dreams stop. The Officers, bereft, ask whether the flame can be turned down a bit.

events.text: A rain of offerings falls on {b3_clan}, from the wrong direction: flowers, rice, a small carved bird, all arriving from the west instead of the long road from below. The Reader of Omens traces it. Somewhere to the west, another Lineage is praying to your Line by mistake, and with great sincerity.

choices.text: Send an embassy west to find the mistaken worshippers

effects.log: You send one. They find a small kingdom of fishers who have merged two names, and are very happy, and the Line gains its first western shrine.

choices.text: Accept the offerings and let the mistake stand

effects.log: You accept. The west goes on praying to a god who is slightly the wrong one, and you answer them anyway.

events.text: A lesser god of a drainage ditch in the domain of {b3_clan} petitions to be raised to a Domain. He has a long list of reasons. He brings a model of the ditch. The ditch is, he says, the most overlooked body of water in the whole of the world. The petition is quite touching and wildly out of order.

choices.text: Raise him to Keeper of the Waters, a post but not a Domain

effects.log: You do. He weeps. The ditch is, from then on, a place of low-key pilgrimage and unshakeable cleanliness.

choices.text: Send his petition to the Thrones with a kind letter

effects.log: You send it. The Thrones lose it, as they lose most things, but the ditch-god is touched that someone tried.

events.text: The younger gods of {b3_clan} have swapped the order of the name-pillars during the night. Every elder is now standing in the wrong place at the Feast of Names. The prank is flawless and executed with the precision of a coup. {b3_elder} stands under the wrong title, rigid with outrage, as the herald calls it.

choices.text: Let the Feast go on, in the wrong order

effects.log: You let it. The elders wear their new titles with wounded grace, and the Feast is the best attended in a thousand years.

choices.text: Send for the ringleaders and ask for a pillar-by-pillar restoration

effects.log: You send for them. The ringleaders restore the order with ceremonial care, in an afternoon, and are, privately, thanked.

events.text: A boundary dispute has reached {b3_clan}: a god of the next domain has moved the river-bend a hundred paces east, into the Line's water-meadow, and says it was always so. The meadow is not important. The principle is. The Officers have already drawn a map in red.

choices.text: Walk the new bank with the other god and talk it over

effects.log: You walk it, with a flask. By the third bend the two of you agree that the river wanted to move anyway.

choices.text: Move the river back at midnight, quietly

effects.log: You move it back. The other god discovers it at dawn, and sends you a grudging note of praise.

events.text: The shrine of {b3_clan} at the edge of the domain has been robbed by mortals, and the thieves are caught. They are children, in rags. The village wants an example. The god of the shrine, a minor, soft-hearted spirit, has appeared in the dock and is pleading for the children.

choices.text: Hear the village and the shrine-god together, in a dream

effects.log: You hear them. The village relents, the children work off the theft at the shrine, and the shrine-god is, finally, listened to.

choices.text: Send a small sign to the village: let the children go

effects.log: You send a sign. The village lets them go, uneasy, and the shrine-god weeps with gratitude into a bowl.

events.text: A young god of {b3_clan} has lost a tooth. Gods of the Line lose one, once, in the thousandth year; it is a rite. The tooth is placed on a pillow and left under the Oracle Pool. The god is mortified and about a hundred years old. The Officers behave with great gravity. Something is left in exchange.

choices.text: Leave a coin of starlight for the tooth

effects.log: You leave it. In the morning the young god finds it and believes in the Oracle Pool forever.

choices.text: Keep the tooth in the Book, in a small pouch

effects.log: You keep it. The young god, grown, comes to look at it every century and laughs.

events.text: A prayer reaches {b3_clan} from a dying soldier, on a field far below, who asks for nothing but to be told he was not a coward. The prayer is quiet and absolutely clear. The Reader of Prayers has stopped writing and set down the pen, and is watching you across the Hall.

choices.text: Answer him, in a dream of his mother's kitchen

effects.log: You answer him. He dies at peace, and the Reader of Prayers writes the entry in the largest letters in the Book.

choices.text: Send him a single feather and no words

effects.log: You send the feather. He dies with it in his hand, and the Line is quiet for a day.

events.text: A question of precedence has arisen on the stair to the Thrones: whether {b3_clan} may go up before the Lineage of the Nine Wells or after. The question has been asked for seven thousand years and answered each time by the Wells arriving early. This year you could arrive first.

choices.text: Arrive first, at dawn, in your plainest robe

effects.log: You arrive first. The Wells arrive second, and are gracious, and you are both so tired of the question that you share a flask on the stair.

choices.text: Arrive second, as always, and let the Wells have it

effects.log: You arrive second. The Wells, startled, offer you the first step at the next convocation, and the question is closed.

events.text: A hymn has been sung at {b3_clan} for ten thousand years in a language no longer spoken. This year a visitor from the Lineage of the Root says, kindly, that the hymn is not a hymn. It is a recipe. Specifically, for a soup. The Officers stare. The visitor says, "it is quite good."

choices.text: Cook the soup, and sing the hymn over it

effects.log: You cook it. The soup is excellent, the hymn is a revelation, and the Line has a new dish for the Feast.

choices.text: Keep the hymn a hymn, and the recipe a private joke

effects.log: You keep it. The soup is made, in secret, on feast nights, and shared in the kitchen only.

events.text: The archivist of {b3_clan} needs one volume of the Lineage of the Unlit Lamp, a record of how the Line's first domain was drawn. The Unlit Lamp lends nothing to anyone. The archivist has written six letters. The seventh arrives with a reply, in the dark-ink of that Lineage: "come, and read it here. Bring no lamp."

choices.text: Go yourself, and read it in the dark

effects.log: You go. The Unlit Lamp lets you read by touch, in a cold stone room, and what you learn is a page of how the Line was nearly never made.

choices.text: Send the archivist, with a sealed question for you

effects.log: The archivist goes and returns with a headache, a stammer and an answer. The Unlit Lamp, you note, has read your question.

choices.text: Decline; the Line has done without it for ten thousand years

effects.log: You decline. The archivist keeps the seventh letter, grimly, as a small trophy of dignity.

events.text: A letter from the Lineage of the Unlit Lamp arrives at {b3_clan}, written in the dark and unusually warm. It says the Lamp has noticed that the Line is the first in an age to read a record without asking to take it. The Lamp would like to offer, in return, one favour: the right to ask a question of them that they will answer truthfully.

choices.text: Ask what the Lamp most fears

effects.log: The answer takes nine years to arrive, and is two words long. You tell no one, and treat the Lamp ever after as a friend.

choices.text: Hold the favour in reserve for a day of need

effects.log: You hold it. The Unlit Lamp respects it; a favour kept is a bond kept, and the Lamp sends a small lamp, unlit, as a token.

events.text: A day of need has come for {b3_clan}: an accuser at the Thrones says the Line's first domain was taken by fraud. The only proof is in the Unlit Lamp's records. You hold a favour. The Lamp is bound by its word and its habit, and the habit is stronger. A single dark-robed scribe stands at the gate, waiting.

choices.text: Spend the favour: ask the Lamp to speak for the Line

effects.log: The scribe speaks, once, at the Thrones, in a voice like a snuffed wick. The accusation falls, and the Lamp is owed nothing, and the Line is owed more.

choices.text: Spare the Lamp, and answer the accuser yourself

effects.log: You answer, with the Line's own records. It is a closer thing, and the favour is kept, and the Lamp sends a note that says only "noted."

events.text: Ember, heir to {b3_clan}, and Sill, heir to a rival Lineage, have been sending each other dream-letters for a century. Not love-letters: insults, rated for wit. The letters have grown elaborate. Several have been printed. The Officers of both Lineages read them aloud on feast days, with the exact enjoyment of people at a play.

choices.text: Quietly arrange for the two to meet at a neutral shrine

effects.log: You arrange it. They come, glare, and talk for nine hours. The dream-letters get shorter and stranger.

choices.text: Let the war go on; it is better than most diplomacy

effects.log: You let it go. The two Lineages learn each other's moods through the letters better than any embassy could have taught them.

events.text: Ember and Sill, finally face to face at the neutral shrine, have discovered that they have the same sense of humour. The shrine-keeper, a small god of crossroads, is hiding behind the altar. The Officers of both Lineages are waiting outside. They hear peals of laughter, followed by the sound of something being broken.

choices.text: Go in, and find out what was broken

effects.log: You go in. It was a centuries-old rivalry, formally, in the form of an ornamental treaty. The two are sitting on the shards, helpless with mirth.

choices.text: Stay outside, and tell the Officers it is a family matter

effects.log: You stay out, and tell them so. The matter becomes, in a quiet way, exactly that.

events.text: Ember and Sill have asked for a Covenant of the two Lineages. Not a marriage: a Covenant of Neighbours, with shared shrines, a standing exchange of heralds, and a clause that each will, once a century, write the other an insult in the open. The Officers of both are charmed, appalled, and scrambling for precedents.

choices.text: Sign the Covenant at the shrine, in the open

effects.log: You sign. It becomes the model for a dozen others, and Ember and Sill, in their old age, are insufferable about it.

choices.text: Sign it privately, and let the public learn in time

effects.log: You sign privately. The Covenant takes root quietly, unremarked, and works the better for not being celebrated.

events.text: Tirk, Warden of the Domain Gate of {b3_clan}, is two-thirds faded, and has begun to let people through who should not be. He is not wrong; he is only tired. A candidate has come: Lacy, a god of thresholds, twice his height, half his age, and certain that every rule is a poem.

choices.text: Appoint Lacy and keep Tirk as Warden Emeritus

effects.log: You do. Tirk takes it with the dignity of a man being given a cushion, and sits in the gate-house for five thousand years, saying "no" to the wind.

choices.text: Test Lacy for a year before appointing

effects.log: You test. Lacy lets in exactly three people who should not have come, and is exactly right about each, and is appointed.

choices.text: Keep Tirk in the post, and find a quieter helper

effects.log: You keep him. He carries on, drowsy, and the Gate lets in a mild river of inappropriate visitors.

events.text: Lacy, new Warden of the Domain Gate of {b3_clan}, has reformed the rules of entry. Visitors must now declare, at the gate, one true thing about themselves. The Officers think it is a mockery. The visitors find it, in practice, disarming. The first week, three rival Lineages confess to being lonely.

choices.text: Support the new rule, and declare a true thing yourself

effects.log: You declare one at the gate on your way back from a convocation. It is small and embarrassing, and the Warden bows to you for the first time.

choices.text: Retain the old rules, but let Lacy keep the true-thing custom for guests

effects.log: You compromise. Lacy is rueful, the Officers relieved, and the guests carry the custom out to the rest of the world.

events.text: A hundred years on, the true-thing custom has spread. At the Gate of {b3_clan} a Lineage of enemies arrives to negotiate, and each is made to say one true thing, and one says, with a trembling voice, "I am afraid we will lose." The other side laughs, kindly, and says the same. Lacy looks smug.

choices.text: Convene the talks at once, in the gate-house

effects.log: You convene them. The talks take nine days instead of nine centuries, and the peace is the Line's best work in an age.

choices.text: Let Lacy run the talks, with you watching from the gallery

effects.log: Lacy runs them. It is the finest hour of a Warden in the Line's history, and Tirk, from his chair, weeps.

events.text: The Lineage of Ash and Morning has sent {b3_clan} a vial of the first fire, kept in a bone of the first beast. The note says: "if you ever need to remember what it was like." The Officers are afraid to touch it. The vial is warm, and hums in a key that makes the Gate of Incense stand to attention.

choices.text: Light the Line's great vigil flame from it, once

effects.log: You light it. The flame burns white for a day, and the Line remembers, briefly, being new.

choices.text: Seal the vial in the Hall of Names and tell no one

effects.log: You seal it behind the third pillar. The Line carries a secret, and a secret warmth, from then on.

events.text: The Lineage of the Long Tide holds a funeral for one of its own at the edge of the world, and has invited {b3_clan} to stand on the shore. The sea-gods wail in a pitch that bends the horizon. The Herald of the Line is expected to speak. The Herald, never before at a funeral that moved the sea, has run out of words.

choices.text: Speak yourself: a few plain words about the dead

effects.log: You speak. The tide stills, an inch, and the sea-gods turn to look at you, wet-eyed, and the Long Tide counts the Line a friend.

choices.text: Stand silent beside the Herald and hold their sleeve

effects.log: You stand. The Herald says nothing, which is the best speech, and the sea takes it for grace.

events.text: The Lineage of the Nine Wells has decided that {b3_clan} is, after all, the tenth well, and has begun to draw water from it, in metaphor, to settle disputes. The Line has been quoted, three times, as "a well of good sense." The Officers are flattered and suspicious. {b3_elder} says: "it is a loan, and they will want interest."

choices.text: Accept the title, and ask for a seat on the Wells' council

effects.log: You accept. The Wells are surprised, and then pleased, and the Line gains a vote and a lot of tedious meetings.

choices.text: Politely decline; the Line is its own well

effects.log: You decline. The Wells are amused, and send a small jar, and say they will be back in a thousand years.

events.text: The Silent Drum has been heard in {b3_clan}, across a whole season, as an absence: the Hall goes still at dusk, every dusk, for the length of a heartbeat, and then returns. The Officers have started to hold their breath in time. The Lineage of the Silent Drum has sent no message, as is its way.

choices.text: Hold the dusk-silence as a rite of the Line

effects.log: You make a rite of it. The Line is quiet, one heartbeat, each evening, and finds itself kinder.

choices.text: Send a drum of your own, with a skin, in reply

effects.log: You send a drum with a skin. It is returned, a year later, without one, and no note, and the Line takes this as a courtesy.

events.text: The Laughing River has sent {b3_clan} a gift: a barrel of its water, laced with the faint unmistakable sound of a joke. Anyone who drinks it will laugh once, at an inconvenient moment, for a year. The Officers, solemnly, have refused. A young god has already taken a cup and is going to be funny at the Thrones.

choices.text: Drink a cup yourself, and trust the Thrones

effects.log: You drink. You laugh, once, at the exact moment an ancient Throne is pronouncing a sentence, and the Throne laughs too.

choices.text: Pour the barrel back into the river, with thanks

effects.log: You pour it back. The river laughs, a long way off, and the Officers sigh with relief and, privately, regret.

events.text: The Keeper of the Offerings of {b3_clan} has found something strange in the weekly tally: a handful of offerings with no sender, left at the Gate of Incense each night, in a style the Line does not know. Small clay animals, neatly glazed. By morning they are warm. The Keeper has started to keep them in a cabinet.

choices.text: Watch the Gate one night, and see who leaves them

effects.log: You watch. It is a child-spirit of the clay, lost, nameless, shy, who flees when seen, and leaves another by the gate.

choices.text: Leave out a bowl of milk and a note of thanks

effects.log: You leave it. The clay animals come in pairs after that, and the cabinet becomes a menagerie.

events.text: The Reader of Omens reports that a long-dead god of {b3_clan}, whose pillar is the oldest and plainest in the Hall, is stirring. Not waking: stirring. The pillar has begun to sweat a very faint smell of rain. The Officers argue about whether this is an honour, a threat or a leak.

choices.text: Keep a night vigil at the oldest pillar

effects.log: You keep it. At the third hour the pillar sighs, once, and a smell of rain drifts through the Hall. Nothing else. It is the finest night of your year.

choices.text: Wrap the pillar in cloth and have the Reader watch by day

effects.log: You wrap it. The stirring stops; the cloth gets damp; the Reader writes a long report.

events.text: A pantheon-wide convocation is being held, and {b3_clan} has been given the least favourable seat, between a god of boils and a Throne asleep on his feet. The Officers are livid. The seat is a message, and the message is: you are a young Line. The sleepy Throne begins to snore on your shoulder.

choices.text: Sit, and charm the god of boils

effects.log: You sit and talk. The god of boils turns out to be a charming conversationalist, and by the end the seat is the most popular in the room.

choices.text: Stand throughout, with the Line behind you

effects.log: You stand. The Line stands. The whole convocation looks, and the seat is changed by the next session.

events.text: A rite of the Lineage requires that on the longest night, the head of {b3_clan} wake the youngest god and tell them one thing the Line has never told anyone. This year the youngest is a tiny shy god of puddles. The thing, you realise, is probably small, and probably embarrassing. You have not chosen yet.

choices.text: Tell them what really happened to the third pillar

effects.log: You tell them. The tiny god listens, nods gravely, and says, "I will tell no one," and means it, and keeps it for ten thousand years.

choices.text: Tell them the Line's most embarrassing joke

effects.log: You tell the joke. The tiny god laughs so hard they hiccup, and the Line has acquired a very happy future Officer.

events.text: A pair of mortals who wish to marry in the shrine of {b3_clan} have come a long way, and are told by the priest that a god must bless the rings. The god on duty, a harvest cousin, is asleep. The mortals wait on the steps, holding hands. The priest sends up a prayer so frantic that it arrives like a flushed bird.

choices.text: Bless the rings yourself, in the cousin's place

effects.log: You bless them, in a whisper. The mortals feel a warmth and take it for the sun, and the cousin, awake, hides in embarrassment.

choices.text: Wake the cousin and send them down in a fine mood

effects.log: You wake the cousin. The rings are blessed with a great deal of grain, and the wedding feast is excellent.

events.text: The Hall of Offerings of {b3_clan} has a drain. Nobody knows where it goes. For ten thousand years, a small share of the libations has run down it.
