A curious young Officer, with a lamp and a rope, goes down and returns in an hour, speechless, covered in glittering mud. "There is," says the Officer, "a lake."

choices.text: Descend yourself and see the lake

effects.log: You go down. The lake is vast and dark and full of ten thousand years of libation, and something in it drinks, politely, and says thank you.

choices.text: Send an expedition and map the lake at leisure

effects.log: You send one. The lake is mapped in a century, and found to be an old, quiet god of wells, very glad of the company.

events.text: An old rival Lineage has sent {b3_clan} a wedding invitation for a cousin. In the same envelope is a smaller card, on thicker stock, uninvited: an invitation to a duel, at a date to be agreed, over a matter of a river from nine thousand years ago. The Officers are fascinated. The Warden of the Domain Gate has already begun to polish the Line's old sword.

choices.text: Attend the wedding, and answer the duel with a toast

effects.log: You go. You raise a cup to the rival, and the card is torn up and added to the cake. The quarrel settles into legend.

choices.text: Accept the duel, with a champion of the Line's choosing

effects.log: You name a champion. The duel is a stylised, solemn affair, won by a feint, and the Line has a hero and a river.

events.text: A mortal artisan has carved a statue of {b3_clan}'s ancestor that is the most beautiful thing the Officers have seen in an age. It is also, plainly, a portrait of the artisan's late wife. The ancestor, if they were awake, would be bemused. The statue is already working small miracles at the hill shrine where it stands.

choices.text: Let the statue keep its face; send the artisan a dream of thanks

effects.log: You send it. The artisan wakes weeping, and the hill shrine becomes a place where those who miss someone go.

choices.text: Have a priest quietly alter the face to match the old icons

effects.log: A priest does. The miracles fade, and the artisan stops carving, and the Line has a more correct and less loved statue.

events.text: The Reader of Omens of {b3_clan} has predicted, correctly, nine small disasters in a row, and is now so feared that the Officers hesitate to ask them anything. The Reader is lonely. They invite you to dinner. They say they would like to be asked about something pleasant, just once.

choices.text: Ask them what sort of morning tomorrow will be

effects.log: They say, with obvious joy, that it will be a warm one with a good breakfast and a letter from an old friend. You wake up to exactly that.

choices.text: Ask them to read nothing for you tonight, and just talk

effects.log: You talk until dawn. The Reader of Omens is, in the end, a very good talker, and the Officers resume their questions with more tenderness.

events.text: The young gods of {b3_clan} have decided, without asking, to hold a competition among themselves to see who can answer the smallest prayer. The record is a prayer for a lost button. The new champion has answered a prayer for the colour of a dream. The Officers say it is frivolous. The mortals below keep praying smaller.

choices.text: Judge the competition yourself, and give a prize of dawn

effects.log: You judge. The prize is a morning to themselves, and the winner, a girl-god of lost things, uses it to find the button.

choices.text: Ban the competition, but quietly keep a scoreboard

effects.log: You ban it. The Hall keeps a scoreboard in the stacks, in pencil, and it grows every year.

events.text: The Line of {b3_clan} has two hymnals, the Dawn Book and the Dusk Book, and two choirs. For ten thousand years they have sung at different hours. A new Officer, Harl, has noticed the choirs sing the same prayers in a different order, and has proposed uniting them. Half the Hall is thrilled. Half has gone pale.

choices.text: Unite the choirs for the Feast of Names

effects.log: You unite them. The first rehearsal is a catastrophe, the second is a tolerable noise, and at the Feast the Hall hears something it has never heard.

choices.text: Keep the two, and add a third hymn that both sing

effects.log: You commission one. It becomes the fiercely loved compromise, and both choirs claim to have written it.

choices.text: Rule the Dawn Book older and drop the Dusk

effects.log: You rule so. The Dusk choir sings once more, at midnight, outside the Hall, and the Line learns what a schism sounds like.

events.text: The united choirs of {b3_clan} have a problem: they cannot agree who leads. The Dawn precentor, Odel, is thunderous. The Dusk precentor, Maré, is exact. Each offers to resign, with exquisite spite, if the other will lead. Harl, who started the whole thing, sits at the back of the Hall hiding behind a hymn-book.

choices.text: Appoint both as joint precentors and watch them squirm

effects.log: You appoint both. They hate it for forty years and then make the best music the Line has had.

choices.text: Ask Harl to choose, since the trouble is Harl's

effects.log: Harl, appalled, chooses neither, and nominates a shy second-alto. The Hall, stunned, agrees.

events.text: Four hundred years later, the united choir of {b3_clan} is the best in the pantheon. It is invited to sing at the Thrones. The Silent Hall has sent word that it will attend, and sit through the whole thing without a sound, as a courtesy. The choir has never sung for a silence, and rehearses, nervously, in the dark.

choices.text: Go, and sing the Dusk hymn with no accompaniment

effects.log: You go. The Silent Hall listens like a held breath, and at the end a single Throne weeps without a sound, and the Line is named in the Book of Fates.

choices.text: Go, and let the choir fall silent for the last verse

effects.log: The choir falls silent, as one. The Silent Hall inclines their heads. It is the greatest honour the Line has had.

events.text: A shrine of {b3_clan} stands on an island that has begun, very slowly, to drift. The mortals who tend it are three families who have never lived anywhere else. The island moves a pace a year. In ten generations it will reach a coast that does not worship the Line. The head priestess, Zane, is asking what to do.

choices.text: Anchor the island with a chain of prayers

effects.log: You send a chain of prayer-dreams to the families. They sing together each dusk, and the island, sulkily, stops.

choices.text: Let the island drift, and send heralds ahead to the coast

effects.log: You send heralds. The coast, warned in a generation, prepares a welcome, and Zane's families become travellers of a kind.

choices.text: Tell Zane the island is the mortals' business

effects.log: Zane receives this with a silence you can feel through the dream. The island drifts on.

events.text: The drifting shrine island of {b3_clan} has reached the coast, a generation early, and a town has come down to the beach to look at it. The three families, on the shore, are dressed in their best and have no idea what to say. The town, uncertain, has brought a basket of bread. Zane's granddaughter steps forward.

choices.text: Send a dream of welcome to the town, in its own tongue

effects.log: You send it. The town wakes knowing the families' names, and the bread is accepted, and the island is, within a year, a district.

choices.text: Let the families meet the town unaided

effects.log: You hold back. Zane's granddaughter says the first words, the wrong ones, and they are right, and the town laughs.

events.text: Under the shrine on the drifted island, the town has found a set of old stairs that lead down into the sea. They are not the Line's. The Lineage of the Long Tide is said to have built them, for a purpose it has not shared. The town, impatient, wants to open the first door.

choices.text: Ask the Long Tide what is behind the first door

effects.log: You ask. A tide-god arrives, wet and amused, and says: "a cellar." It is, truly, a cellar, and in it are ten thousand years of preserved wedding gifts.

choices.text: Tell the town to leave the door alone, with the Line's authority

effects.log: You tell them. The town, grumbling, closes the stairs, and the Long Tide sends a quiet barrel of thanks.

events.text: A rival god has begun to take the prayers of {b3_clan}'s eastern villages by the simple method of answering faster. Offerings from the east have halved in a decade. The Officers want a counter-miracle. The rival is a harvest god with a cheerful face and a very efficient system of paper slips.

choices.text: Visit the rival, and ask to see the slips

effects.log: You go. The slips are a wonder of order. You borrow the system, with permission, and the rival, startled to be flattered, is thereafter an ally.

choices.text: Answer faster yourself; drown the east in prompt grace

effects.log: You surge the Line's answering. The east returns to the fold, exhausted and delighted, and the Officers are hoarse.

events.text: A mortal heresy is spreading below: that {b3_clan} is not a Line of gods at all, but a long conspiracy of very old humans. Its preachers are earnest, dull and half-right. The Officers want them silenced. The heresy, you notice, is the first thing to have made the mortals curious about the Line in a thousand years.

choices.text: Answer the heresy in a dream: come and see

effects.log: You send the dream. A dozen preachers climb the stair of dawn, and the Hall hosts them, and some stay, and the heresy turns into a school.

choices.text: Send storms of rebuke to the preachers' hills

effects.log: You send a modest storm. The heresy burns hotter in the wet, and the Line is quietly embarrassed.

events.text: A faithful old family of worshippers below has prayed to {b3_clan} for forty generations, and tonight the last of them, a widow, prays for the first time for something for herself: a quiet death. The Reader of Prayers has set down the pen. The Warden of the Domain Gate has set down the lamp. Everyone looks at you.

choices.text: Grant it gently, with a dream of the whole family waiting

effects.log: You grant it. She goes in her sleep, smiling, and the Line, for a week, keeps its lamps lit for her.

choices.text: Answer with a long life, a last spring, and a visit

effects.log: You send her a spring and a visit from a grandchild. She lives six more years, and dies at the end of a sentence, content.

events.text: The Book of Fates has a clerical error: a mortal in the domain of {b3_clan} is recorded as dying at ninety, when by every other register they are twenty-two. The error will come due on a certain day. The clerk who made the entry has gone to the Silent Hall in shame and will not come out.

choices.text: Go to the Silent Hall and ask the clerk to correct it

effects.log: You go. The clerk emerges, shaking, and corrects it in a hand like a priest's. The mortal lives a plain, long life and never knows.

choices.text: Write a note of your own into the Book, in the margin

effects.log: You write it. The Book of Fates accepts the margin with a faint indignant sound, and the mortal goes on.

events.text: A younger sibling of {b3_clan}'s old head has come back after nine thousand years with a claim to a share of the Line's domain. They are charming and plausible. They have papers. They are, you find on checking, perfectly right. The Officers are furious. The sibling is very kind about it, which is worse.

choices.text: Grant the share in full, and invite them to stay

effects.log: You grant it. The sibling, half-expecting a fight, is thrown, and stays, and makes the Line more interesting for the next thousand years.

choices.text: Negotiate a smaller share, with a seat on the Officers

effects.log: You negotiate. The sibling takes a smaller share and a larger seat, and spends a century reforming the Hall.

events.text: A deep rumour reaches {b3_clan} that the Lineage of the Hidden Star is not hidden at all, but merely out of the way. The star-gods are said to be tired of being sought, and to prefer being left to mend. A delegation of Officers wishes to go and look. {b3_peer} says it would be unforgivable.

choices.text: Forbid the delegation, and send a gift of silence

effects.log: You send a gift: a month of the Line holding its tongue. The Hidden Star acknowledges it with a single faint light on the horizon.

choices.text: Allow a single quiet envoy, with orders to say nothing of what they see

effects.log: The envoy returns, pale, calm, and silent for a century. The Line wonders and does not ask.

events.text: A new mortal religion has arisen that holds the gods to be a sort of weather. {b3_clan} is, in their reckoning, a mild front. The priests of the new faith are polite, clever and entirely certain. They have a following of millions. They have not, yet, noticed that the weather replies.

choices.text: Reply, once, with a gentle rain

effects.log: You send it. The priests gape, then write it into their doctrines, and the faith grows more devout and a good deal more accurate.

choices.text: Ignore the faith; it will find its own level

effects.log: You ignore it. It finds its level in a century, quietly converted by its own cleverness to a plain, grateful piety.

events.text: A very old goddess of {b3_clan} has asked for a favour that has never been asked: to be forgotten. Not die; be forgotten. She has had her fill of being a pillar, a hymn and a title. She would like to wander the world as no one in particular. The Book would have to be rewritten. The Officers are aghast.

choices.text: Grant it: strike her name, and send her out with a staff

effects.log: You strike it. She goes out, quiet, light, delighted. Once a century she sends a postcard from a different life.

choices.text: Grant a century of leave, and keep her name warm

effects.log: You grant leave. She returns in a hundred years, brown, wise and tired, and asks, again, for it. Then you grant the rest.

events.text: The Hall of Names of {b3_clan} has a mouse. Not a spirit: a mouse. It has lived there for three hundred years, and has bred a long line of mice, and the Hall is a kingdom of them. They are small, respectful, and have never touched a single offering. The Officers have begun leaving them crumbs, and then, in secret, little names.

choices.text: Let the mice keep the Hall, and record their lineage in the Book

effects.log: You record it. The Book of the Line has one page of the mice, and the mice, on feast nights, sit in rows.

choices.text: Give the mice a small shrine in the east wall

effects.log: You give them one. The mice are, thereafter, very good at keeping the Hall free of far worse.

events.text: A flood of prayer from a plague district falls on {b3_clan}, so many that the Hall is full to the roof with paper. The Officers cannot read them all. They start to triage, which means choosing who to hear. The Reader of Prayers, white-faced, asks you to sit down and read, one by one, for as long as it takes.

choices.text: Read them yourself, through the night and the next

effects.log: You read for three days. You answer nine hundred, and are hollow, and the Hall silently, gratefully, takes over the rest.

choices.text: Open the Hall to every god of the Line to take a stack each

effects.log: You open it. A hundred gods read a hundred stacks, and the plague district is answered in a day, and the Line is, for once, entirely one thing.

events.text: The Gate of Incense of {b3_clan} has started to smell of a particular thing, a different one each morning: bread, snow, a wet dog, an old book. The Officers say it is a malfunction. The Warden says the Gate is remembering. {b3_peer} says each morning smells like something the Line has loved and forgotten.

choices.text: Keep a register of the morning smells in the Book

effects.log: You keep it. After a century, the register is the most intimate record of the Line's heart ever made.

choices.text: Ask the Gate what it is trying to say

effects.log: The Gate smokes in a long thoughtful curl, and then, for a week, smells of nothing at all, as if embarrassed.

events.text: The Officers of {b3_clan} have discovered that the Line's oldest law, carved at the foot of the first pillar, has been misread for eight thousand years. It does not say "the Line shall be first." It says "the Line shall be first to forgive." Several Officers have gone quiet. A few have started to pray.

choices.text: Recarve the law as it was meant, and make forgiveness a rite

effects.log: You recarve it. The Line spends a century being, awkwardly, the first to forgive, and its enemies are baffled and then, one by one, disarmed.

choices.text: Keep the old reading, and teach the true one in the school

effects.log: You keep both. The school teaches the true one, and the Hall, slowly, begins to behave accordingly.

events.text: A pestilent little god of {b3_clan}, a minor deity of itches, has acquired a worshipper: a man who is delighted by him. The man leaves daily offerings of scratching posts and feathers. The god of itches, who has never been loved, has grown insufferably smug and is itching the entire Hall in thanks.

choices.text: Accept the god of itches as a gift of the Line and let the Hall cope

effects.log: You accept him. The Hall scratches, and laughs, and in a year the god of itches is almost bearable.

choices.text: Ask the man to move his devotions to a better-appointed shrine

effects.log: The man is hurt, and moves them, and the itching stops, and the god of itches sulks in the larder.

events.text: The Warden of the Domain Gate of {b3_clan} reports that a mortal has been standing outside for nine years, not asking to enter, only watching. The mortal is a cartographer. They have mapped every approach, every shrine, every sunbeam. The map is exquisite. It is also, the Warden says, the best defence plan the Line has ever failed to make.

choices.text: Invite the cartographer in, and commission the map for the Hall

effects.log: You invite them. The map hangs in the Hall of Names, and the cartographer, an old person with ink on their sleeve, sits under it each night.

choices.text: Buy the map with a boon and have the Warden burn the copies

effects.log: You buy it. The cartographer takes the boon, a good harvest, and goes home, and the Line sleeps a little easier and a little poorer.

events.text: The Reader of Omens has foreseen a visitor to {b3_clan} who will ask a question the Line cannot answer. The Hall has been preparing for forty years. Today the visitor comes: a child with a toy boat, who asks where the sea goes at night. The Hall of Names is silent. The Reader, relieved and humiliated, giggles.

choices.text: Answer the child with the best guess you have

effects.log: You answer: it goes home. The child nods, satisfied, and the Hall, which had expected the end of the world, is a little undone.

choices.text: Ask the Lineage of the Long Tide to answer for you

effects.log: The Long Tide sends a small wave to the child's feet with a note that says, "it goes wherever it likes." The child is delighted.

events.text: A god of {b3_clan} has fallen out of love with their domain. They are the god of frost, and they have grown tired of the cold. They want to be a god of kettles, or of cats. The domain, left unattended, is thawing. The Officers are horrified. The god is weeping, quietly, into a scarf.

choices.text: Let them trade domains with the cat-god, by consent

effects.log: You arrange the trade. Frost gets a gentler master, the cat-god gets a frozen lake to watch, and everyone is, surprisingly, relieved.

choices.text: Ask them to hold the frost one more age, and promise a holiday

effects.log: They hold. The holiday, when it comes, is a hundred years in a warm country, and they return a better frost.

events.text: A herald of the Thrones reads out the roll of the Lineages, and {b3_clan} is called a place higher than last time. Nobody tells you the cause. The Herald of the Line, in the gallery, is trembling with the effort of not cheering. {b3_elder} says the roll is never wrong, only late.

choices.text: Take the new place with a plain bow

effects.log: You bow. The Lineages that had not noticed you now do, and the Hall of Names, that night, rings with the Line's own old hymn.

choices.text: Send each Lineage on the roll a libation by name

effects.log: You send them. The roll is followed by a week of replies, most gracious, a few frosty, one in a rhyme.

events.text: The other Lineages have begun to quote {b3_clan} in disputes. "As the Line would have it," they say, meaning you. Your sayings, tidied and slightly wrong, circulate among the pantheons. A young god of the Silent Hall has your most careless remark embroidered on a scarf.

choices.text: Correct the scarf, gently, in a note

effects.log: You correct it. The Silent Hall embroiders the correction beneath the original, in smaller thread, and the scarf becomes a minor heirloom.

choices.text: Let them quote you wrong; it is the price of being quoted

effects.log: You let it. The sayings grow stranger and wiser than you ever were, and the Line wears them well.

events.text: A mortal king below has named his firstborn for a god of {b3_clan}. The prayers that follow arrive tinged with the particular hope of a new parent. The Keeper of the Offerings reports, in a voice of wonder, that the name is spreading: the child has eleven namesakes by the end of the season.

choices.text: Bless the child, and every namesake

effects.log: You bless them all. The Line is astonished at what it has begun, and eleven children grow up with a small warm certainty that someone is looking.

choices.text: Bless the firstborn, and mark the rest in the Book

effects.log: You mark them. The Book of the Line has a new page headed "Those Named For Us," which grows every century.

events.text: The Warden of the Domain Gate reports an increase in the quality of petitioners at the gate of {b3_clan}. Fewer beggars of favour, more heads of Lineages. A god of the Throne of Storms, who has not visited in four thousand years, is among them, with a gift and a stiff little bow.

choices.text: Receive the Storm god as an equal, at the gate itself

effects.log: You go out to the gate. The Storm god is nonplussed, and then moved, and the Throne of Storms, from that year, counts you among its friends.

choices.text: Receive the Storm god in the Hall, with full ceremony

effects.log: You receive them in state. The ceremony is long, the god is gracious, and the Line is noted, in the Throne's archive, as correct.

events.text: The Oracle Pool of {b3_clan} has started, unprompted, to show visitors the Line's future instead of their own. Visitors do not like it. They find it flattering and alarming. The Reader of Omens says the pool is bragging. The pool, in a ripple, appears to agree.

choices.text: Let the pool show what it will, and post a sign of warning

effects.log: You post a sign. The pool's visions are, thereafter, taken with a smile, and the Line is mildly feared.

choices.text: Cover the pool for a season, so the Line is not seen preening

effects.log: You cover it. The pool sulks, then settles, and the Line's reputation for modesty grows by the same amount as its reputation for secrecy.

events.text: A rival Lineage has formally conceded {b3_clan} a point of precedence it has held for nine thousand years. The concession arrives by a messenger with a very short speech and a very large cake. The Officers are stunned. {b3_peer} says it will cost more than it saves.

choices.text: Accept graciously, and send back half the cake

effects.log: You send back half. The rival's head, receiving it, laughs, and writes you the warmest letter of the age.

choices.text: Accept, and ask what it will cost them to concede

effects.log: You ask. They tell you, honestly, and you realise it is the sort of loss only a good friend would take. You thank them in earnest.

events.text: Children of the Line are suddenly in demand as fosterlings. Other Lineages send gifts with their requests. A weeping elder asks whether the Line is selling its young. {b3_elder} says it is the opposite: the Line is being asked, and it is the highest compliment gods have.

choices.text: Accept three fosterlings and send three of the Line's own out

effects.log: You accept three. The exchange is awkward and tender, and in a century the Line has cousins in four households.

choices.text: Accept none, and let the young choose their own paths

effects.log: You accept none. The young of the Line grow up proud of it, and a few, in time, ask to go anyway.

events.text: A god of the Silent Hall tells {b3_clan} that a record of the Line has been placed in the Book of Fates: a good page, in the ordinary hand, that reads simply "they stayed." Nobody knows what it means. The Reader of Omens frowns. The Archivist, to everyone's surprise, begins to weep.

choices.text: Ask the Archivist why they weep

effects.log: The Archivist says: "It is the only thing a Line wants written." You sit with them until the lamps burn low, and the Line is quieter for it.

choices.text: Add a line of your own to the page, in the margin

effects.log: You write: "and will." The page is, you are told, still being read.

events.text: A prince of the Green Assembly has invited {b3_clan} to the planting of a tree. It is the first tree of an orchard that will be old when the stars are cold. Each Lineage plants one seed. You are given the last spade. The Assembly's old Gardener, ancient as moss, says you may dig as deep as you like.

choices.text: Dig deep, and plant the seed with a prayer

effects.log: You plant it deep. The Gardener nods, and the seed, in its own time, becomes the tallest tree in the orchard.

choices.text: Dig shallow, and promise to tend it for a thousand years

effects.log: You plant it shallow and tend it. The tree grows slow, bent, and loved, and the Gardener, in a century, sends you a pear.

events.text: A shy and brilliant young god from a fallen Lineage has asked to be taken into {b3_clan} as a ward. Their Line is not great and not clean; it lost a war and its name. The Officers murmur. The young god stands in the Hall with a very small bundle and an expression that dares you to be kind.

choices.text: Take them in, and give them a seat at the Line's table

effects.log: You take them in. They sit stiffly, and eat politely, and by the end of the year they are arguing with the Archivist, which is the clearest sign of belonging.

choices.text: Offer them a place as a pupil of the rite-tutor first

effects.log: You offer it. They study hard, and in a century are the best rite-keeper the Hall has had.

events.text: A traveller god of the road has stopped at the Gate of {b3_clan} with a story: that in every pantheon, at every hall, the name of the Line is now said a little more carefully than before. The traveller found it endearing. "Like a name said by someone who might one day be asked for a loan," they add.

choices.text: Laugh, and share a libation with the traveller

effects.log: You laugh and share a cup. The traveller leaves richer in stories, and the Line is spoken of kindly, and, in a few years, lent to.

choices.text: Ask the traveller what is said when the name is spoken carelessly

effects.log: The traveller tells you, with relish. It is mostly accurate, and you act on three points.

events.text: The Book of the Line of {b3_clan} has acquired an unexpected visitor: a copyist from the Lineage of the Unlit Lamp, who wants to copy the whole Book by hand, in the dark, for their own archive. It is the first time the Lamp has ever copied anyone. It takes six years and the copyist is a bat of a person.

choices.text: Let them copy it, and offer them a lamp they may decline

effects.log: You offer. They decline, politely, six times, and finish the copy by touch, and leave a note of such grace that you add it to the Book.

choices.text: Let them copy it, and ask for a copy of their own in return

effects.log: You ask. The Lamp, startled into a laugh, sends a single page, and it is precisely the page you needed.

events.text: A hymn composed for {b3_clan} by a Lineage you had never spoken to arrives at the Gate of Incense, carried by a choir of a hundred, who sing it at dawn without warning. It is very beautiful, and a trifle presumptuous. The Officers are in tears. The choir-master hands you a bill of gratitude.

choices.text: Hear the whole hymn, and ask the choir to stay for the Feast

effects.log: You hear it out. The choir stays three weeks, and the Line has a new, reluctant, devoted ally.

choices.text: Thank them, and send the hymn to your own Herald for revision

effects.log: The Herald revises it. The choir is offended, then won over, and the hymn survives, a fairer thing.

events.text: The Lineage of the Root has come to the gate of {b3_clan} with a very small gift: a single seed. The goddess who brings it says it is for the day the Line is old. It is not a request. The Officers think she means a threat. She means a kindness, the Root being what it is.

choices.text: Plant it now, in the courtyard, and tend it

effects.log: You plant it. The seed sends up a green shoot in the first spring, and the Line learns what it is to be waited for by the earth.

choices.text: Keep it in the Hall, and show it to the young

effects.log: You keep it in the Hall. The young gaze at it, and ask what it is for, and you tell them, "for later," and they remember.

events.text: Your Line is spoken of now with the particular brand of envy that gods reserve for those who are doing well quietly. A rival Lineage sends a letter of congratulation in which every compliment is slightly wrong. The Officers are delighted to be hated so well. {b3_elder} writes the reply in four sentences, each correct.

choices.text: Send the reply, and a small gift to match the insult

effects.log: You send both. The rival is startled to be understood, and the correspondence becomes the best entertainment of the Silent Hall.

choices.text: Keep silent and let the next letter come

effects.log: You keep silent. The next letter is warmer, and a year later the rival is at the gate, asking a favour.

events.text: The Heart-Bell of {b3_clan} has not rung in nine thousand years. This morning it rang, once, on its own, a low note that rattled every cup in the Hall. The Archivist swears it was struck by nothing. The Reader of Omens swears it was struck by someone. The Warden of the Domain Gate has gone to check the roof.

choices.text: Ring it again, deliberately, and see who answers

effects.log: You ring it. Far below, in the domain, somewhere, a bell answers, three times. The Line learns it has a twin.

choices.text: Wrap the bell and let it be silent again

effects.log: You wrap it. It stays silent for another thousand years, and the Line feels, for the first time, lightly watched.

events.text: A pale god of the Silent Hall is sitting on the doorstep of {b3_clan}, saying nothing. They have been there nine days. They accept tea but not conversation. The Officers want to know what the Silent Hall wants. The pale god, asked, says only "to be near someone who is still deciding."

choices.text: Sit with them and decide something small, aloud

effects.log: You sit and decide, aloud, about the colour of a curtain. The pale god listens as to a hymn, and leaves in the morning, restored.

choices.text: Leave them be, and send tea

effects.log: You send tea. The pale god stays a month, drinks forty cups, and leaves one behind, filled to the brim.

events.text: It is the Feast of the First Fire, and the Lineage of Ash and Morning, who say they were there, are insisting on lighting the Line's hearth themselves. The Line has lit its own for ten thousand years. The Officers bristle. The oldest Ash god, tiny, upright, with a spark in each eye, is already kneeling at the grate.

choices.text: Let Ash light it, and kneel beside them

effects.log: You kneel. The fire takes on the first stroke, white and unpretending, and Ash says, softly, "yes, like that," and means it.

choices.text: Thank Ash and light it yourself with their flint

effects.log: You light it, with their flint. Ash watches, approves, and the Feast is the warmest in an age.

events.text: A scholar of {b3_clan} has discovered that the Line's oldest prayer, said at every dawn, is a lullaby. It was meant to be sung to a child. Nobody can say which child. The dawn-singer, an old god with a voice like gravel, has begun to sing it more softly. The Hall has gone very still.

choices.text: Ask the dawn-singer to sing it to the youngest god of the Line

effects.log: The dawn-singer does. The youngest, a tiny god, sleeps through it. The lullaby, you suspect, has at last found its child.

choices.text: Make the lullaby the Line's official evening rite

effects.log: You make it so. The Line goes to its rest, every night, in a hush, and wakes calmer.

events.text: A pair of hostile Lineages are using the courtyard of {b3_clan} as neutral ground to negotiate. The talks have stalled for forty years. The Officers bring them tea in shifts. Today one of the negotiators, a god of locks, has fallen asleep at the table, and the other, a god of keys, has covered them with a cloak.

choices.text: Quietly end the day's session, and leave them to the quiet

effects.log: You end it. The god of locks wakes to find the cloak, and the talks resume with a thaw so gentle that nobody mentions it.

choices.text: Stay and watch, and offer to be witness to whatever comes

effects.log: You stay. They talk through the night, at last, and the treaty is sealed at dawn in your courtyard.

events.text: The name-pillars of {b3_clan} shiver, one after another, down the whole length of the Hall, as if something had walked by that nobody saw. The vigil flames lean after it. The Gate of Incense swings. The Warden asks who passed. The Reader of Omens, white as paper, says: "someone who was owed an entrance."

choices.text: Light every flame in the Hall and wait for them to speak

effects.log: You light them all. Nothing speaks, but the Hall is warmer by dawn, and the dust on the pillars is arranged in a small neat line.

choices.text: Follow the shiver to the end of the Hall

effects.log: You follow it. It ends at an empty alcove, in which is a stool, a cup, and a name nobody has ever carved.

events.text: Visitors from a Lineage of the Hidden Star have been seen standing in the courtyard of {b3_clan} in the dead of night, with their faces turned up, doing nothing, for hours. They are not stargazers. They say they are checking that the sky is where they left it. They would like to be left alone and also given soup.

choices.text: Bring soup and say nothing

effects.log: You bring it. The star-gods eat with great gravity, and one of them murmurs, "it is there still," and the others nod.

choices.text: Ask them what they are afraid of

effects.log: They tell you, in whispers, and you are afraid of it too for a month, and kinder.

events.text: A god of {b3_clan} has been summoned to the Thrones on a charge of overlooking a prayer. The prayer, it emerges, was from a dying infant; the god was ill, and slept through it. The Thrones are not cruel, only exact. The god is standing in the dock with their hands folded, and they ask for nothing.

choices.text: Speak for them before the Thrones, and share the blame

effects.log: You speak. The Thrones hear you, and the sentence is a year of penance that you serve beside them, scrubbing the Hall of Prayers.

choices.text: Ask the Thrones to weigh the god's ten thousand years of service

effects.log: You ask. The Thrones weigh them, and the penance is lessened, and the god weeps.

events.text: The kites of {b3_clan}, great paper birds flown at the festival of winds, have all been cut loose at once by an unseen hand. They rise in a single flock and drift off west. The children cry. The Officers say it is an omen. A mortal child far below catches a string and holds on.

choices.text: Follow the flock and see where the kites land

effects.log: You follow. They land in a field where a lonely shepherd looks up, startled, and the Line has a new shrine by evening.

choices.text: Send the children fresh kites and a good wind

effects.log: You send them. The festival goes on, and the old kites are, the Officers insist, a sign of favour.

events.text: The Archivist of {b3_clan} has fallen in love with a pillar. Not a god: a pillar, a plain one in the corner, said by the Line to have no name. The Archivist visits it daily, brings tea, and says it listens beautifully. The Officers whisper. {b3_elder} says the pillar once bore a name and lost it, and the Archivist is the first to ask.

choices.text: Ask the Archivist to read the pillar by touch

effects.log: The Archivist reads it. The stone gives up a name, small and clear, and the pillar, for the first time in nine thousand years, hums.

choices.text: Let the Archivist keep their private tea-hour

effects.log: You let them. The pillar goes on listening, and the Archivist goes on loving, and the Line is quietly improved.

events.text: A messenger arrives from the lowest rung of the Thrones asking, with great embarrassment, whether {b3_clan} could lend them a cup of salt. Their own stores have been, through an error of record, sent to the wrong pantheon. They are famous for pride, and the request has cost them. The Officers prepare to laugh. {b3_peer} does not.

choices.text: Send a barrel, with a note that it is a gift and not a loan

effects.log: You send a barrel. A day later, a note in perfectly formal hand: "owed, and not forgotten." The Line has a Throne's gratitude in its pocket.

choices.text: Send a cup, as asked, with a graceful joke

effects.log: You send a cup. The joke lands. The Throne's messenger laughs, once, in a very small way, and the debt is a friendship.

events.text: The first morning after the Hidden Ancestor of {b3_house} is awake, the Hall is full of prayers addressed to {b3_anc}, not to you. A thousand petitions from the faithful, in every hand. The Officers politely forward them. {b3_anc} reads three, frowns, and hands the pile back, saying: "you are the head; they are yours."

choices.text: Answer the petitions in the sleeper's name, and in yours

effects.log: You answer them jointly. The faithful of the Lineage are astonished to be addressed by two gods at once, and the Line's name rings through the hills.

choices.text: Ask {b3_anc} to answer the oldest of them in person

effects.log: The sleeper chooses one, a baker's prayer for rain on a field. It rains. The baker never knows, and the Line is not so cold.

events.text: The Feast of Names of {b3_house} falls on your first year as its head. You are expected to open it with the name of the founder. You have practised it for months. At the lectern you find that the founder's name has been quietly changed overnight in the Book, to yours. The Herald of the Line is looking at the ceiling.

choices.text: Open the Feast with the founder's name, and strike yours

effects.log: You say the founder's name, and strike yours with your own hand. The Lineage applauds, softly, in the manner of a people relieved.

choices.text: Ask the Herald to explain the change before all

effects.log: The Herald explains: the Lineage wished to honour you. You thank them, and keep the change, until you can undo it politely.

events.text: The Elder Lineage you head, {b3_house}, owes a debt that its previous head never mentioned: a promise to a mortal village to hold back a flood, once, in a single bad year. The village has just sent word that the year has come. The Officers of {b3_house} search the Book. The clause, they find, is real.

choices.text: Honour the promise and hold back the flood

effects.log: You hold it, and are tired for a century. The village erects a shrine, and the Lineage learns that it has promises that bind.

choices.text: Send a lesser god of rivers to share the burden with you

effects.log: You share it. The flood is held by two, and the village praises both, and the lesser god of rivers is no longer lesser.

events.text: A delegation from the faithful of {b3_house} arrives in the Hall to ask a delicate thing: a change in the Lineage's greatest rite, which has been held at the new moon since the world was young. They would prefer it at the full. It would, they say, be more comfortable for the old and for children. They are afraid of you.

choices.text: Move the rite to the full moon, and bless the first

effects.log: You move it. The faithful come in their thousands, and the old and the children sit together in the light, and the Lineage is warmer for it.

choices.text: Keep the new moon but add a full-moon vigil for the weak

effects.log: You add the vigil. Both rites stand, and the Lineage has a new custom, and some Officers a new grievance.

events.text: On the anniversary of your taking the head seat of {b3_house}, the Lineage presents a gift: a painting of you, as the Officers imagine you. It is magnificent and wrong. In it you are tall, stern and radiating. You are, in life, none of these. The Officers watch you look at it with the nervousness of those who are about to find out.

choices.text: Hang it in the Hall, and laugh

effects.log: You laugh, and hang it, and the Hall laughs with you, and the painting is thereafter fondly mocked and never moved.

choices.text: Ask the painter to come and see you as you are, and paint again

effects.log: The painter comes. The second portrait is smaller, truer and kinder, and hangs beside the first.

events.text: {b3_peer} has told the younger gods that the seal of the Line was meant to pass by descent and never by choice, and that you, whatever else, were chosen. It is an old argument and not wholly wrong. The young gods of {b3_clan} are listening, with the bright attention of those who have always wanted to be asked.

choices.text: Call {b3_peer} in and ask what they want

effects.log: You call them in. They want a seat on the council, and an apology for a slight of four thousand years ago, and both are easier than the argument.

choices.text: Say it before the Hall: the seal was chosen, and why

effects.log: You say it plainly. The young gods hear the reasons, which are better than the descent, and the argument loses its edge.

events.text: The Book of the Line of {b3_clan} is short by a handful of names. They have been scraped from a page and the page re-inked, by someone careful. {b3_elder} found it, and comes to you with the cold grief of a person who knows that only four people touch the Book, and one is {b3_elder}.

choices.text: Hold a quiet reckoning with the four

effects.log: You hold it. The names were of three gods who disgraced the Line a thousand years ago, and the scribe who erased them was trying to spare the young. It is a hard conversation and a kind one.

choices.text: Restore the names from memory, and say nothing of who

effects.log: You restore them. The four are left wondering which of you knows, and are, for a decade, scrupulous.

events.text: The Keeper of the Offerings reports that the Line of {b3_clan} has offered, this year, twice as many libations as it has received. The Line is, in the language of the ledger, in deficit of faith. {b3_elder} says the Line has simply been generous. The Keeper says generosity is how Lineages die.

choices.text: Cut the libations to match the receipts, for a decade

effects.log: You cut them. The Line is thinner, steadier, and slightly less loved, and the Keeper sleeps again.

choices.text: Keep giving, and send heralds below to inspire more worship

effects.log: You send them. The faith returns in a trickle, then a stream, and the Line is a little proud and a little worn.

events.text: An old custom of {b3_clan} says the Hall of Names must be swept by the blood of the Line, never by servants, once each season. The Line now numbers thousands, and the custom is kept by fewer each year. {b3_elder} has begun doing it alone, at dawn, loudly, so that everyone can hear the broom.

choices.text: Take up a broom yourself, and be seen to

effects.log: You sweep. By the second week a dozen young gods are sweeping with you, embarrassed, and the Hall is clean.

choices.text: Replace the custom with a rota of duties of other kinds

effects.log: You write the rota. The sweeping is shared with cooking, guarding and carving, and nobody can say they have been spared.

events.text: The Herald of the Line has been asked by a rival Lineage to call the names of their dead at a funeral, a courtesy of the highest order. The Herald is delighted and has already begun to rehearse. {b3_peer} says the request is a trap: the dead include a god who was your Line's enemy.

choices.text: Let the Herald go, and trust the rite

effects.log: The Herald goes. The enemy's name is spoken in the Line's voice, correctly, and the rival Lineage is silent with astonishment.

choices.text: Send the Herald with a written statement of the Line's feelings

effects.log: The statement is read aloud first. It is graceful, brief and exact. The rival respects it, and the funeral goes on.

events.text: A god of the Line, Dasseth, has been taking his seat at the council in the clothes of a mortal farmer, and speaking only in proverbs of the soil. He says he is in mourning for his domain, a field that was sold. The Officers are alarmed. The field was not his.

choices.text: Visit the field with Dasseth, and see it for yourself

effects.log: You go. The field is a small bare plot with a well, and Dasseth's grief is real and out of proportion, and you listen for an afternoon.

choices.text: Buy the field back from the new keeper, with Lineage offerings

effects.log: You buy it back. Dasseth stops wearing the clothes, and the field becomes a small shrine to the plain pleasures of tilling.

events.text: A scribe of {b3_clan} has changed the spelling of the Line's founding name in the Book, from the old to the modern, in a moment of tidiness. The change has been noticed by one Officer, who has not slept since. The Line has been spelled wrong, the Officer says, for forty-one years, and nobody noticed.

choices.text: Restore the old spelling and thank the Officer

effects.log: You restore it. The Officer is nearly weeping, and the scribe is let off with a rebuke and a lecture on the history of vowels.

choices.text: Adopt the modern spelling across the Book

effects.log: You adopt it. The old Officers are appalled, the young delighted, and the Line enters its next age spelled differently.

events.text: The Warden of the Domain Gate of {b3_clan} has been asked by a visiting god for the loan of the gate's key. Just for an evening. The god says it is a matter of sentiment. The Warden, uneasy, has said neither yes nor no. The god is standing very politely in the rain.

choices.text: Lend the key, and send a young god along to keep it

effects.log: You lend it. The god returns it at dawn, polished, and leaves behind a small iron flower as thanks.

choices.text: Refuse, and offer the god the gate-house fire instead

effects.log: You offer the fire. The god accepts, warmed and a trifle abashed, and they tell the Warden a story about a locked door in their youth.

events.text: The vigil flames of {b3_clan} have been mismatched. Seven flames burn blue, six burn red, and one burns green, and no one lit them that way. The Officers argue whether it is an omen. The flame-keeper insists it is a prank. The green flame is by the Oracle Pool and is, you note, making the pool look seasick.

choices.text: Sit with the green flame and ask what it wants

effects.log: You sit. The flame says nothing, but burns very slowly and very close, and in the morning you remember a conversation from childhood.

choices.text: Order the flames relit in their proper colours

effects.log: You order it. The flames resume, and the green one, at the last, gutters back, a little offended.

events.text: A boy of the mortals below has been stealing prayers from the Line. He writes them in his own hand and sends them to {b3_clan} as if they were his, making wishes in other people's names. The prayers are heartfelt and mostly for the benefit of others. The Reader of Prayers does not know whether to forgive or complain.

choices.text: Send the boy a dream and ask him why

effects.log: You send it. He confesses, mortified: nobody listens to him, but they listen to a prayer. You decide to listen to him too.

choices.text: Quietly answer his borrowed prayers, one in ten

effects.log: You answer one in ten. The boy never knows, and grows up quietly good, and sends a hundred more.

events.text: Two sets of Officers of {b3_clan} have taken to meeting in separate halls to discuss the same questions. The Day Council meets by the sun and the Night Council by the moon. They have not, in a century, agreed on the date of the Feast. {b3_elder} says the Line has two heads and does not know it.

choices.text: Call a joint council at the eclipse, when sun and moon meet

effects.log: You wait for the eclipse and convene both. They are so startled to be in the same room that they agree on everything in ten minutes, and are appalled.

choices.text: Make the Feast fall on whichever date is the first of the two

effects.log: You decree it. The Night Council grumbles, the Day Council smirks, and the Feast is held at dusk, so that neither is wrong.

events.text: The Herald of {b3_clan} has been called to explain a mispronunciation at the last Feast, in which the name of a revered ancestor was said as "Orsh" instead of "Orth." The ancestor, if awake, would have taken offence. The Herald is mortified. {b3_peer} points out that "Orsh" was the original form.

choices.text: Ask the Herald to keep "Orsh" and explain why

effects.log: The Herald keeps it, and explains. The Line is charmed by its own history, and the ancestor is, silently, flattered.

choices.text: Apologise to the ancestor with a libation, and say "Orth"

effects.log: You pour the libation. The Hall breathes out, and the ancestor, wherever they are, does not object.

events.text: A young god of {b3_clan} wishes to be Keeper of the Offerings, an office held by Ossel for six thousand years. The young god is clever, honest and plainly better at the arithmetic. Ossel, who is old and kind, has said nothing. The young god, hesitant, has come to you at night with a ledger.

choices.text: Make the young god Keeper-Designate, and Ossel their guide

effects.log: You do. Ossel, hurt, says it is long overdue, and teaches harder than anyone, and the Line gains a Keeper and a lesson.

choices.text: Tell the young god to wait, and to serve Ossel gladly

effects.log: You tell them. They wait, and serve, and in a century are the Keeper and the dearest friend Ossel has.

events.text: The mortals of a fishing district below have started to pray to {b3_clan} with their boats still in the water. The prayers are salty, brief and usually followed by a splash. The Reader of Prayers says the district is in trouble: a reef has shifted. The district's priest is not asking for help. He is asking forgiveness.

choices.text: Send a calm sea and a dream of the reef's new shape

effects.log: You send it. The district is saved, and the priest asks again for forgiveness, and does not get an answer, because there was nothing to forgive.

choices.text: Send a herald in the shape of a gull to lead the boats home

effects.log: The gull leads them. The district puts up a small stone gull, and, for centuries, the birds are not eaten.

events.text: The old stair of dawn leading up to {b3_clan} has been worn by ten thousand years of pilgrims into a smooth, deep trough. A pilgrim, last week, slipped and was caught by a Warden. The Officers recommend repairing it. The pilgrims, asked, say the worn stair is part of the prayer.

choices.text: Repair only the top three steps, the dangerous ones

effects.log: You repair three. The rest stays smooth and ancient, and the pilgrims treat the new steps with a wary respect.

choices.text: Leave the stair alone and post a Warden to catch the falling

effects.log: You post one. The Warden catches nine pilgrims in a year, and the number goes into the Book, and into legend.

events.text: The Gate of Incense of {b3_clan} burns a smoke that can be read, by a trained eye. {b3_elder} has been reading it for years and has been wrong twice. Today it has formed a clear, trembling shape in the air: a hand, open, held out. Nobody knows whose.

choices.text: Take the hand in the smoke, and see what follows

effects.log: You reach out. The smoke closes around your fingers like a handshake, and a name you did not know comes to you, and you write it down.

choices.text: Wait for a second shape before acting

effects.log: You wait. A second shape forms, a door, and you realise the hand was an invitation, and you are glad you did not grasp.

events.text: A bequest has come to {b3_clan} from a minor god who has faded: a modest shrine, a cat, and an instruction to "see that the cat is not sad." The shrine is in a bad district, and the cat is vast, ancient and highly critical. The Officers don't know what to do with either. The cat is looking at you.

choices.text: Take both, and give the cat the run of the Hall of Names

effects.log: You take them. The cat, appraising the Hall, finds the warmest pillar and declares it a throne, and the Hall is thereafter ruled gently.

choices.text: Send the cat to the shrine with a good keeper and a dish

effects.log: You send them. The cat is moderately content, and the shrine, in its bad district, becomes a haven for strays.

events.text: The faithful of a hill-town below have begun to compare {b3_clan} unfavourably with another Line, in public, and to leave the second Line's offerings on your altar as a form of rebuke. The Keeper has stacked them. The pile is unwieldy. It includes a live goat, who is looking resentful.

choices.text: Return the offerings and the goat with an elegant note

effects.log: You return them. The other Line, mortified, sends the goat back to you again with a worse note, and the hill-town is entertained.

choices.text: Accept the goat and answer the rebuke with a miracle

effects.log: You accept the goat. The rebuke is answered with a plain, practical miracle, a well, and the town forgets the comparison.

events.text: A Reader of Omens at {b3_clan} has seen a deathless god of the Line weeping in a dream, and has been unable to say which. The Line is afraid. Several gods, over the next week, make small cautious confessions, to each other, in corridors. It is the best week for forgiveness the Hall has had in a century.

choices.text: Invite the Line to confess, formally, in the Hall of Names

effects.log: You invite them. A hundred small things are said aloud, and absolved, and the Hall is lighter than it has ever been.

choices.text: Let the corridors do their work; do not formalise it

effects.log: You let them. The corridor-confessions continue for a decade, and are the Line's most honest rite, for being unofficial.

events.text: The Line of {b3_clan} has a library cat, a library owl and a library moth. The three do not get on. The owl wants the cat banned, the cat wants the moth banned, and the moth has no opinions but is eating the minutes of the dispute. The Archivist, besieged, has come to you for judgment in a mock-solemn voice.

choices.text: Rule that each has the stacks on alternate days

effects.log: You rule so. The Archivist pins up a rota in three scripts, and the three obey it with feline, owlish and mothlike resentment.

choices.text: Appoint the moth to guard the minutes and see how it likes it

effects.log: You appoint it. The moth, to the astonishment of all, takes it to heart, and eats nothing for a century.

events.text: An old tale says that on the thousandth anniversary of the Line's founding, its head must walk the boundary of the domain alone, barefoot, at dawn. You have forgotten that this is the year. {b3_elder} reminds you at breakfast, in a voice of terrible gentleness, with a pair of unworn sandals held in both hands.

choices.text: Walk the boundary barefoot, as the old tale requires

effects.log: You walk. The domain is long, cold and strangely kind, and you come home at dusk with new lines on your soles and a clear head.

choices.text: Walk it in the sandals and write a note of apology to the tale

effects.log: You walk it shod. The tale seems not to mind, and the Officers decide, over dinner, that it was meant as a metaphor.

events.text: The faithful of {b3_clan} below have begun to leave their children with the shrine's priests for the harvest season, and the priests cannot cope. The shrine is full of small mortals sticky with plums. The Reader of Prayers reports that the prayers are now mostly for the children's safety, said by the priests in a ragged chorus.

choices.text: Send a herald in the shape of a wet-nurse to help for the season

effects.log: You send one. The shrine is saved, the plums are eaten, and the children grow up with a firm belief that gods help with sticky hands.

choices.text: Build the shrine a proper nursery wing from the Line's stores

effects.log: You build it. The wing stands for a thousand years, and the Line is spoken of in a hundred villages as the god of full cradles.

events.text: The tutor of rites at {b3_clan} has quit, in a letter written entirely in the passive voice. "A decision has been made." "It is regretted." The young gods are lost without her. She is sitting, they discover, in the gate-house, ostentatiously not teaching, with her tea and a small pile of unmarked rites.

choices.text: Ask her what would bring her back, and mean it

effects.log: You ask. She wants the young given real work earlier, and an end to a ritual she thinks is cruel. You agree to both, and she returns with a stiff nod.

choices.text: Ask the best of her pupils to teach a season in her place

effects.log: The pupil teaches, and does well, and the tutor, listening at a door, returns in a month, wounded and glad.

events.text: A god of {b3_clan} has built a shrine to themself, in secret, on a hill, complete with offerings. They have been leaving the offerings themselves. The shrine is small, tidy and rather sweet. The god is in tears. "I thought if I started," they say, "someone might come."

choices.text: Come to the shrine yourself, with an offering, and sit

effects.log: You come. You sit for an hour. The god, watching you from behind a tree, sobs, and the hill has its first real visitor.

choices.text: Quietly send a mortal shepherd that way, in a dream

effects.log: You send one. The shepherd stays, and tells his friends, and the shrine is a place of modest, true devotion.

events.text: The dust on the lower shelves of the Book of the Line has been disturbed by something small and determined. Tiny footprints cross the vellum and end at a hole in the wall from which a faint ticking can be heard. {b3_peer} says it is a mechanical mouse. {b3_elder} says it is the Line's conscience, escaped.

choices.text: Open the wall and find out what is ticking

effects.log: You open it. It is a tiny clock made by an ancestor to keep the Line's time, still working, nine thousand years old, very slow.

choices.text: Leave the hole alone and put out a saucer

effects.log: You leave the saucer. The ticking continues, and the Hall hears it as a sort of heartbeat, and is the calmer.

events.text: A sudden fashion has swept {b3_clan}: the young gods have begun to speak entirely in the tongue of an obscure pantheon, to the despair of the Officers. The meetings are conducted in a language only half understood. Decisions are being made, and nobody is quite sure which.

choices.text: Ask the young gods to translate for you, to learn the tongue

effects.log: You ask them. They beam, and teach, and by the end of the year you speak it badly and are loved.

choices.text: Rule that Council business be conducted in the common tongue

effects.log: You rule so. The young are sulky, and, in the corridors, still use the other tongue, and the Line acquires a slang.

events.text: The Oracle Pool of {b3_clan} has shown the same vision, for nine nights, to the same Reader: a door in a wall in a country the Reader has never visited. On the tenth night the Reader walked out of the Hall and has not returned. A small note is left on the Reader's desk: "gone to see."

choices.text: Send a trusted herald after the Reader to bring news

effects.log: The herald finds them after a year in a small market-town in a far domain, fixing a pump. The door was a pump-room door. They are very happy.

choices.text: Wait, and trust the Reader to return in their own time

effects.log: You wait. The Reader returns after eleven years, brown and strange and quiet, with a seed, and plants it by the Pool.

events.text: A new Officer of {b3_clan}, Nesh, is deeply devout and very tiring. They kneel at every pillar. They correct the pronunciation of every hymn. They have proposed an additional seven rites. {b3_elder} says Nesh is what the Line was, and has forgotten it was. The Hall is wary of Nesh the way it is wary of a mirror.

choices.text: Give Nesh a rite of their own to lead, and watch

effects.log: You give them one. Nesh leads it flawlessly, and the Hall, to its irritation, is moved. The seven proposed rites are reduced to one.

choices.text: Thank Nesh, and ask them to teach the young gods to kneel

effects.log: You ask. The young kneel crookedly and Nesh teaches them with a patience nobody expected, and is, for the first time, loved.

events.text: A babe is born to the Line of {b3_clan}, and the stone-cutters are waiting at the name-pillars with their chisels. The rule is that a child is named when it first laughs. This one has not. It is eleven years old, which is young, but the cutters are bored and the aunts are anxious. The child watches everyone gravely.

choices.text: Wait for the laugh, and tell the aunts to stop counting

effects.log: You wait. The child laughs at fourteen, at the sight of a goose in a hat, and the name is cut that evening, and is "Goose."

choices.text: Tell a joke to the child, privately, and see

effects.log: You tell it. The child considers it with a grave air and says, "no," and you try three more, and one lands, and the child is named with a surprising dignity.

events.text: An inspector from the Thrones is visiting {b3_clan}, quietly, to assess the Line's accounts of belief, behaviour and rite. They are very polite. They ask to see the kitchen first. {b3_elder} is sweating. The Archivist has hidden the worst ledger under a cat.

choices.text: Show the inspector everything, the worst ledger first

effects.log: You show it. The inspector is silent for an hour, and then says it is the most honest Line she has seen. The ledger, thereafter, is a point of pride.

choices.text: Walk the inspector round the domain and let it speak for itself

effects.log: You walk. The domain is lived-in and cared for, and the ledger is forgiven in the face of it.

events.text: A god of {b3_clan} has fallen in love with a mortal, and not in the old, clumsy, godly way, but properly: reading her letters, learning her dialect, carrying her water. She is a fishwife of forty. The Officers consider it a disgrace. {b3_peer} considers it the first interesting thing the Line has done in a century.

choices.text: Meet the fishwife yourself, in disguise, and see

effects.log: You meet her. She is shrewd, funny, and wholly unimpressed, and you understand at once. You tell the god so.

choices.text: Tell the god to go carefully, and keep the Officers off

effects.log: You tell them. The god goes carefully, and the Officers are kept off, and a quiet courtship becomes, in time, a quiet marriage.

events.text: The offering-stores of {b3_clan} are being pilfered, slowly, by a thief of great delicacy. A cake from here, a bowl from there. The thief has been seen only as a shadow, and a faint scent of cinnamon. The Keeper of the Offerings, in despair, has laid a trap of cakes. The cakes remain, and the Keeper's own breakfast has gone.

choices.text: Sit up in the stores with a plate of cinnamon rolls

effects.log: You sit up. At the third hour a very small, very elegant god of hunger arrives, and shares a roll, and a long conversation.

choices.text: Set a standing dish for the thief in the stores

effects.log: You set a dish. The thief takes only from the dish, thereafter, and sends a thank-you in cinnamon.

events.text: The young gods of {b3_clan} have sat their yearly exam in the rites, and the results are in: half have failed. The tutor wants the exam made easier. The Archivist wants it made harder. A third voice, a young god who passed, says the exam is not testing the right thing and she has a list.

choices.text: Read the young god's list, and consider her reforms

effects.log: You read it. It is very good. The exam is changed, and the next year's pass-rate is no higher, and everyone is learning more.

choices.text: Keep the exam, and offer the failed a second year with the tutor

effects.log: You offer it. The second year is humbling and useful, and the tutor takes it as a sign of trust.

events.text: The Oracle Pool of {b3_clan} will not answer you. It will answer anyone else; a scullion got a full reading of her future this morning. But when you lean over it, it ripples, shows your face, and goes calm. The Reader of Omens says the pool is shy. The pool, at this, ripples in indignant disagreement.

choices.text: Sit by the pool every dawn until it relents

effects.log: You sit. Forty days later it shows you, in a long silence, a table laid for dinner with an empty chair. You take it as a courtesy.

choices.text: Ask the Reader to ask the pool for you

effects.log: The Reader asks. The pool answers the Reader, at length, and the Reader returns white and says only: "they said you know."

events.text: A deserter from the army of a rival Throne has come to the Gate of {b3_clan} asking for refuge. A tall, tired god of war with a notched sword and a face like a shut door. The Warden has let him in as far as the gate-house. The Throne's herald is already at the foot of the stair, requesting him back.

choices.text: Grant refuge, and answer the herald with a lawful refusal

effects.log: You grant it. The herald leaves in a cold temper, and the god of war sits in the gate-house, and for the first time in an age, sleeps.

choices.text: Hear the deserter first, and then decide what is just

effects.log: You hear him. It is a long, plain story of orders he would not follow. You grant the refuge, and the Throne, when it hears, is oddly silent.

events.text: The mortal shrine-keepers who tend {b3_clan}'s lowest shrines have sent a petition: they would like one day in the year when the god of their shrine is asked, not asked of. They would like to bring the god a cup of tea and listen to its problems. Several of the Officers think this absurd. The Reader of Prayers has wiped his eyes.

choices.text: Grant the day, and attend one shrine yourself

effects.log: You attend. The shrine-keeper pours the tea with trembling hands and says, "tell me how it is up there," and you do, and she cries a little, and so, ever so slightly, do you.

choices.text: Grant the day, and send a herald to each shrine in your stead

effects.log: You send heralds. The tea is drunk, the problems heard, and the Line is spoken of at a hundred hearths as the god who listens back.

events.text: A fire has started in the Archive of {b3_clan}: a small one, in a corner, caused by a lamp tipped by a cat. It is put out in a minute. But the pages it touched are of the oldest records. The Archivist is on their knees on the ash, gathering charred flakes and sobbing. {b3_peer} is holding the cat, who is unrepentant.

choices.text: Put the Line's scribes to reconstructing the lost pages

effects.log: You do. It takes forty years, and some pages are guessed at, and the Archivist insists on marking the guesses with a small red star.

choices.text: Ask the Unlit Lamp for a copy of what was burnt

effects.log: You ask. The Lamp, who keeps copies of everything, sends them in a month, and a short note: "we noticed you were busy."

events.text: The Line of {b3_clan} has a banner, old, faded, hung over the Hall of Names. Its colours have bled so that no one can say what the original device was. Two factions want it restored. Each remembers the original differently. The banner, between them, is turning slowly to dust in a draught.

choices.text: Have the banner copied as it is now, faded, and keep the original

effects.log: You do. The new banner is a pale ghost of the old, and the Line, looking at it, remembers precisely how it was to be young.

choices.text: Commission a new banner from the Line's children

effects.log: The children make it, with paint and glue. It is garish and splendid, and hangs over the Hall, and is the Line's true device from that day.

events.text: A messenger of the Throne of Storms arrives at {b3_clan} with a demand: the Line must send a god to stand a century on a mountain in the Storm's service. The post is boring, cold and honourable. The Officers draw lots, and the lot falls on {b3_peer}, who goes pale. They are not strong. They are the best-read among you.

choices.text: Go yourself, instead of {b3_peer}

effects.log: You go. The mountain is cold and windy, and you learn how thunder talks, and return with a new respect for weather.

choices.text: Send {b3_peer}, with the Line's best books and its blessing

effects.log: {b3_peer} goes. They return a century later weather-beaten and wise, and have written a treatise on the winds, and the Storm sends a gift.

events.text: The Gate of Incense has started to open, on its own, on the stroke of midnight, to nothing. The Warden has stood in the doorway each night and seen no one. The gate swings wide, and shuts. The Reader of Omens suggests a prayer. The Warden suggests a cup of cocoa, and a short chat with whoever it is.

choices.text: Stand in the gate at midnight and say, "welcome"

effects.log: You stand. At the stroke, the gate opens, and a chill passes through you, like a bow, and the gate is quiet thereafter.

choices.text: Leave a chair and a cup in the gateway each night

effects.log: You leave them. By morning the cup is empty, and warm, and the gate has ceased its opening.

events.text: A god of {b3_clan} has been caught practising the voice of the Herald in the bath. It is flawless. The Herald, listening at the door, is torn between fury and a sort of ghastly pride. {b3_elder} says the young god has an ear. The young god says it was only an experiment. The Herald is staying very still.

choices.text: Make the young god the Herald's understudy

effects.log: You do. The Herald fumes, and teaches, and in a century has a successor who calls the names with a new music.

choices.text: Ask the pair to call the Feast of Names together, in alternation

effects.log: They call it so. It is the best Feast in recent memory, and the Herald, dignified, unbends.

events.text: A god of {b3_clan} is dying, slowly, of the oldest ailment: no one has said their name in a thousand years. They are in the infirmary, grey, polite, apologising for the trouble. The Officers have forgotten who they are. The infirmary-keeper has the name written on a slip and cannot bring herself to read it aloud.

choices.text: Read the name aloud at the bedside, and bring the Line to hear

effects.log: You read it. The Line crowds in. The god sits up, and weeps, and lives another thousand years.

choices.text: Carve the name on a pillar, tonight, with your own hand

effects.log: You carve it. By dawn the god is breathing easier, and the Line has a new pillar and a new rule: no name unsaid.

events.text: The lowest shrine of {b3_clan} has asked for an exemption from the yearly tithe of worship. The shrine's mortal community is in a bad year. They are offering all they have: songs, a pig, a dried fish. The Keeper of the Offerings is moved, and appalled at the precedent. The pig is sitting at the Keeper's feet, entirely at ease.

choices.text: Grant the exemption and send a granary-load as a gift

effects.log: You grant it. The shrine weeps with gratitude, and the pig is allowed to live out its days in the Hall.

choices.text: Accept the songs only, and return the pig and the fish

effects.log: You accept the songs. They are surprisingly good, and the shrine is thereafter known for its choir.

events.text: A decorator of the Line has proposed to repaint the Hall of Names in a cheerful yellow. The Officers have lost their composure. The Hall has been grey-gold for nine thousand years. The decorator, an unflappable young god of colour, says he has tested a small patch behind the third pillar. It looks, he says, like a smile.

choices.text: Visit the test patch, and judge it with open eyes

effects.log: You visit. It is a rather lovely yellow. The Hall is not repainted, but the patch is kept, and the Hall smiles, a little, at that corner.

choices.text: Allow the repainting of one wall, in the yellow, for a decade

effects.log: You allow one wall. By the decade's end, the Line is arguing about whether the second wall should follow.

events.text: A rumour in {b3_clan} says the head of the Line must, by an old rule, sleep one night in each year on the bare floor of the Hall of Names, to remember the first night. Nobody has told you this. It is not written anywhere. Three Officers are quietly watching to see whether you will do it, or ask, or rail.

choices.text: Sleep on the floor, and say nothing of it

effects.log: You sleep. The floor is hard, cold and full of voices, and you wake with a new understanding of the word "founding."

choices.text: Ask the three, plainly, whether the rule exists

effects.log: You ask. It does not. They invented it as a test, and are mortified, and you laugh, and the Hall relaxes.

events.text: A hostile Lineage has sent {b3_clan} a gift of a hundred blue lilies, with a note that says, in impeccable calligraphy, "to brighten the Hall." The lilies are lovely. They are also, the Reader of Omens says, a flower of grief in that Lineage's tradition, sent only to Lines they intend to outlive.

choices.text: Plant the lilies in the courtyard, and send a thank-you

effects.log: You plant them. They bloom in an unexpectedly bright shade, and the hostile Lineage, discovering the thank-you, does not know where to look.

choices.text: Send the lilies back with a basket of cedar branches

effects.log: You send cedar, the tree of long life. The message is understood, and the Lineages continue their polite feud.

events.text: The Line of {b3_clan} has a tradition of holding the Feast of Names with an empty chair for the god who has not yet been named. This year an unknown god sat in it, uninvited, and ate three courses before anyone noticed. They are small, ragged, and have the faint smell of rain. The Warden stands over them. They say, mildly, that they were told it was their seat.

choices.text: Let them sit, and ask who told them

effects.log: You ask. The god says: "a voice in the rain." They are new, nameless, and for centuries unclaimed. You are the first to ask.

choices.text: Offer them a name and a pillar of the Line

effects.log: You offer one. They accept shyly, and the Line has a younger sibling and a stranger one.

events.text: The mortals below have started to bury offerings for {b3_clan} in their fields instead of burning them, on the theory that the god is in the earth. The harvest is excellent. The Officers are thrown. The Reader of Prayers says it is not a heresy so much as a reasonable adjustment, and the Line should perhaps learn to live in dirt.

choices.text: Accept the buried offerings, and take a field into your care

effects.log: You accept. The Line acquires a taste for clods, and the harvests are, for a century, the pride of the district.

choices.text: Send a dream: the Line is in the air, but loves the soil

effects.log: You send it. The mortals nod, and bury half and burn half, and everyone is satisfied.

events.text: A rite of {b3_clan} requires the exchange of gifts between the head and the youngest god of the Line at each turning of the age. This age, the youngest is a sullen little god of splinters who has never spoken to you. You have a gift. They have, you see, a gift for you, wrapped in a leaf, clutched like a weapon.

choices.text: Open the leaf-wrapped gift first, and be pleased

effects.log: It is a carved sparrow, rough, with one wing too long. You carry it for the rest of the age, and the little god, noticing, speaks to you for the first time.

choices.text: Give your gift first, plainly, and wait

effects.log: You give it. The little god looks at it for a long time and then gives you the leaf, and walks away fast.

events.text: A visiting scholar from the Lineage of the Root has noticed that the Hall of {b3_clan} stands on the same spot as a much older hall, whose foundations show in the cellar. The older hall belonged to a Line that is no more. Its name is carved on the cellar wall, in a script no one reads. The scholar reads it aloud, gently.

choices.text: Ask what the name says, and the scholar to stay

effects.log: It says: "we were glad." The scholar stays a year and teaches the Line the script, and the cellar is hung with lamps.

choices.text: Light a lamp in the cellar for the earlier Line, once a year

effects.log: You light one. The earlier Line, if it hears, does not answer, but the cellar smells of warm stone thereafter.

events.text: The singer of the Line, a god of old ballads, has started to forget the words. A verse is lost, then another. The singer covers with a hum and a flourish. The Line has not noticed, but the singer has told you, in confidence, and asks that no one be told. They are sitting beside you, too proud to weep.

choices.text: Sit with the singer and write down the ballads, word by word

effects.log: You sit. It takes six years. At the end you have a book of songs, and the singer has a friend.

choices.text: Ask the young to learn the ballads from the singer, one a month

effects.log: You ask. The young learn them, and the singer, surrounded, is the happiest god in the Hall.

events.text: A priest of the lowest shrine of {b3_clan} has climbed the stair of dawn to deliver a grievance in person: the god of their shrine, a small thing, has been neglected for two centuries and is going translucent. The priest has carried the god up in a pot. The god, in the pot, waves at you faintly.

choices.text: Take the god in, and set the pot in the warmest alcove

effects.log: You take them in. In a decade the god is solid and chatty and has opinions on the Hall's curtains.

choices.text: Send the priest home with a vigil flame for the shrine

effects.log: You send it. The shrine is warm again, and the god, restored, sends you a thank-you in shell.

events.text: The Feast of Names of {b3_clan} has run past dawn, for the first time. The Herald's voice has held, the Hall has not tired, and the names keep coming: thousands, and thousands, until the sun is well up and the doors are thrown open. Mortals below have noticed the Line's lights are still on. A shy crowd has gathered on the stair.

choices.text: Invite the crowd in, to hear the last names

effects.log: You invite them. They enter on tiptoe, mortals among gods, and listen to the last thousand names, and weep, without knowing why.

choices.text: Close the Feast gracefully at the next name and greet them at the gate

effects.log: You close it. The mortals are greeted at the gate with bread and wine, and the Line is, that day, a host.

events.text: The Warden of the Domain Gate has found a baby dragon in the Line's gatehouse. It is the size of a cat and has eaten the Warden's lunch, and the lunch of the Warden's lunch.
