It is also, according to its markings, the heir of a very old and very angry Lineage. {b3_elder} says to send it home. The dragon has started to purr.

choices.text: Send a courteous letter to the dragon's Lineage, with the baby

effects.log: You send it. Its Lineage, which had thought it lost, is so grateful that a century of grudge is dropped.

choices.text: Keep the baby dragon for a season, and teach it manners

effects.log: You keep it. It learns two tricks and a fear of the Archivist, and goes home, a changed dragon.

events.text: A dispute has arisen over whose turn it is to light the great vigil flame of {b3_clan} on the longest night. The turn passes in order of birth, and two cousins were born in the same breath. Both are certain they are the elder. Both have witnesses. The flame is waiting. The cousins are standing on either side of it, not speaking.

choices.text: Have them light it together, one hand each

effects.log: They light it together. The flame leaps high, and the cousins are so startled they laugh, and the quarrel ends in a draw.

choices.text: Light it yourself, and settle the turn by lot for the next age

effects.log: You light it. The lot, when drawn, is a cause of general amusement, and the quarrel is shelved in a drawer.

events.text: The mortals of a river-district below have discovered that {b3_clan} has a tendency to answer prayers made at dawn more readily than those made at dusk. They have organised a vast, orderly queue to pray at dawn, to the despair of the dusk-prayers and the astonishment of the Officers. The Reader of Prayers assures you the pattern is quite real.

choices.text: Even out the answering, and give dusk its hour of grace

effects.log: You do. The dusk-prayers flower, and the queue disperses, and the district is, for a while, calmer.

choices.text: Embrace the dawn queue and make a rite of it

effects.log: You embrace it. The queue grows, and the dawn becomes the Line's great hour, and the mortals keep it with a rare discipline.

events.text: A grief-stricken god of {b3_clan} has asked permission to retire to the cellar and not come up. They say they will be fine. They say the cellar is quiet. They have packed a trunk, a candle and a book of poems. {b3_peer} has said, in a very small voice, that this is how it started with the last one.

choices.text: Go down with them, and sit a while in the dark

effects.log: You go. You sit, saying nothing, and after an hour they begin to talk, and you listen until the candle is a stub.

choices.text: Let them go, and promise to bring supper and the news each night

effects.log: You promise, and keep it. The cellar fills with light by degrees, and in a year they come up for the Feast.

events.text: A flock of the Line's sacred geese has broken out of the cloister of {b3_clan} and occupied the Oracle Pool. They are standing in it, in rows, hissing at the Reader of Omens. The geese are eight thousand years old, were bred for divination, and have never once been wrong about anything but manners.

choices.text: Ask the geese what they foresee, politely

effects.log: The geese, flattered, honk a verdict. It is, the Reader decides after a week, "be kind to the next stranger," and you are.

choices.text: Lure the geese out with a procession of barley-cakes

effects.log: You lure them. The Pool is reclaimed, the geese are offended, and for a year they refuse to foresee anything for the Line.

events.text: The quarrel of the two Councils of {b3_clan} has found a new subject: whether the Hall of Offerings should face east or west. Both sides produce ten-thousand-year-old arguments. The Hall has faced north since the founding. Nobody has noticed. A servant, sweeping, asks quietly whether anyone has a compass.

choices.text: Take the compass, and show the Councils the Hall faces north

effects.log: You show them. The Councils are stunned, and then united in a baffled shame, and the quarrel ends in a draw.

choices.text: Let the Councils fight it out, and avoid the compass

effects.log: You let them. The quarrel gains weight, and in a century is a rite, and no one can say how it began.

events.text: A scroll has arrived at {b3_clan} from a stranger god, claiming to be a long-lost child of the Line, with a genealogy as long as an arm. It is very persuasive. The Herald, who has read it, is silent. {b3_elder} says the claim is almost certainly false, and also that the stranger has the Line's nose.

choices.text: Invite the stranger to the Hall and look at them properly

effects.log: You invite them. They are not of the Line. They are of the Line's heart, and they stay anyway, and the Book makes room.

choices.text: Test the genealogy against the Book, line by line

effects.log: You test it. It fails on the fifth generation, and the stranger confesses with a laugh, and is made a friend of the house.

events.text: At the gate of {b3_house} the Warden asks which pantheon you owe, and writes it down. Then which pantheon your teacher owed. Then which your teacher's teacher refused. It is how they decide where to seat you. The Warden waits, pen lifted, with the look of someone who has heard every possible answer and is still hoping.

choices.text: Answer truthfully, down to the refusal

effects.log: You answer all three. The Warden stops writing at the third, looks up, and seats you nearer the fire than you were going to be.

choices.text: Say you owe no pantheon, and let the Warden make of it what they will

effects.log: The Warden writes "unaligned" with visible interest. The seat you get is by the window, which is where they seat people they have not yet decided about.

events.text: The Hall of {b3_house} is warm, and its libation is served in cups of a thin white clay that has no right to be so old. The cup is pressed into your hand by a god who says nothing and looks at you intently. You understand the cup is the question. You do not understand what the answer might be.

choices.text: Drink, then pour the last drops on the floor for the dead

effects.log: You pour them. A murmur goes round the Hall, approving, and the silent god nods once.

choices.text: Drink it all, and compliment the clay

effects.log: You drink it all. The silent god smiles faintly, as at a harmless mistake, and the Hall resumes its murmur.

events.text: Your name is read aloud in the Hall of Names of {b3_house}, from the guest-roll, and a heavy hush falls. Not hostile: uncertain. Somewhere in the Hall a very old god has begun to cough. The Herald of the house, reading, has frozen on the second syllable, as if a different name had been hoped for.

choices.text: Step forward and say your name once more, slowly

effects.log: You say it. The Herald resumes, relieved, and the old god stops coughing and says, "ah, you are that one," in a tone you take for fair.

choices.text: Wait for the Herald to finish the name in their own time

effects.log: You wait. The Herald finishes, a little pink, and the Hall exhales, and your seat is two places nearer the head.

events.text: The young heir of {b3_house} meets you on the stair of the Lineage seat and has been told to be civil. The heir manages it for one sentence, which is about how few outsiders are allowed past the second landing. The heir is proud, bright and wrong in a very particular way. They have never lost an argument and are about to start one.

choices.text: Let the heir win this one, and enjoy the heir's surprise

effects.log: You concede. The heir blinks, and talks for an hour, and the Lineage hears about it for a century, kindly.

choices.text: Out-talk the heir on the subject of landings

effects.log: You do. The heir is furious and fascinated, and you are, in some wing of the house, remembered.

events.text: You are taken through the Lineage seat of {b3_house} to see the name-pillars, which are the pride of the house and a quiet burden. A line of silent attendants stands at each, dusting. The tour is long. The guide, an elderly god, murmurs each name, and the attendants echo it, and by the fiftieth you are no longer sure who is dusting whom.

choices.text: Ask to be told the story of one pillar in full

effects.log: You choose one. The story is long, tender and not flattering, and you listen, and the guide looks at you as at a person who has asked a real question.

choices.text: Walk the length in silence and touch one name

effects.log: You touch one. The attendants stop dusting. The guide says, softly, "that one is mine," and the tour ends there, for that day.

events.text: A banquet is given in your honour at {b3_house}, and you are seated between two gods who are not speaking to each other. The Lineage has done this deliberately. It is an old trick to test a guest's tact. The soup arrives. The god on your left says to the soup that it is a disgrace. The god on your right says to the soup that it is perfect.

choices.text: Praise the soup, the quarrel, and the ladle

effects.log: You praise all three. Both gods, offended and pleased in equal parts, address you at once, and the soup is excellent.

choices.text: Ask the god on your left what is wrong with the soup, in detail

effects.log: You ask. It is a long answer. It is actually a very good complaint, and the god on your right, listening, starts to nod.

events.text: The Oracle Pool of {b3_house} is offered to you as a courtesy: a look into the water, for a guest, once. The Lineage watches with that tightness of a house that knows the Pool is honest and has been embarrassed by it. The Pool is clear. It shows, you think, a thing about you. They will not say what.

choices.text: Look, and say what you saw, plainly

effects.log: You say it. The Lineage is silent, then laughs, because it was a thing they had also seen in the Pool, and had not dared to say.

choices.text: Look, and keep what you saw to yourself

effects.log: You keep it. The Lineage nods, a house respecting a secret, and the Pool ripples approvingly.

events.text: The Keeper of the Offerings of {b3_house} shows you the offering-stores with a faint pride and a heavier burden. They are enormous: rice in jars the size of houses, bales of silk, rows of lamps. The Keeper has been counting for six thousand years. The Keeper asks, in a whisper, whether your own Lineage is as tired of counting.

choices.text: Say yes, and share the dullest ledger story you know

effects.log: You say yes, and share. The Keeper, at last, laughs, and tells a story of their own, and you are at the same table in the same sense.

choices.text: Say no, politely, and praise the order of the stores

effects.log: You praise the order. The Keeper glows, and the visit goes on with the formal ease of those who have each said the right thing.

events.text: A very old goddess of {b3_house}, said to have been alive when the Line first quarrelled with its neighbour, asks to see your hands. She turns them over, looks at the palms, and tuts. "You have not worked in a while," she says. "Come." She takes you to a loom in the gallery and shows you how to weave.

choices.text: Sit at the loom, and learn the pattern

effects.log: You weave a row of the Line's old pattern. It is crooked, and she approves, and the house has a small piece of your hands in its tapestry.

choices.text: Politely decline, and ask her to tell you of her loom instead

effects.log: She tells you. It is a long story with three wars and a wedding, and you listen with your chin on your hand.

events.text: You are asked at {b3_house} to name one thing you would give up for the good of a Lineage. It is a ritual question. Nobody expects a true answer. The Lineage is watching the guest's face rather than hearing the reply. The question has been asked of gods for ten thousand years, and no two have given the same answer.

choices.text: Give a true answer, small and honest

effects.log: You say what you would give up. It is a small, odd thing, and the Hall is silent, and then the oldest god says, "that is the right size."

choices.text: Give a grand answer, as the Lineage will expect

effects.log: You give a grand one. It is applauded, and filed, and forgotten, and the Lineage thinks no worse and no better of you.

events.text: The ancestor of {b3_house} is mentioned at table in the tone of a family that has a sleeping relative upstairs. The Lineage is anxious about the visitor who might wake them. The cook has been told to cook quietly. A little girl-god keeps asking, aloud, whether the guest has come to wake the ancestor. The adults are pretending not to hear.

choices.text: Tell the child you have come only to visit, and to sit quietly

effects.log: You say so, to the child. The Hall relaxes, and the child, satisfied, climbs into your lap, and the house forgives the question.

choices.text: Tell the child you would like to know the ancestor's name

effects.log: You ask. The Hall freezes, and then the oldest god tells you, slowly, because nobody has asked in a thousand years.

events.text: The Gate of Incense at {b3_house} is a fine one, with nine censers, and the incense is a blend that smells of things you have lost. You are made to walk through it, slowly, as the custom requires. The attendants watch you from the walls. By the sixth censer you are weeping a little. By the ninth you understand why.

choices.text: Walk it slowly to the end, and thank the attendants

effects.log: You do. The attendants bow, as one, and the Lineage knows that you can be moved, and trusts you accordingly.

choices.text: Walk it briskly, and mention the fine smell, and move on

effects.log: You walk briskly. The attendants murmur. You are not rude, but you are marked as one who keeps their own counsel.

events.text: In the gallery of {b3_house} hang the portraits of its heads, thirty of them, each more severe than the last. The twenty-ninth is smiling. It is the only one that is, and the painter has been dismissed. A servant mutters that the twenty-ninth is the happiest head the house ever had, and the one who nearly ruined it.

choices.text: Ask the servant for the twenty-ninth's story

effects.log: The servant tells it, with relish and in a whisper, and it is an excellent story of a feast, a flood and a loan.

choices.text: Admire the twenty-ninth's smile, aloud, in front of the others

effects.log: You admire it. The Lineage sucks in its breath, and then, one by one, begins to smile, and the gallery, for a moment, is warm.

events.text: A messenger runs into the Hall of {b3_house} during your audience, panting, bearing news of a quarrel in the lower district, and the Lineage must send a god to settle it. The head looks round the room, and then, pointedly, at you. The head asks whether the guest might be so kind. It is half a joke. It is half a test.

choices.text: Go, and settle it, and return by supper

effects.log: You go. The quarrel is about a goat. You settle it, and return by supper, and the house is amused and impressed.

choices.text: Offer your good offices, but send a herald in your name

effects.log: You send one. The goat is settled, and the head thanks you for your tact and your laziness in equal measure.

events.text: The elders of {b3_house} have a custom of testing a guest's patience by making them wait in a hall with no chairs for an hour. You have been standing for fifty-eight minutes. The elders are watching through a crack in a screen. One of them is knitting. The door is about to open.

choices.text: Remain standing, and say nothing, and be gracious at the end

effects.log: You remain standing. The door opens, and you greet the elders with an easy bow, and they are, to your surprise, honestly moved.

choices.text: Sit on the floor, cross-legged, and begin to hum

effects.log: You sit and hum. The elder who is knitting cannot hold it, and laughs aloud, and the door opens at once.

events.text: At {b3_house} a god of the Lineage insists on teaching you its greeting: a complex arrangement of the hands, the breath and the tongue, said to be older than speech. You are an indifferent student. The Lineage waits for you to get it right with great and visible courtesy, which makes it worse.

choices.text: Get it wrong, loudly, and laugh at yourself

effects.log: You get it wrong, and laugh. The Lineage laughs with you, helplessly, and the greeting is taught again, with more love.

choices.text: Practise it in a corner until it is right

effects.log: You practise. It takes three hours. At the end you greet the Lineage with it, and they are speechless, and a little tearful.

events.text: The Lineage of {b3_house} keeps a pet, an enormous, ancient, lethargic hound that has sat in the Hall of Names for four thousand years and is believed to be the soul of the founder. The hound, asked to approve of a guest, must be shown one. It lifts its head and looks at you for a very long time.

choices.text: Hold out a hand, palm up, and wait

effects.log: You hold it. The hound sniffs, sighs, and puts its chin on your palm, and the Hall gasps, because it has done that for no one.

choices.text: Sit down on the floor at the hound's level

effects.log: You sit. The hound studies you, and then lies down, with its back to you, and the Hall decides this is high praise.

events.text: The Lineage of {b3_house} gives you a small sealed gift on your arrival and tells you not to open it until you have left. You are given, also, an escort to the border. At the border, the escort looks at you meaningfully and says nothing. It is a lovely, anxious little ritual. You can feel the whole house waiting for you to open it.

choices.text: Open it at the border, in front of the escort

effects.log: You open it. It is a pressed flower and a note: "come again." The escort smiles, and the house, watching in a mirror far away, cheers.

choices.text: Keep it sealed, and open it at home

effects.log: You keep it sealed until home. It is the same flower and note, and you write back that night.

events.text: A younger god of {b3_house} has a grievance against their own Lineage and sees in you a stranger to whom it can be told. They corner you in the larder, whispering about an old injustice, an unpaid honour, a pillar left uncarved. They ask, hopefully, if outsiders can intercede. They are shaking.

choices.text: Listen fully, and promise nothing but to remember

effects.log: You listen. You promise only to remember. The young god weeps with relief, and the Lineage, in time, is changed by your remembering.

choices.text: Tell them gently that you cannot meddle in a house that hosts you

effects.log: You tell them. They nod, ashamed, and the Lineage hears of it, and thinks well of your discretion.

events.text: The Lineage seat of {b3_house} is built on a cliff, and the guest-room hangs over the drop. The window has no glass. The wind sings through it in a ghostly note that keeps you awake until dawn. In the morning the host asks politely whether you slept well, with the faintest edge of a smile. Everyone who visits has this room.

choices.text: Say you slept very well, and ask for the wind's tune

effects.log: You say so. The host is delighted and teaches you the tune, and you hum it all the way home.

choices.text: Admit you did not sleep a wink, and laugh

effects.log: You admit it. The host laughs too and you are moved to the room with the carpet.

events.text: At {b3_house} you meet the Reader of Omens, an old god with eyes like wet stones, who says that she saw your visit in a dream, and in the dream you left a bowl of something warm on the table. She does not say what it was. She watches you with growing expectation. The Lineage is looking at the table.

choices.text: Quietly ask for a bowl of soup and leave it half-eaten

effects.log: You do. The Reader laughs till she weeps. "That was it," she says. "Exactly that." The Lineage chuckles and the dream is paid.

choices.text: Tell her you do not fit into dreams, and thank her

effects.log: You tell her. She says that is the sort of thing a person in a dream would say, and pats your hand.

events.text: The house of {b3_house} has a small garden in its courtyard, where its gods are said to go when they cannot bear to be gods. You are shown it at the end of the tour, without comment. In it is a single bench, a single tree, and a gardener, an elderly god who is at the moment pulling up a weed with great tenderness.

choices.text: Ask the gardener what the tree is

effects.log: The gardener tells you it is a plum, and why. It is a long answer, and you are invited, after, to the bench.

choices.text: Stand quietly at the edge, and do not enter

effects.log: You stand at the edge. The gardener looks up and nods, and the house, learning of it, thinks you a person of manners.

events.text: The Lineage of {b3_house} has a ritual of honest speech, performed on the last night of a guest's visit: the guest is asked to tell the house one thing it does badly, and the house is asked to tell the guest one thing too. The Hall settles. The head of the house, to your surprise, goes first. The thing is brief, and true, and you are not sure how to answer.

choices.text: Tell the house the one thing, kindly and exactly

effects.log: You tell them. It is something they had half-known for a thousand years, and they take it with an exhalation, and thank you.

choices.text: Tell the house you are not worthy to judge, and ask them to continue

effects.log: You decline. They are charmed and a little disappointed, and say, with great gentleness, that you will do better next time.

events.text: On the stair of dawn at {b3_house}, an attendant stops you, politely, and asks for the oldest offering you carry. You are not sure what the attendant means. The attendant is patient. The attendant says: "the oldest thing you are carrying, whether you know it or not." You search your pockets, then yourself.

choices.text: Offer a memory, and say what it is

effects.log: You name a memory. The attendant bows and says it is accepted, and you find, ever after, that the memory is a trifle less sharp, and a little warmer.

choices.text: Offer a coin of starlight from your sleeve

effects.log: You offer it. The attendant weighs it and says it is a decent answer, though a bit literal, and lets you pass.

events.text: You are invited to a rite at {b3_house} in which each guest places a flower on the pillar of a god they have wronged. The Lineage does not ask which. You are left alone with a basket of flowers. The Hall is empty but for the pillars, and the quiet. You have one flower in hand and a great many names to read.

choices.text: Place the flower on a pillar of a god you did wrong

effects.log: You choose one. The act costs you something and gives you something and you leave the Hall lighter by a small, strange weight.

choices.text: Place it on the pillar of the oldest god, as an act of respect

effects.log: You place it. The Hall seems satisfied, and you are not quite honest, and know it, and say nothing.

events.text: A wedding procession of {b3_house} meets you on the road and, by custom, a guest must be invited to join. The couple are two gods of rival domains, and the procession is half joy, half barely suppressed hostility, with the hostility arranged in bands of colour. You are handed a ribbon and a lantern and a fan.

choices.text: Walk in the procession, and sing the wedding song

effects.log: You walk and sing, off-key. The couple glances back, and laughs, and the two halves of the procession laugh too, and the hostility softens.

choices.text: Walk in the procession, but keep to the middle, and say nothing

effects.log: You walk in the middle. The sides keep their colours, and you are a decent, forgettable link.

events.text: The Warden of the Domain Gate at {b3_house} is a huge, scarred god with a face like a cliff, and he has taken a dislike to you, for no reason. He lets you in with every muscle clenched. At dinner, he sits opposite and watches you eat. Halfway through the second course he leans over and says, in a rumble: "you hold your cup like my sister."

choices.text: Ask about his sister, and listen to the answer

effects.log: You ask. His sister was a god of the winter wells, long dead, and he tells you about her over three cups, and the Warden is your friend.

choices.text: Say, "I hope that is a good thing," and continue eating

effects.log: You say so. He grunts, and the grunt is, you will learn, a considerable compliment.

events.text: The head of {b3_house} receives you in a hall of mirrors, where each mirror shows the guest a slightly different version. In one you are older, in one younger, in one in the robe of a Throne. The head says that the guest may take one version for the length of the visit. It is a gift. It is also an experiment.

choices.text: Take the version in the robe of a Throne, for the visit only

effects.log: You take it. The house treats you with wary deference, and you learn exactly what it is like to be afraid of, and you set it down gladly at the gate.

choices.text: Take the plain version in the plainest mirror

effects.log: You take it. The head nods, delighted, as at a correct answer, and you are treated as yourself.

events.text: The Lineage seat of {b3_house} is enormous, and the guide has lost you. You find yourself in a small round room, windowless, with a single pillar in the middle, on which no name is carved but on which, very faintly, the Lineage's hymn is playing. It hums. It hums to you. The pillar is warm. Somewhere, a door closes quietly behind.

choices.text: Sit at the foot of the pillar and listen to the hum

effects.log: You sit for an hour. When you leave, the guide is waiting with a face of relieved reverence, and says nobody has found the room in a thousand years.

choices.text: Retrace your steps quietly and say nothing of the room

effects.log: You retrace them. The room is not on the map you are shown afterwards, and you wonder.

events.text: A child of {b3_house}, about four hundred years old, sits next to you at dinner and asks, loudly, why your hair is like that. The entire table goes silent. The child's mother turns scarlet. The head of the house freezes with a spoon in the air. The child waits, interested.

choices.text: Explain, seriously, with a long and false history of your hair

effects.log: You do. It involves a storm, a bird and a lost argument. The table roars, and the child is delighted, and the Lineage loves you.

choices.text: Say, "I do not know, why is yours like that?"

effects.log: The child considers, and says, solemnly, "because I am four hundred." The table collapses. You are in.

events.text: You are shown, at {b3_house}, the shrine of their lost: a long hall with a lamp for each god of the Lineage who has faded, or been exiled, or simply not come home. There are many lamps. The oldest are dimmest. The newest burns bright, as if the god might walk in. The attendants say nothing, and watch your face.

choices.text: Light a lamp of your own, for someone you lost

effects.log: You light one. The attendants nod. The Lineage knows you for a person who has also lost, and is gentler with you thereafter.

choices.text: Stand a while at the brightest lamp and say nothing

effects.log: You stand. The attendants are moved, and the house says afterward that you have a good heart, and the lamp flickers, once, in thanks.

events.text: The libation-master of {b3_house} offers you a rare vintage, one made from the first harvest after the Line was founded. It is nine thousand years old. It is, the master admits, probably vinegar. But it is the Line's vinegar, and it is offered with such love, and such terror of what you will say, that you hold the cup like a baby bird.

choices.text: Drink it with every sign of rapture

effects.log: You drink. It is vinegar of a venerable and horrible kind, and you keep a straight face, and the master weeps, and the house adopts you.

choices.text: Say, with tenderness, that it is vinegar, and perfect vinegar

effects.log: You say so. The master roars with laughter and tears, and says nobody has ever dared. You are given a jar to take home.

events.text: A quarrel breaks out in the Hall of {b3_house} over whether the guest may be given the Lineage's second-best cup or must be given its best. The head sits in the middle, cold as stone, listening to a hundred voices. The tradition says the guest should decide. You have just realised it is you, and the room has gone quiet.

choices.text: Ask for a simple wooden cup from the kitchen instead

effects.log: You ask. The Hall freezes and then explodes in approval, and the kitchen's cup, brought in on a tray, is treated like a relic.

choices.text: Ask for the second-best, graciously, and let the best go unused

effects.log: You ask for it. The Hall relaxes, and the best cup is put away with a sigh of relief, and your tact is the talk of the evening.

events.text: On the roof of {b3_house}, at night, you find the Reader of Omens lying flat on her back with a blanket and a flask, watching the sky. She pats the tiles. "Sit," she says. "You are about to be told something, and it is easier lying down." The stars wheel. You sit.

choices.text: Lie down beside her and ask for the telling

effects.log: You lie. The telling is gentle, odd and far-reaching, and by dawn you and the Reader are friends, and you have a new thing to carry.

choices.text: Sit upright, and say you would rather not know

effects.log: You sit. She laughs, softly, and says that is the wisest thing, and tells you only the weather.

events.text: The grandmother of {b3_house}, a goddess so old that she is mostly a smell of camphor and an attitude, asks you in front of the entire Hall to name three gods of her Lineage who ever did anything useful. The Hall waits. The grandmother's eyes are very small and very bright. She is not joking.

choices.text: Name three, with a reason for each, and a flourish

effects.log: You name three. You have done your reading, and the grandmother nods, and says, "the fourth is a secret," and you are granted a place at her side.

choices.text: Name only one, and say the others are modest

effects.log: You name one. The Hall hums. The grandmother laughs, a dry laugh, and says, "that is the right number," and the Lineage thaws.

events.text: You are given a tour of the stables of {b3_house}, where the cloud-chariots are kept. The animals are unusual: great pale elk with antlers of branching light. A groom introduces each by name, and then, with a conspiratorial wink, offers you the reins of one for a short spin. The head is watching from a balcony.

choices.text: Take the reins and drive the elk gently round the yard

effects.log: You drive. The elk is serene and wise, and the yard is a blur of gold, and the head claps from the balcony.

choices.text: Decline, and stroke the elk's nose, and ask its name

effects.log: You stroke the nose. The elk breathes on your hand, and the groom says it has never done that, and the house hears of it.

events.text: At the end of your first day at {b3_house}, a servant leaves a note beneath your door. It reads, in careful handwriting: "do not trust the soup." The next morning there is no soup, and a different note: "do not trust the first note." You have no idea which of these is a joke, a warning, or a trap, and whether the house has more than one author.

choices.text: Ask the head of the house, openly, who writes the notes

effects.log: You ask. The head looks at you with great gravity and says: "which one?" and you are not sure you have been answered.

choices.text: Eat the soup, and burn the notes in the lamp

effects.log: You eat it. It is excellent. The notes burn, and the house has the grace to look disappointed.

events.text: The head of {b3_house} takes you aside during your visit to say, in the manner of a person confiding a secret that is not one, that the Lineage does not like you. Not you personally: your pantheon. "But you," the head says, looking at you straight, "are not a pantheon." There is a very long pause in which something is being decided.

choices.text: Say: "I am what I am, and I would like to be liked as such"

effects.log: You say so. The head nods, slowly, and the Lineage begins, from that evening, to see you as a god and not as a banner.

choices.text: Say: "I have not come to be liked, only to be heard"

effects.log: You say so. The head smiles with one side of the mouth, and you are heard, and respected, and not quite liked.

events.text: A tiny god of the Lineage of {b3_house}, no bigger than a hand, attaches himself to your shoulder on your arrival and rides there for the whole visit, commenting on everyone. He is a god of small observations. His observations are devastating and accurate. The Lineage seems to find this normal and rather affectionate.

choices.text: Ask the tiny god what he makes of you

effects.log: He tells you, at some length, to your face and to the whole Hall. You are dumbfounded, and he is right on every point.

choices.text: Politely ask him to keep his remarks for the stairs

effects.log: He does. On the stairs he is a torrent, and you carry him down like a very small, very candid judge.

events.text: The Lineage of {b3_house} asks all guests to sign the Book of Visitors with a verse. You are bad at verse. The book is open at a page where a previous guest, a god of war, has written something rude, and a very beautiful goddess something gentle, and a god of thunder has simply drawn a storm. The pen is held out. The Hall is watching.

choices.text: Write a short, honest, rhymeless line

effects.log: You write one. It is plain and true, and the book is closed on it with a satisfied clap, and the head says it is the best entry in a century.

choices.text: Draw a bird next to the storm

effects.log: You draw one. It is a bad bird. The Hall loves it, and it is copied into the Lineage's crest the next year, as a joke that became a custom.

events.text: On your last evening at {b3_house} the head presents you with the choice of three gifts, wrapped, without labels. One is said to be worth a province. One is said to be worth a friend. One is said to be nothing at all. You may choose, and the Hall is dead quiet. The head's eyes are calm and kind and tell you nothing.

choices.text: Take the one that feels warmest in the hand

effects.log: You take it. It is the friend. The head nods, surprised and pleased, and the house, thereafter, is yours.

choices.text: Take the one that feels heaviest

effects.log: You take it. It is the province, or rather the deed to a small green valley, and the head says: "you may regret it," and you do not.

events.text: The Lineage seat of {b3_house} has a tradition that a guest who stays for nine nights must help with some work of the house. You have been there nine nights. You are handed a mop. The task is the washing of the front step, which has been washed, by custom, by every visitor for ten thousand years. It is a long, shallow, polished step, and it is wet.

choices.text: Wash the step with great care and no complaint

effects.log: You wash it. The step gleams, and the attendants look on, and the house learns that you are a guest who can be humbled.

choices.text: Wash it fast, and leave a flower on it

effects.log: You wash it fast. The flower is found by the head, who holds it thoughtfully, and the step is remembered as yours.

events.text: A stranger in the guest-hall of {b3_house} tells you, over a shared bench, that she has come to petition the head and has been waiting nineteen years. She is not bitter. She has a very good knitting project. She asks, mildly, whether a guest might be seen sooner. She is not asking for herself.

choices.text: Ask the head to hear her petition before your own audience

effects.log: You ask. The head, surprised, hears her, and the petition is a request for a lamp for her village. It is granted at once, and she weeps over her knitting.

choices.text: Wish her well, and keep your place in the queue

effects.log: You wish her well. She nods, without reproach, and goes on knitting, and the head hears her in the autumn.

events.text: The house of {b3_house} has a rule that every guest must be shown to the Wall of the Unnamed, where the Lineage keeps the names of gods it betrayed. Your guide stops before it and says nothing. There are many names. Some are recent. The guide looks at the floor.

choices.text: Read three names aloud, quietly, to the wall

effects.log: You read them. The guide breathes out, and the house, hearing, remembers that its shame can be spoken.

choices.text: Ask the guide who carved them, and why

effects.log: The guide says: "we did, to remember." You nod, and the Wall takes you in, for a moment, as a sort of family.

events.text: It rains at {b3_house} the whole length of your visit, a heavy warm rain that falls only on the roofs and not on the courtyard. The head apologises: it is the house's mood. They have not had an unclouded visit in six hundred years. A servant offers you an umbrella of cedar bark, with an ironic bow.

choices.text: Walk in the rain with the head, uncovered, and talk

effects.log: You walk. The rain is warm and the head talks, at last, of the thing that has been clouding the house for six hundred years.

choices.text: Take the umbrella and compliment the cedar

effects.log: You take it. It is a good umbrella. The house, hearing the compliment, is warmed, and the rain lightens by a degree.

events.text: On the road from {b3_house} an attendant overtakes you with a small basket, panting. It holds the remains of your dinner, wrapped in a cloth, and a note: "you left this." It is the sort of absurd, thoughtful courtesy that makes you realise the house has been watching you with care. It is also, of course, a message.

choices.text: Send back a basket of your own, with a better note

effects.log: You send one. The two baskets pass back and forth for a decade, and the Lineage and you are friends by correspondence.

choices.text: Eat the dinner on the road, and write a plain thank-you

effects.log: You eat it. The thank-you is plain, and the house prefers it to a clever one.

events.text: A very small dispute breaks out in the guest-hall of {b3_house}: whose turn it is to light the lamp. Three gods of the house, each polite, each in earnest, have a precise claim. They turn to you, the neutral visitor, to settle. It is, you realise, the real test of the visit, and nobody has said so.

choices.text: Light the lamp yourself, and set the turn by the guests' age

effects.log: You light it. The three accept, with the grace of those who have been rescued from themselves, and the house laughs.

choices.text: Ask them to light it together, hands touching

effects.log: They do. It is awkward and sweet, and the lamp is the brightest in the guest-hall for the rest of the visit.

events.text: The Lineage of {b3_house} asks you to witness a promise in its Hall of Names. A young god is to take the oath of the Line. The oath is long, old, unsparing. The young god falters in the middle. The Hall is silent. The head turns to you, the guest, and with a barely perceptible nod asks whether you will say the next line, as a courtesy.

choices.text: Say the line, quietly, from memory

effects.log: You say it. The young god recovers, and finishes, and weeps, and the house takes your help as a deep and discreet kindness.

choices.text: Shake your head, kindly, and let the young god find it

effects.log: You shake your head. The young god finds the line, alone, and is stronger for it, and the head nods to you, approving.

events.text: Your first month in the service of {b3_house} is spent at the Gate of Incense, tending the censers, and the steward, a brisk goddess of tallies, explains that the incense is graded by how much it hurts to lose. The cheapest is for the weak-hearted. The dearest is for the dying. You are given a little spoon.

choices.text: Learn the grades by smell, by the week's end

effects.log: You learn them. The steward watches you sniff the dearest, and say nothing, and she says: "good. You will do."

choices.text: Ask which of the grades the steward uses herself

effects.log: The steward looks at you for a long moment. "The middle," she says. "It is a mistake to feel too much." She does not smile.

events.text: In the service of {b3_house} you are made, for a season, the reader of the Lineage's prayers. The prayers are not for the Lineage: they are for a deep-sea god on the far side of the world, misdirected by a postal error of the gods ten thousand years ago. The prayers have piled in a corner. You read one aloud.

choices.text: Answer them all, in the Lineage's name, as a favour

effects.log: You answer them. The house is surprised and a little embarrassed, and the deep-sea god, when told, sends a pearl as large as a skull.

choices.text: Forward them with a letter to the proper god

effects.log: You forward them. The deep-sea god replies in a hundred years, with thanks, and a rather alarming offer of friendship.

events.text: The head of {b3_house} sends you for a year to the lowest shrine of the Lineage, a hill-top affair with a leaking roof and three exhausted priests. You are told to find out why the offerings have fallen. The roof is the reason. So is the priest who sleeps through the dawn. So, partly, is the god.

choices.text: Mend the roof, wake the priest, and speak to the god

effects.log: You do all three. The offerings return, and the god of the shrine, who has not been spoken to in a century, is a sensitive, shy sort, and cries.

choices.text: Report back to the head on the shrine's state and let them act

effects.log: You report. The head, who had expected a miracle, is quiet, and the shrine is mended at the Lineage's expense.

events.text: You are lent to the Herald of {b3_house} for a season, to learn the calling of names. It is a harder art than it looks. Each name has a weight, a breath and a pitch, and a mistake is an insult to the dead. The Herald corrects you for six weeks without a word of praise, and on the seventh says: "that one was almost right."

choices.text: Take the correction, and call the same name until it is right

effects.log: You call it until you can sleep to it. On the thirtieth day the Herald says nothing, which is, you now understand, praise.

choices.text: Ask the Herald to teach you the oldest name instead

effects.log: The Herald does, slowly, in a whisper, and the name is longer than a breath. You learn it, and tell no one.

events.text: A year in {b3_house} teaches you its hierarchy of silences. There is the silence of the head, of the steward, of the aunts, and each says something different. You are learning to read them as one reads weather. By winter, the silence of the cook is the loudest in the house, and you are not sure why.

choices.text: Befriend the cook, and learn what the silence means

effects.log: You do. The cook is silent from grief, for a child lost nine hundred years ago, and you carry a dish to the child's pillar every year after.

choices.text: Keep to your own duties, and listen

effects.log: You listen. The silence resolves itself into a pattern, and you are wiser than the steward by spring, and say nothing.

events.text: In the service of {b3_house} you are made keeper of the lamps in the north gallery. The lamps burn for gods who have gone out of the world. One burns brighter than it should; its god has been dead four thousand years. The head of the house walks past it each night, and does not look.

choices.text: Ask the head about the bright lamp, privately

effects.log: You ask. The head says: "that is my sister, and I have not forgiven her," and goes on walking, and next night, pauses.

choices.text: Trim the lamp to burn with the others, and say nothing

effects.log: You trim it. It flares up again at midnight, defiant, and the head, passing, says only "thank you for trying."

events.text: You are sent by {b3_house} to collect an overdue offering from a hill-village. The village, you find, is at war with itself over a well, and its priest has fled. The people are polite, tired and hungry. They have no offering. They have a well. They have a grievance against the Lineage, which they air in a long, patient list.

choices.text: Hear the list, and mend the well-quarrel before collecting anything

effects.log: You hear it out. The well is mended, the quarrel quieted, and the offering, when it comes, is a gift and not a due.

choices.text: Collect what is owed in kind, and leave a note of regret

effects.log: You collect it. The village gives, grudging, and your note is read aloud at the well, in silence.

events.text: The steward of {b3_house} asks you, in the service year, to draw up a map of the Lineage's quarrels, who owes what to whom. It is a map of ten thousand years of grievance and it takes three seasons. By the end the map covers a wall. The steward looks at it for a long time and says: "we are not so bad."

choices.text: Mark each quarrel with a small gold dot where it was settled

effects.log: You mark them. The wall glitters, and the house sees, for the first time, how much it has forgiven.

choices.text: Keep the map in plain ink, and offer it to the head

effects.log: You offer it. The head hangs it in the hall, and refers to it, quietly, in every dispute for a century.

events.text: You spend a season guarding the Oracle Pool of {b3_house}. The work is dull until a night when a figure rises from the Pool, wet, silver, and asks you for a towel. It is the Pool's own spirit, who has not been out in nine thousand years, and wishes to look at the moon. You have no authority to refuse.

choices.text: Give it your cloak and walk with it by the water

effects.log: You give the cloak. The spirit walks, looks at the moon, and goes back in, and the Pool, thereafter, is a little clearer, and a little warmer for you.

choices.text: Tell it that the Pool needs it, and ask it to wait for the head

effects.log: The spirit sighs, and waits. The head, when told, is aghast, and orders the moon to be brought to the Pool for one night a year.

events.text: The head of {b3_house} sends you into the lower stacks of the Lineage's archive to fetch a book. You come back with the wrong one. It is a book of lullabies, in the Lineage's own hand, signed by a god of war. The head looks at it for a long time, and takes it, and says, "I had forgotten."

choices.text: Ask the head to read one aloud

effects.log: The head does, hoarsely. It is a lullaby of a god of war to a child, and the house, listening, is very still.

choices.text: Return to the stacks for the right book, and say nothing

effects.log: You go. When you come back the head has the lullabies on the desk, and a small, private, absent look.

events.text: A season of your service in {b3_house} is spent teaching the Lineage's young. They are brilliant, spoiled and bored. The lesson of the day is patience. You tell them a story. The youngest, a girl-god of mice, asks whether patience is not just fear with good manners. You realise you do not know.

choices.text: Say you do not know, and ask the class to find out

effects.log: You ask them. The class works at it for a month, and the answer they bring back is better than yours.

choices.text: Say it is the same as courage, held still

effects.log: You say so. The girl-god writes it down, and in a century, quotes it to a Throne.

events.text: The house of {b3_house} sends you to a convocation as its proxy. You are to sit in a corner and say nothing. A quarrel breaks out between two Thrones over a disputed river. Both look at your seat. The house you represent is the only one the Thrones both trust. Everyone is waiting for you to be the house.

choices.text: Speak for the house, in a few precise words

effects.log: You speak. The quarrel stops, startled, and the river is shared, and the house is credited with a peace you made.

choices.text: Remain silent, and let the Thrones settle themselves

effects.log: You remain. They settle, grumbling, and the house, told of it, is touched by your discretion.

events.text: The stores of {b3_house} are in turmoil: the kitchen accounts and the shrine accounts have been swapped, and the Keeper of the Offerings is weeping into a ledger. You are given a week to unscramble it. The task is both dull and delicate. By the third day you have discovered a fraud of nine hundred years' standing, and a very sad, small motive.

choices.text: Confront the fraud's author with the evidence, in private

effects.log: You do. The author, a retired god of grain, confesses, and the Lineage forgives, and you are the one who made it kind.

choices.text: Report it to the Keeper in writing, with the facts and no judgment

effects.log: You report. The Keeper reads it twice, and takes the matter in hand, and your cool report is a model for others.

events.text: Your service at {b3_house} includes a night vigil by the cradle of a sick child-god of the Lineage, a baby with a fever of stars. The parents have gone to sleep for the first time in a week. The baby burns, softly, and every so often hiccups, and a star falls out of the window. You catch some in a cup.

choices.text: Sing the baby the lullaby of your own childhood

effects.log: You sing. The fever breaks in the small hours, and the baby sleeps, and the stars in the cup glow on the sill until morning.

choices.text: Keep the cup of stars safe, and wake the parents at the first sign

effects.log: You keep watch. The parents wake, and the baby does, and the stars are hung over the cradle, and the house never forgets.

events.text: You are lent to the Warden of the Domain Gate of {b3_house} to help with a surge of petitioners from a flood-struck region. They fill the stair, the court, the roofs. They are quiet and frightened. The Warden has a list. The list has room for forty. There are nine thousand.

choices.text: Open the courtyard and the Hall of Offerings to the petitioners

effects.log: You open them. The house is a refuge for a week, and the Warden, who protested, brings out the good soup.

choices.text: Triage with the Warden, fairly, by need, and send heralds for the rest

effects.log: You triage. It is a long and thankless night, and the Warden, at dawn, shakes your hand without a word.

events.text: In the service of {b3_house} you are given the task of copying the Lineage's genealogy for a visiting scholar. Midway through the third volume you find an entry for a god who does not appear in any other record, with a single line: "lost on purpose." The date is 4,000 years ago. The ink is fresh.

choices.text: Ask the scholar if the entry is known to them

effects.log: The scholar goes pale. "That is my grandmother," they say, "and the Lineage has been looking for her for 4,000 years." The mystery thickens, and you are in it.

choices.text: Copy the entry as written and say nothing

effects.log: You copy it. The scholar leaves with the volume, and you hear, a century later, what became of the lost.

events.text: The Lineage of {b3_house} sends you with a long-awaited dowry to a distant Lineage for a marriage. The journey is two years. The dowry is a chest of lamps and a very old, very rude parrot. The parrot talks. The parrot has opinions about the marriage, and about the bride's family, and about you.

choices.text: Gag the parrot politely with a blanket for the final week

effects.log: You gag it. It sulks, but the marriage goes on, and the parrot is later seen, amid the wedding guests, spitting out the blanket and holding forth.

choices.text: Let the parrot speak at the wedding, and trust the families

effects.log: You let it speak. The wedding is saved by the parrot's honesty, and it is given a ribbon.

events.text: The steward of {b3_house} asks you to take over the evening reading of the Roll of the Faded. It is a long list of gods the house has lost. The reading is done aloud, each night, and the reader is expected to remember something of each. You have not met any of them. You are given a lamp and a stool.

choices.text: Read it slowly and ask the old attendants for a word on each

effects.log: You read. The attendants, one by one, murmur a word, and by midwinter the Roll is a living thing.

choices.text: Read it plainly, with respect, and no embellishment

effects.log: You read it. The attendants nod, and the Roll is read with a quiet that is more eloquent than any story.

events.text: In your year with {b3_house}, the Lineage faces an inspection by a delegation from the Silent Hall. The delegation will spend a week and notice everything. The house is in a flap. You are asked to be the guide. They want a quiet, plain, honest face. They do not want you to say anything memorable. The Silent Hall arrives.

choices.text: Guide them truthfully, and let the house speak for itself

effects.log: You guide them. The delegation notices everything, and writes it down, and the report, in the end, is kind.

choices.text: Guide them smoothly, and steer them from the worst corners

effects.log: You steer them. The report is fair, and the corners are quietly mended, and you are very tired.

events.text: The head of {b3_house} sends you to bring back a runaway: the Lineage's youngest, a boy-god of kites, who has left home for a life as a clown at a mortal fair. The boy is happy. He is good at it. The fair is a joy. The head wants him back. You are sitting in the front row, with a bag of sweets.

choices.text: Watch the whole show, then go and talk to the boy

effects.log: You watch. The boy is brilliant. You talk. You return with a message: "I will come home for the Feast, and go back after."

choices.text: Bring him home as ordered, and plead his case to the head

effects.log: You bring him. The head, hearing the plea, sulks for a month, and then buys tickets.

events.text: You are asked to take the night shift at the gate-house of {b3_house}, and a figure arrives at the third hour, cloaked, with a heavy chest, and asks to be let in quietly. The figure says it is the Lineage's own exiled elder, back with a gift. The Warden is off duty. The rule says to wake the head. The figure says please not.

choices.text: Let the figure in, and wake the head gently afterward

effects.log: You let them in. The head, woken, comes down in a dressing-gown, and the reunion is, you gather, a long-awaited one.

choices.text: Keep the figure at the gate until the head can be woken

effects.log: You keep them. It is cold, and the figure shivers, and the head arrives and is moved by your care.

events.text: The house of {b3_house} has a small, secret custom: on the longest night, the service-gods swap places with the Officers, and the Officers do the dishes. You are, by chance, the Officer's Officer for the night. A trembling Archivist is handed the apron. You have never seen anyone so afraid of a pot.

choices.text: Show the Archivist how to scour a pot, patiently

effects.log: You show them. The Archivist, flushed and wet to the elbow, discovers that there is a pleasure in it, and the dishes are clean.

choices.text: Take the pot yourself, and keep the Archivist company

effects.log: You scour. The Archivist talks, at last, of the Archive, and it is the first time you hear what they love in it.

events.text: During your service in {b3_house}, the Lineage goes into mourning for its eldest. The funeral is a three-day affair in which every attendant must sing a verse. You have no verse. The steward hands you a slip of paper with the first line: "He was not an easy man." The rest, she says, is up to you.

choices.text: Sing a true, unflattering verse, kindly

effects.log: You sing. The house, startled, laughs through its tears, and the verse is added to the funeral song.

choices.text: Sing the traditional verse, as practised

effects.log: You sing it. The house nods, and the funeral goes on, and you are one of the family for those three days.

events.text: In your year at {b3_house}, a lesser god of the Lineage is accused of an indiscretion. You are asked to sit as one of three judges. The accused is a mild, sad god of the evening who, it turns out, did it for love. The two other judges want a harsh sentence. They look at you for the swing vote.

choices.text: Argue for mercy, and a year of service in the gardens

effects.log: You argue. The sentence is mercy, and the garden is the evening god's for a year, and he plants a tree for each of you.

choices.text: Vote with the others for the harsher term, and hate it

effects.log: You vote with them. The term is served, and the god returns subdued, and the house is orderly and cold.

events.text: A dispute over a boundary stone comes to {b3_house}, and you are sent as the house's eyes. The stone is on a barren hill. Both claimants are gods of the same Line, brothers, aged twelve thousand. Each brings his own surveyor. Both surveyors are the same god, wearing different hats.

choices.text: Declare the stone moves a hand's breadth each year, and so settles nothing

effects.log: You declare it. The brothers laugh, sheepishly, and meet at the stone every year after to put it back.

choices.text: Settle it by the old measure, and plant a tree on the line

effects.log: You settle it. The tree is planted, the brothers wearily shake hands, and the hill is no longer barren.

events.text: The head of {b3_house} has you read, aloud, the Lineage's accounts of faith to a hall full of drowsy Officers. Halfway through the third year of figures, you notice a pattern: the faith has been falling for forty years in one region. No one has said so. Everyone has noticed. The Officers are watching you to see what you will do with it.

choices.text: Say the pattern aloud, plainly, to the whole Hall

effects.log: You say it. The Hall stirs, and the region is attended to, and the head thanks you in front of everyone.

choices.text: Whisper it to the head after the reading, privately

effects.log: You whisper. The head acts without saying so, and the Hall learns to respect your tact.

events.text: You are lent by {b3_house} to a mortal king, in disguise, as an adviser, for a year. The king is a boy of fifteen, anxious and proud, and his council is full of wolves. The Lineage wants the realm kept stable. The boy asks you, in private, whether he should trust his uncle. You are the god in the room.

choices.text: Tell him to trust no one for a year, and watch

effects.log: You tell him. He watches. The uncle is, in the end, loyal, and the boy learns to look, which is better than trust.

choices.text: Tell him to trust his own judgment, and let him err

effects.log: You tell him. He errs, and recovers, and by year's end the council respects him.

events.text: The Lineage of {b3_house} puts you on the night-watch of its sleeping ancestor. The cave is cold, swept, still. You sit with a lamp and a book. In the small hours the ancestor mutters a word. It is a name. You do not know it. You write it in the margin, and the lamp gutters, and the cave seems to listen.

choices.text: Tell the head of the house the name you heard

effects.log: You tell the head. The head is silent for a long time. It is the name of a god the house believed had gone without trace.

choices.text: Keep the name to yourself, and wonder

effects.log: You keep it. For years you carry it, and whisper it sometimes, and, once, in a far place, you meet its owner.

events.text: The steward of {b3_house} gives you the key to the Lineage's private library and tells you not to open the seventh door. For a year you do as you are told. In the twelfth month a small, bright voice calls from behind the seventh door: "please." It is a child's voice, and quite cheerful, and you are the only one in the corridor.

choices.text: Open the seventh door, a crack, and look

effects.log: You open it. It is a child-god, shut in by an error nine hundred years old, and cheerful, and hungry. You give it your lunch.

choices.text: Fetch the steward and let them open it

effects.log: You fetch her. She turns grey, opens the door, and the child bounds out, and the house is in an uproar for a week.

events.text: The house of {b3_house} asks you, in your year of service, to compose a hymn for the dedication of a new shrine. You are not a poet. The deadline is ten days. The shrine is in a marsh, and the god of the shrine is a heron. You go to the marsh, and sit on a stump, and the heron looks at you with great suspicion.

choices.text: Write the hymn in the heron's own idiom, a long silence and a splash

effects.log: You write it. It is mostly silence. The dedication is the quietest on record, and the heron, deeply moved, takes a step closer.

choices.text: Write a plain hymn, and sing it at dawn to the marsh

effects.log: You sing. It is a bad hymn, and the marsh enjoys it, and the heron, at the end, flaps once.

events.text: In the service of {b3_house} you are made steward of the guest-hall for a season. Your first guest is a god of death, tall, grey, and unexpectedly shy. He asks for tea and a quiet room. He says he is on holiday. He looks, over the rim of the cup, deeply tired. The other guests are edging away from him down the corridor.

choices.text: Seat him at your own table, and talk about nothing

effects.log: You do. He talks about gardening, and laughs once, and the other guests, seeing it, drift back, and he is, for a week, simply a guest.

choices.text: Give him the quiet room and leave him alone

effects.log: You do. He leaves a note of thanks on the pillow, and a single white flower that does not wilt.

events.text: The head of {b3_house} sends you to inspect a vineyard on a distant slope that is said to be producing sour grapes. You find a perfectly good vineyard, and a vintner god in despair. The grapes are not sour; they have been secretly tasting of every grief the vintner ever had. He cannot sell it. He cannot stop it. He offers you a glass.

choices.text: Drink the glass, and listen to the vintner's story

effects.log: You drink. It tastes of a house you lost, and a person, and a spring, and you listen to the vintner until dawn.

choices.text: Suggest he sell it as medicine for the grieving

effects.log: He thinks about it. By next autumn the vineyard is a place of quiet pilgrimage, and the vintner a sort of healer.

events.text: You are put in charge of the cloud-chariots of {b3_house} for the season. One of them is old, wilful and rude, and bolts with you across the sky at the worst possible moment: over a convocation, a wedding, and the sacred precincts of the Thrones. You are holding the reins with both hands. Below, a hundred gods look up.

choices.text: Wave, graciously, at the Thrones, and land with dignity

effects.log: You wave. The chariot comes down, bruised and rueful, and the Thrones, watching, applaud, and the house is the talk of the season.

choices.text: Haul the reins hard and bring it down on the nearest cloud

effects.log: You haul. The chariot lands with a crash in a field of wildflowers, and you are lightly bruised, and the field is sacred ever after.

events.text: The Lineage of {b3_house} asks you to take charge of its annual census of worship: a wearisome tour of a thousand shrines to count the faithful. The count is a polite fiction; the Lineage has always rounded up. You find that one shrine has far more worshippers than reported, and another far fewer. The numbers will cause a stir.

choices.text: Report the real figures, shrine by shrine, with a gentle preface

effects.log: You report. The head, reading, is quiet, and then reorganises the Lineage's priorities, and thanks you for the honesty.

choices.text: Round the figures as the Lineage has always done, and note the oddities in a margin

effects.log: You round them. The margin is read, and acted on, quietly, and the peace is kept.

events.text: The Lineage of {b3_house} sends you to mend a quarrel between its two oldest shrines, which have not exchanged a bow in a thousand years. Their priests are courteous, cold and exact. Each recites the grievance, which begins before either was built. A third party, a small god of stairs, has been waiting between them to be asked.

choices.text: Ask the god of stairs what they have seen of the quarrel

effects.log: The stair-god has seen all of it, and tells you, quietly, that it began over a borrowed ladder. You send a ladder to each, and the bows resume.

choices.text: Walk between the shrines every day for a season until they meet you halfway

effects.log: You walk. By the third month the priests are walking too, and meet at the stair, and are embarrassed, and bow.

events.text: You spend a year as a night-reader of the Oracle Pool of {b3_house}, which means sitting by it, awake, noting what it shows. Most nights it shows nothing. On the two-hundredth night it shows your own hand, writing the note you are about to write. You put down the pen, and the Pool shows your hand, putting down the pen.

choices.text: Write the note anyway, and see what the Pool does

effects.log: You write it. The Pool shows nothing for a month, and then a long, unexpected image of a person you have not met, laughing.

choices.text: Walk away from the Pool for the night, and report it in the morning

effects.log: You walk. The report is received with raised brows, and the Pool, the next night, shows only the moon.

events.text: A famine in the hills below {b3_house} sends a stream of the faithful to the Lineage's gate, begging not for rice but for a word of reassurance. You are the one at the gate, with a ledger of rice and a heavy heart. The Keeper of the Offerings cannot spare a grain, by the rules. The faithful, in the cold, are counting heads.

choices.text: Break the rule quietly and open the stores

effects.log: You open them. The Keeper finds out, and says nothing, and pays the debt out of her own cup for a century.

choices.text: Give them a word, a prayer, and a promise to plead to the head

effects.log: You plead. The head, hearing, opens the stores in a day, and the faithful never learn how close it was.

events.text: The head of {b3_house} has you play the part of the Lineage in a rehearsal of a trial before the Thrones. Another servant plays the accuser. The accuser is good. The accuser knows the Lineage's weak points. It becomes clear, in the second hour, that the accuser is the head, in a wig, to see how you hold.

choices.text: Hold the line, calmly, answering every charge with the Lineage's own record

effects.log: You hold. The head removes the wig with a smile and says, "the Thrones will not be so kind," and you are given a seat at the table.

choices.text: Break character and ask the head what they are really afraid of

effects.log: You ask. The head, startled, answers truthfully, and the rehearsal becomes a conversation, and the real trial is better prepared.

events.text: You are asked to take down the old banners from the hall of {b3_house} for cleaning. Behind the oldest you find a small door, no higher than your waist, with a child's hand-print in dried paint upon it. The steward, when told, goes still. "That was the nursery," she says. "We bricked it up after the war."

choices.text: Ask permission to open the door, and clean what is inside

effects.log: You open it. Inside are the toys of children long gone, and the house, hearing, weeps, and keeps a single shelf.

choices.text: Leave the door shut, and hang the banner back with care

effects.log: You hang it. The steward thanks you, in a small voice, and you know that you have been trusted with a secret.

events.text: On the last night of your service with {b3_house}, the head invites you to sit at the family table for the first time. It is a plain meal. The head says nothing of your year. The Officers pass the dishes in silence. At the end, the youngest god of the house puts a small stone by your plate: a river-pebble, with a hole in it, for luck.

choices.text: Thank the youngest, and wear the stone on a thread

effects.log: You wear it. The house sees you leave with it round your neck, and counts you one of theirs.

choices.text: Ask the head, over the plates, what the year has meant to the house

effects.log: The head answers, briefly, honestly. It is the best thing said to you in an age, and you carry it for a thousand years.

events.text: The cave is cold and swept. {b3_anc} sits at the back of it with eyes shut and one hand open on a knee, and on the open hand a spider has spun a small web with great care. On the floor, a bowl of this morning's rice. Nothing about the sleeper has aged. The sweeper, an old goddess, has not stirred from her post at the mouth.

choices.text: Sit across from {b3_anc} and wait for something

effects.log: You sit through the afternoon. The spider finishes a thread. The sleeper does not wake. But you understand you were looked at, once, from very far in.

choices.text: Leave an offering of your own and go quietly

effects.log: You leave a cup of libation. In the morning the sweeper pours it on the floor of the cave, and nods, and the cave smells of rain.

events.text: The sweeper of the back mountain, a goddess too old to give her age, is on her knees at the mouth of the cave with a broom, sweeping a floor already clean. She says the house of {b3_house} has paid for this sweeping every morning since before it had a name. She asks you, not unkindly, not to disturb the dust on the sleeper's side.

choices.text: Take a second broom and help her

effects.log: You sweep. The floor was already clean, and you sweep it anyway, and she tells you, grudgingly, her name.

choices.text: Ask how long she has swept, and why

effects.log: She tells you: since the last god of her Line died, and the sleeper was left. It is a long answer, and you listen to all of it.

events.text: On the wall of the cave behind {b3_anc} are scratches: tallies, in groups of nine, hundreds of thousands of them. Someone has been marking days, or years, or breaths. The most recent is fresh. The sleeper's open hand has a tiny callus on the forefinger. The sleeper is counting in their sleep.

choices.text: Add one scratch to the wall, in the old style

effects.log: You add it. The sleeper's finger twitches, once. You leave the cave wondering whether you have helped or interrupted.

choices.text: Count the tallies, and carry the number back to {b3_house}

effects.log: You count: 41,000 groups of nine. The Lineage, hearing, is silent, for the number is an ancient date.

events.text: A deer has wandered into the cave of {b3_anc}, and lies down across the sleeper's feet. It has done so for centuries, says the sweeper; it is the fourth of the line. The deer opens one eye at you, closes it. The cave is warm. The deer has the bearing of a creature on a long, comfortable guard.

choices.text: Kneel and offer the deer a handful of barley

effects.log: You offer it. The deer takes it with polite indifference, and the sweeper smiles for the first time.

choices.text: Step round the deer and look closely at the sleeper's face

effects.log: You look. It is a calm face, and an unfinished one, as if a thought had been put aside for a moment.

events.text: A spring rises in the corner of the cave of {b3_anc}, clear, silent, welling over a lip of stone into a pool the size of a wash-basin. It never overflows. The sweeper says it is the sleeper's breath, condensed. She says that to drink from it is a form of intimacy. She says it with a strict face.

choices.text: Drink a cupful, and bow to the sleeper

effects.log: You drink. It tastes of nothing, and of morning, and you walk down the mountain with a clear head and a foolish smile.

choices.text: Do not drink; wash your hands in it, as a courtesy

effects.log: You wash. The water is cold and slow and good, and the sweeper nods, since this is the safer respect.

events.text: On a stone shelf in the cave of {b3_anc} are letters: thousands of them, from the Line, left over the ages, addressed to the sleeper. They are petitions, confessions, jokes. A few are open. The sweeper says the sleeper has read none. The sweeper says she reads them aloud, on feast days, for company.

choices.text: Read one letter aloud to the sleeper, yourself

effects.log: You read one. It is from a god, nine thousand years ago, complaining about a neighbour. It is very funny, and you laugh in a cave that has not heard laughter in ages.

choices.text: Leave a letter of your own among them

effects.log: You write one. It is short and honest, and you leave it on the shelf. You will never know whether it was read.

events.text: The back mountain above {b3_house} has a path swept by someone nobody ever sees. At its end, the cave of {b3_anc}. You arrive at dawn and the path is clean, though no one has passed. At the cave the sweeper is not at her post. A small cup of tea, still warm, is set at the mouth of the cave, and a second cup beside it, for you.

choices.text: Drink the tea, and wait for the sweeper

effects.log: You drink it. The sweeper arrives after an hour, out of breath, and says she did not know she would have company.

choices.text: Leave the tea untouched, and go in alone

effects.log: You go in. The sleeper is as ever, and the tea cools, and when you come out the cup is empty and the sweeper at her post.

events.text: The air in the cave of {b3_anc} changes when you step across a certain line of stones: a pressure behind the ears, a hum, a light like the one before thunder. The sweeper tells you most visitors stop here. The ones who do not, she says, come out with gentler faces. She says it without recommending either.

choices.text: Cross the line of stones, and sit down in the hum

effects.log: You cross. The hum is enormous, and you sit in it for an hour, and when you stand your hands are steady and your tongue is slow.

choices.text: Stay at the line, and listen from there

effects.log: You stay. The hum comes to you in pieces, and you learn one thing: it is not meant for you, and it is, anyhow, kind.

events.text: Painted on the roof of the cave of {b3_anc}, in a style older than the house, is a mural: a figure, enormous, holding a lit lamp over a darkened plain. Below, tiny figures turn their faces up. The lamp has a crack in it, and from the crack, the painter has left a thin line of gold dripping down the stone, which is real gold.

choices.text: Trace the gold line with a finger to the floor

effects.log: You trace it. It ends at the sleeper's open hand, where the spider has caught a single bead of gold in its web.

choices.text: Sit and study the mural until the light changes

effects.log: You sit for a day. The tiny figures seem to turn, with the light, and by evening you understand what they are asking for.

events.text: A young god of {b3_house} is already at the cave of {b3_anc}, on his knees, whispering. He looks up, caught, and goes scarlet. He says he comes every night to read to the sleeper. He says it is a secret, and he would be grateful. He reads from a book of poems he wrote himself. He asks, shyly, what you think.

choices.text: Listen to a poem, and tell him honestly what you think

effects.log: You listen. It is rough, sincere and good, and you tell him which lines are best, and he is rapt.

choices.text: Tell him his secret is safe, and leave him to his reading

effects.log: You leave. He is grateful, and the poems, you learn in time, grow better by the year.

events.text: The rice offered to {b3_anc} each morning is, the sweeper confides, always eaten by night. By what, nobody knows. She has watched, and fallen asleep, three nights running. Tonight she asks you to keep watch with her, since she says you have the face of someone who stays awake. The bowl is full, steaming. The cave is dark.

choices.text: Keep watch with her, and see who eats the rice

effects.log: You watch. At the third hour, the sleeper's open hand twitches, and a single grain rises, and vanishes. You say nothing to anyone but the sweeper.

choices.text: Eat a handful of the rice yourself, as an experiment

effects.log: You eat. It tastes of an old, plain comfort. The sweeper says nothing, and the next morning the bowl is full and untouched.

events.text: The cave of {b3_anc} has a visitor's book. Not for gods: for the faithful who, over the ages, have climbed the mountain and stood at the mouth to pray. Their names go back ten thousand years. Most are mortal. Most are ordinary. The sweeper turns the pages for you, slowly. A recent entry reads: "I have nothing to ask. I only wanted to say that I came."

choices.text: Sign the book yourself, in the plainest hand you have

effects.log: You sign. The book is closed gently, and the sweeper puts it back in its niche, as if a small, pleasing thing had occurred.

choices.text: Read the book backwards, a few pages, in silence

effects.log: You read. The names go back and back. By the last page you are weeping a little, and the sweeper offers you her handkerchief.

events.text: There is an echo in the cave of {b3_anc}, a deep, delayed echo that returns your words a little changed. You say "hello." The echo returns "hello, child." You say "I am no child." The echo says "not yet." The sweeper, in the corner, stirs her tea and pretends to hear nothing.

choices.text: Ask the echo a question and hear what returns

effects.log: You ask: "who are you?" The echo returns the same question, and then, after a pause, a different one: "who are you, to ask?" You leave without an answer.

choices.text: Whisper a secret to the echo, and listen to it come back

effects.log: You whisper. The echo returns it, gentler, and lighter, and you leave a little unburdened.

events.text: A band of mortal pilgrims is camped outside the cave of {b3_anc}, dozens of them, singing very softly. They do not know whose cave it is. They know only that the mountain is holy, and that the sweeper once gave one of them a cup of water. They are polite, grave and poor. They offer you a share of their bread.

choices.text: Share their bread and sit with them in the singing

effects.log: You share. The bread is coarse and sweet, and the singing is a lullaby, and you fall into a light, long sleep in the open air.

choices.text: Thank them, and quietly leave a store of rice and a lamp

effects.log: You leave them. They find them in the morning, and give thanks, to the mountain.

events.text: The sleeper {b3_anc} is not alone. On a ledge above, hidden from the mouth of the cave, a child sits in the dark, a mortal child, perhaps seven, with a lantern and a bowl of rice. The sweeper has not seen the child. The child puts a finger to the lips. The child has been coming, evidently, for a long time.

choices.text: Sit beside the child and share the lantern

effects.log: You sit. The child whispers that the sleeper snores, softly, on the second night of each month, and you listen for it, together, in the dark.

choices.text: Tell the sweeper quietly, so the child can be fed and kept safe

effects.log: You tell her. The sweeper, shaken, climbs the ledge with a blanket and a bowl, and the child has two friends instead of one.

events.text: On the floor of the cave of {b3_anc}, between the sleeper's feet and the spring, lies a sword. It is plain, battered, and has not been drawn in an age. The sweeper does not sweep around it; she sweeps over it, tenderly, as if it were a sleeping animal. She says it is the sleeper's own, and has not been touched since the Line's first war.

choices.text: Lay a hand on the hilt, for the length of a breath

effects.log: You lay it. The sword is warm. You feel, for a second, the weight of a first war, and withdraw with your heart racing.

choices.text: Do not touch the sword; bow to it, and to the sleeper

effects.log: You bow. The sweeper nods, approving, and says: "the right answer to a sword is not to pick it up."
