events.text: The sweeper of the cave of {b3_anc} asks a favour of you: to carry a message down the mountain to the head of {b3_house}. It is a note, folded small. The message, she says, is the same one she has sent every year, and has never been answered. She doesn't ask you to read it. She asks you only to put it in the head's hand.

choices.text: Take it, deliver it, and ask for the head's reply

effects.log: You deliver it. The head reads it, and blanches, and says: "she has been asking me to visit for six thousand years." A visit is planned.

choices.text: Read it on the way down, and decide what to do

effects.log: You read it. It says only: "come up, I am lonely." You carry it to the head with a gentle word.

events.text: At the foot of the sleeper {b3_anc}, scratched into the floor, is a diagram, a design of nine circles and a line. The sweeper does not know what it means. The circles are not equal in size. One is much smaller than the others, and a thin thread of light connects it to the rest. It looks like a map. It looks like a family.

choices.text: Copy the diagram, and ask the Archivist of {b3_house} to read it

effects.log: You copy it. The Archivist stays up three nights, and says: it is a seating plan, for a dinner that was never held.

choices.text: Add a tiny tenth circle in chalk, beside the smallest

effects.log: You draw it. The thread of light, in the night, grows a fraction brighter, and you are not sure whether to be pleased.

events.text: The sleeper {b3_anc} snores. Only once a century, and softly, a sound like a distant river. You are in the cave when it happens. The sweeper stiffens, then smiles. The dust on the floor ripples. The spider stops. The cave seems to listen back. When it ends, the sweeper says, without turning, "you are the first to hear it who was not of the house."

choices.text: Bow to the sleeper, and thank the sweeper for the honour

effects.log: You bow. The sweeper presses your hand. Later the house of {b3_house} will know of it, and look at you with something close to awe.

choices.text: Sit quietly until the dust settles, and tell no one

effects.log: You sit. The dust settles. You keep your own counsel, and the memory of the sound.

events.text: Painted on the floor of the cave of {b3_anc} is a circle, worn almost away by feet. The sweeper says it is where visitors of the house stand to be seen by the sleeper. It is the one spot in the cave where the light falls just so. She asks whether you wish to stand in it. Her face says she hopes you do not.

choices.text: Stand in the circle, and be seen

effects.log: You stand. The light falls, and something old and calm looks you over, once, from a great distance, and the circle hums.

choices.text: Decline, and stand at the edge, where the light is gentler

effects.log: You stand at the edge. The sweeper breathes out, and says, "wise," and brings you tea.

events.text: {b3_anc} comes down the swept path without any hurry, and the Hall of {b3_house} empties around them like water from a basin. They stop in front of you and look you over once, from head to foot, as one regards a piece of furniture one has not seen moved. The first thing they say is "who let you in?"

choices.text: Answer: "the house did"

effects.log: You answer so. A long silence follows, and then {b3_anc} snorts, and the Hall, which had been holding its breath, lets it go.

choices.text: Answer: "nobody. I came because I could"

effects.log: You answer so. {b3_anc}'s eyes narrow, and then, very slightly, brighten, and the Hall is a little more frightened and a little more awake.

events.text: {b3_anc} wakes, and for a long moment looks confused. Then they see the head's seat, and you in it, and the confusion goes. "I slept so that this house would not need me," they say, "and it has needed me four times since breakfast." The Hall waits for a verdict, and the verdict, it appears, is going to be yours.

choices.text: Say the house has done well without them

effects.log: You say so. {b3_anc} considers it, with an exhausted dignity, and says: "then I shall be unnecessary a while longer," and sits.

choices.text: Admit the house did need them, and thank them for sleeping so long

effects.log: You admit it. {b3_anc} gives a short, rusty laugh, and the Hall relaxes, for the sleeper is not, after all, an executioner.

events.text: {b3_anc} stands in the doorway of the Hall of {b3_house}, still blinking, with a spider on their shoulder. The spider has made a very small hat of web. The Hall does not know whether to fall to its knees or to laugh. The Herald of the Line, trembling, begins to call the sleeper's titles. There are forty-one.

choices.text: Cut the Herald off, kindly, and ask the sleeper how they slept

effects.log: You cut in. {b3_anc} says: "badly, for four thousand years, and then very well." The Hall laughs, thinly, and the Herald sits down.

choices.text: Let the Herald finish all forty-one titles in full

effects.log: You let him. {b3_anc} listens to each, nodding, and at the thirtieth says, "that one was a mistake," and the Hall is utterly still.

events.text: When {b3_anc} wakes in the Hall of {b3_house}, the first thing that happens is that every vigil flame in the Hall lights itself, one after another, from the door to the high seat, and then, with a collective sigh, burns blue. The sleeper looks at them with great tenderness. The flames lean, like children, toward the sleeper.

choices.text: Kneel with the Hall, and let the flames do their work

effects.log: You kneel. The flames burn blue for an hour, and the Hall is hushed, and {b3_anc} lays a hand on your head, briefly, without a word.

choices.text: Stand, and meet the sleeper's eyes with all the calm you have

effects.log: You stand. {b3_anc} studies you for a long time and says: "stand a little longer," and you do, and the flames burn white.

events.text: {b3_anc} comes into the Hall of {b3_house} and goes directly to the pillars. They touch each in turn, as if checking a family. At the ninth they stop. A name has been struck out. They turn, slowly, to the head's seat, to you, and to the Officers, and say, very gently, "who did this?" The Hall of Names goes quiet as a held breath.

choices.text: Own up to it, if it was your doing, or the house's

effects.log: You say that the house struck it, long ago, and you inherited the shame. {b3_anc} nods, as at a hard answer, and the name is restored that day.

choices.text: Ask who the name belonged to, and why it was struck

effects.log: You ask. The Archivist answers, shaking, and {b3_anc} listens, and weeps, and the matter is not closed that day.

events.text: The sleeper {b3_anc} has woken in the Hall of {b3_house} and has demanded a bath. The Officers are aghast. The Hall hurries, in a flurry, to produce a tub, warm water, sandalwood. The sleeper steps behind a screen, and from behind it comes a long, shuddering sigh of great contentment. The Officers look at one another. This was not in the rites.

choices.text: Send a servant in with the sandalwood and the soap, and silence

effects.log: You send them. The sleeper emerges an hour later, pink and rejuvenated, and treats the Hall with unusual kindness all day.

choices.text: Speak through the screen, and ask what the sleeper needs

effects.log: You ask. A voice replies: "a good dinner and a clean shirt." The Hall rushes to supply both, and it is the shortest crisis of the age.

events.text: {b3_anc} walks the length of the Hall of {b3_house} and sits not in the high seat but on the bottom step of the dais, and pats the stone beside them. They say, "sit." The Officers hold their breath. This is where children sit. The sleeper wants you to sit at their side, below the high seat, in the dust. Nobody knows what this means.

choices.text: Sit beside the sleeper, on the step

effects.log: You sit. {b3_anc} nods, content, and says: "better," and the Hall realises it has been told something about thrones.

choices.text: Remain standing, politely, and ask to be excused the dust

effects.log: You stand. The sleeper shrugs, and says, "as you like," and the Hall relaxes, a little disappointed.

events.text: The sleeper {b3_anc} wakes in the Hall of {b3_house} and, to the horror of the Officers, begins to laugh. It is a huge, rolling, helpless laugh, the laugh of a person who has been told a joke ten thousand years ago and has just got it. The pillars rattle. The Hall stares. {b3_anc} wipes their eyes and says: "it was the cheese."

choices.text: Ask what cheese, and what joke

effects.log: You ask. The story is long, absurd and shared by the whole Hall within minutes, and {b3_anc} is carried to the high seat on a wave of laughter.

choices.text: Wait quietly for the laughing to subside, and offer a cup of water

effects.log: You wait. {b3_anc} drinks, and is calm, and says, "thank you, that was overdue," and the Hall breathes again.

events.text: When {b3_anc} wakes in the Hall of {b3_house}, the first thing they do is walk to the great doors and look out at the world. They look for a long time. The Officers wait. {b3_anc} says, "the mountains have moved," and the Archivist, ashen, says that is not possible. {b3_anc} says, "I know. I moved them, in my sleep."

choices.text: Ask the sleeper what else moved in the sleeping

effects.log: {b3_anc} lists, in order, seventeen things, including a river, a lake, and a person. The Hall is struck dumb, and you take notes.

choices.text: Ask only that the mountains be left where they are, from here

effects.log: {b3_anc} grunts, amused. "As you wish. I am tired of moving things." The Hall hears the promise and writes it down.

events.text: {b3_anc} wakes in the Hall of {b3_house}, and, before anything else, asks for the sweeper. The old goddess is fetched, breathless, still holding her broom. {b3_anc} rises, crosses the Hall, and takes her hands. "You kept the floor," they say. "I felt it." The sweeper bursts into tears. The Hall looks anywhere but at the two of them.

choices.text: Look away, and ask for tea for the three of you

effects.log: You ask for tea. It arrives. The three of you sit, and no one speaks, and it is the most honest hour the house has had.

choices.text: Offer the sweeper a seat in the Hall, by right, from this day

effects.log: You offer it. The Officers murmur, and {b3_anc} nods, and the sweeper becomes the first of her kind to sit at the table.

events.text: The first words of {b3_anc}, risen in the Hall of {b3_house}, are a question: "what year is it?" The Archivist gives the year. {b3_anc} closes their eyes and counts on their fingers. "Then I am late," they say, "for a wedding." They open them. "Whose is it?" Nobody in the Hall has the heart to tell them the groom is dust.

choices.text: Tell the truth, gently, and offer a libation to the groom

effects.log: You tell them. {b3_anc} is silent, and then pours the libation, and says, "then I shall go to the wedding of his grandson."

choices.text: Say the wedding has been postponed, and ask them to come and eat

effects.log: You say so. {b3_anc} sees through it, and takes your arm anyway, and the Hall is much moved.

events.text: {b3_anc} walks into the Hall of {b3_house} with eyes half-shut, as if still half asleep, and sits in the middle of the floor. The Officers, aghast, wait. {b3_anc} puts a hand on the stone, and says: "this is warm." It is the floor of the Hall. The Officers, in turn, touch it. It is. It has been warm since the sleeper came down.

choices.text: Kneel and lay your hand on the floor, with the sleeper

effects.log: You kneel. The floor is warm as a living thing, and for a moment you feel the Line in your hand, and let go with reluctance.

choices.text: Ask the sleeper what the warmth means

effects.log: {b3_anc} says: "it means they are glad." The Hall, hearing, falls into a long, shy quiet.

events.text: The Hall of {b3_house} has a ceremony for the waking of an ancestor, never used, written ten thousand years ago. It involves a trumpet, a bowl of salt and a child. The Officers rush to produce all three. The trumpet is blown. The salt is spilled. The child, a small, pale, solemn girl-god, steps forward, and says in a clear voice: "please wake up, you are very late."

choices.text: Let the child say it twice more, in her own words

effects.log: The child does. {b3_anc} listens, astonished, and then smiles, and gathers her into their lap.

choices.text: Thank the child, and bow to the sleeper on the Line's behalf

effects.log: You bow. {b3_anc} nods, touched, and the child is allowed to ride in the sleeper's hood for a week.

events.text: {b3_anc} walks to the high seat of {b3_house}, looks at it, and runs a finger along the back. "Hard," they say, "I always said it should be harder." There is a rustle in the Hall. A slow, dry look crosses their face. "Who sat here last?" The Archivist names the previous head. {b3_anc} nods. "A good seat for a bad man. Sit, child."

choices.text: Sit in the seat, as ordered, and keep your back straight

effects.log: You sit. {b3_anc} looks at you a long time, and says: "the seat is not so bad," and the Hall exhales.

choices.text: Ask whether the seat should be softened, now they are awake

effects.log: {b3_anc} blinks, and bursts into a dry delighted laugh, and a cushion is brought, and the Hall is utterly reformed.

events.text: The sleeper {b3_anc} wakes in the Hall of {b3_house} and, after one look at the Officers, asks to see the accounts. The accounts are brought in nine boxes. {b3_anc} reads for six hours without moving. At the end they close the last box and say, quite gently: "someone has been lying to you, and to me, for four thousand years, and it is not the person you think."

choices.text: Ask who, and prepare yourself for the answer

effects.log: {b3_anc} names someone. The Hall is shocked, then quiet, then oddly relieved, because it explains a great deal.

choices.text: Ask only that the truth be told in the morning, and not tonight

effects.log: {b3_anc} nods, and says that is wise. The Hall sleeps, uneasily, and wakes to a gentler truth.

events.text: When {b3_anc} wakes, the first living creature they greet in the Hall of {b3_house} is the cat. The cat has been the Hall's for eight hundred years. It leaps into the sleeper's lap, purring like a small engine, as if it had been waiting all its life. {b3_anc} says, to the cat, "I know," and the Hall is utterly still, and slightly in love.

choices.text: Leave the sleeper to the cat, and clear the Hall for the hour

effects.log: You clear it. An hour later the two are asleep together on the dais, and the Hall steals in on tiptoe.

choices.text: Offer the cat a dish of cream and the sleeper a cup of tea

effects.log: You offer both. The sleeper drinks, the cat laps, and the Hall is witness to an ancient understanding.

events.text: You sit, for the first time, in the head's seat of {b3_house}. It is a hard seat, deliberately; the founder thought comfort led to error. Down the table, a very old god of the blood has not touched his food. He is looking at you the way one looks at a stain on a good cloth. Nobody has spoken for a very long minute.

choices.text: Say a few plain words and offer the first libation

effects.log: You say them. The old god drinks, which is more than he intended, and the table breathes. The seat is no softer, but it is yours.

choices.text: Say nothing, and let the silence be your first act

effects.log: You say nothing. The silence stretches and bends, and the old god looks away first, and the house learns something about you.

events.text: The blood of {b3_house} do not bow to you in the Hall. They stand, correctly, fold their hands, and tilt their heads exactly one finger. It is a perfect, practised insult, and every child of the Line will remember being taught it. The Steward, at your side, murmurs that the blood needs time. The blood has all the time there is.

choices.text: Return the finger's tilt, to each, exactly

effects.log: You return it, to each, god by god. It takes an hour. By the end the blood are wary, which is progress.

choices.text: Bow to each, deeply, as a guest of the Lineage

effects.log: You bow. The blood are startled, then amused, and the Hall decides you are either a fool or a very clever guest.

events.text: The pillars of {b3_house} are hung with white cloth for the old head, whom you displaced. It is not a custom of mourning; it is a custom of reproach. The cloth hangs in every room. The servants pass it with their eyes down. In the Hall, the old head's chair has been left empty at the table, with a place laid and a cup of wine, untouched.

choices.text: Leave the chair, the place and the cup as they are for a year

effects.log: You leave them. The Hall takes this as courtesy, and in a year the cloth is taken down, and the chair is moved.

choices.text: Take the cup and raise it, and send for the old head to be honoured

effects.log: You raise it, and send. The old head comes to the Hall, stiff, and is seated at your right, and the Lineage mends by an inch.

events.text: On your first morning as head of {b3_house}, you wake to find your room full of gifts from the Lineage. They are lovely and useless: a lamp that sings, a cloak of mist, a bowl of ever-warm clay. A card in each is signed, in an identical hand, "with the Line's regard." You have the horrible suspicion that they are bribes in advance.

choices.text: Return every gift, with a courteous note, and keep the lamp

effects.log: You return them. The Lineage is nonplussed; the lamp sings on your desk, and the Steward permits herself a faint, appreciative cough.

choices.text: Accept the gifts, and place them all in the Hall for the Lineage to use

effects.log: You place them. The Lineage, deprived of its leverage, is scandalised and relieved.

events.text: The Herald of {b3_house} calls your name at the first Feast of Names under your headship, and gets it wrong. Not by a syllable: by a title. They have called you "the Interim." The Hall freezes. The Herald freezes. The Herald, who has been doing this for six thousand years, goes the colour of ash. You are the only person in the Hall who can move.

choices.text: Accept the title, with a smile, and make it the Interim until you are not

effects.log: You smile. The Hall laughs, relieved, and the title is used affectionately, in whispers, all year.

choices.text: Ask the Herald to say your name again, slowly, and wait

effects.log: The Herald says it, slowly, correctly, and bows. The Hall understands that your name is not to be fumbled twice.

events.text: The first petition to reach you as head of {b3_house} is from the blood themselves: a long, polite list of eleven requests. Nine are trivial. Two are grave. One of the grave ones would unmake a decision of your predecessor. The other would unmake a decision of your predecessor's predecessor. The Steward waits with a pen, and a face of perfect blankness.

choices.text: Grant the nine trivial ones at once, and study the grave ones

effects.log: You grant them. The blood, startled to be answered, wait for the others with a new respect.

choices.text: Grant none, and call the petitioners to the Hall to explain themselves

effects.log: You call them. The explanations are long, and uneven, and teach you more about the blood than the petition did.

events.text: At your first council as head of {b3_house}, a very young god in a very good robe rises to ask a question. It is a long, careful, reasoned question about the Lineage's policy toward the next Throne. It is, as you realise on the second sentence, a brilliant one. It is also a trap, laid by someone older, who has trained the young god to say it. The Hall is watching.

choices.text: Answer the question honestly, and name the trap

effects.log: You answer. The Hall holds its breath, and then the old god who laid the trap smiles, thinly, and the Hall relaxes, because you have been seen.

choices.text: Ask the young god what they think the answer is

effects.log: You ask. The young god, startled, answers in their own words, and it is better than the trap, and you adopt it.

events.text: The Warden of the Domain Gate of {b3_house} meets you at the threshold on your first day as head, and does not open the gate. He says there is a custom. A new head must be refused, once, to remind them that a gate is a decision. He asks you to wait. It is raining. The Hall, from the windows, watches the new head standing outside their own gate.

choices.text: Wait in the rain, and say nothing

effects.log: You wait. After an hour the Warden opens the gate and bows, and the Hall, which had been prepared to be disappointed, is not.

choices.text: Knock politely, and ask whether the custom has a time limit

effects.log: You knock. The Warden, a straight-faced man, says "the custom has no limit," and then opens the gate, and the Hall roars.

events.text: On the night you take the head seat of {b3_house}, you cannot sleep. You walk the halls. At the third hour you meet the Steward, also awake, carrying a candle. She says that nobody sleeps the first night of a new head. She says she has seen it nine times. She asks whether you would like to see something. You follow.

choices.text: Follow the Steward to what she wants to show you

effects.log: She shows you the Lineage's secret room: a small, plain chamber with a cot and a book, where every head has written one line. She hands you the pen.

choices.text: Ask her to show you tomorrow, in the daylight, and go to bed

effects.log: You go to bed. In daylight the room is plainer still, and the Steward is a little disappointed, and you are rested.

events.text: The elders of {b3_house} bring you, as head, the traditional gift: a key to the cellar of the oldest wine. The wine is eight thousand years old. They say you may drink it, or pour it out, or lay it down. They say the last head poured it out. The one before drank it all in a night. They say it with a gleam in their eyes.

choices.text: Open one bottle, and pour it for the elders in the Hall

effects.log: You open it and pour. The elders say the wine is thin and wonderful and tastes of a world that is gone, and they weep, and love you a little.

choices.text: Lay the wine down, unopened, for the next head

effects.log: You lay it down. The elders nod, a bit disappointed and a bit approving, and the cellar goes on keeping its secret.

events.text: A messenger arrives within the hour of your taking the seat of {b3_house}: from the Throne of the pantheon, with congratulations and, tucked beneath, a request. The Throne wants a favour of the new head, a small one, as a courtesy. It is, on inspection, an enormous one, hidden in a small request. The Steward reads over your shoulder and whistles through her teeth.

choices.text: Decline the hidden favour politely, and grant the small request

effects.log: You decline. The Throne receives the answer in a silence that is almost respect.

choices.text: Grant the favour, and ask a larger one in return

effects.log: You grant it. The Throne, impressed, grants yours, and the Line is a notch more tangled in the pantheon.

events.text: You find, on the head's desk in {b3_house}, a letter from your predecessor, left for you. It is four pages. The first three are advice, practical and wise. The fourth is a single line: "do not believe a word of the first three." You turn the pages over. There is nothing else. The old head, you recall, had a notorious sense of humour.

choices.text: Follow the first three pages for a year, and see

effects.log: You follow them. They work. The fourth line, you decide, was a joke on the reader, and the joke was on you.

choices.text: Follow the fourth line, and ignore the other three

effects.log: You ignore them. It goes badly for a month, then well, and you cannot tell which of the old head's pages was the joke.

events.text: The first act of a new head of {b3_house} is to light the Heart-Flame in the Hall, from which all the Lineage's flames are kindled. It has never gone out. It is a small thing, in a bowl, and as you reach for it, it flares, once, sharply, as if it knew you. The Steward breathes in. The flame settles. It has chosen to be touched.

choices.text: Cup your hands round the Heart-Flame, and warm them

effects.log: You warm them. The flame is gentle, and strangely familiar, and the Lineage, seeing it accept you, falls into a reverent hush.

choices.text: Light your taper from it, and carry it round the Hall

effects.log: You light it. The flame walks with you from lamp to lamp, and the Hall brightens, and the first night is warm.

events.text: A cousin of the blood of {b3_house} mocks you in the Hall in front of the young by repeating your own words in an exact, slow, cruel imitation. It is skilled. It is awful. The young are watching. The aunts have stopped chewing. The cousin knows precisely what is being risked, and is enjoying it.

choices.text: Laugh, and ask for the imitation again, in full

effects.log: You laugh. The cousin falters, caught between triumph and shame, and the young, who had expected a fight, laugh too.

choices.text: Rise, and answer in the cousin's own voice, perfectly

effects.log: You answer. The Hall is stunned, and then roars, and the cousin, red to the ears, sits down and does not do it again.

events.text: You have ruled {b3_house} for some years, and the blood still call you "the head" in a tone that means "for now." It is not hostility; it is an old, steady, unmoving patience. They will outlast you, they believe, and the believing is the strength of the Lineage. The Steward remarks, drily, that they are quite right.

choices.text: Plan a work for a century, and begin it

effects.log: You begin a work that will outlive you, a great library of the Lineage's voices. The blood watch, and begin, grudgingly, to contribute.

choices.text: Accept the tone, and rule lightly

effects.log: You rule lightly. The blood relax, in time, and the "for now" becomes, by degrees, "for as long as you like."

events.text: A matter comes before you as head of {b3_house} that the whole Lineage expects you to decide against the outsider you once were. A distant relative of the blood, a hard case, has come asking for the same chance you took. The blood are watching to see whether you will pull up the ladder.

choices.text: Give the relative a place, as you were given one

effects.log: You give it. The blood are startled by the generosity, and the relative becomes one of the house's steadiest hands.

choices.text: Rule against, citing the Lineage's custom

effects.log: You rule against. The blood are reassured and the relative is not, and you know, as you say it, what it cost.

events.text: The Lineage of {b3_house} has a tradition that the head must, once a decade, sit in judgment on a dispute among the blood, in public, in the Hall of Names, with the full rite. This decade's dispute is over a name. Two cousins each claim to be the "Elder Cousin," an unofficial and much-cherished title. Both are sincerely wounded.

choices.text: Declare both Elder Cousins, and make the title a joint office

effects.log: You declare it. The cousins are aghast to find they are required to sit together, and are, within a year, inseparable.

choices.text: Declare the title abolished, and replace it with a new one that fits neither

effects.log: You abolish it. The cousins are mutually aggrieved, which reunites them against you, and the Hall chuckles.

events.text: A god of the Lineage of {b3_house} comes to you in the small hours with a confession: he has been secretly feeding a hungry mortal village for forty years from the Lineage's own stores, against policy, without telling the Keeper. The village is thriving. The Keeper is going to find out. The god is not sorry. He is only frightened for the village.

choices.text: Make the secret feeding the Lineage's official policy, and thank him

effects.log: You make it so. The god weeps, the Keeper protests and then sighs, and the village is, from then on, the Lineage's own.

choices.text: Tell him to carry on, and keep it from the Keeper a while longer

effects.log: You tell him. The Keeper finds out in a year, and says she knew for thirty, and was only waiting for someone to say something.

events.text: A scholar of the Silent Hall has written a history of {b3_house} that makes the Lineage look ridiculous, accurate, and rather lovable. The blood want it burned. The young want it printed. The scholar, who has stayed in the guest-hall, is the quietest and most alarming person you have met. You are asked to rule.

choices.text: Print the history, with a preface in your own hand

effects.log: You print it. The blood grumble, the young rejoice, and the book is read in the Silent Hall as a model of its kind.

choices.text: Keep it in the archive and let each new head read it once

effects.log: You archive it. The scholar sighs, bows, and leaves a note: "you will wish you had printed it."

events.text: It is the decade of the Great Audit of {b3_house}, in which every office, every shrine and every ledger is inspected. The Officers have prepared for it for years. On the day, the inspector is an eleven-year-old god, small, solemn, with a lantern and a magnifying lens, who has been asked by the Thrones to be very thorough. She starts with the kitchen.

choices.text: Follow her round with a polite expression and open every door

effects.log: You follow. By the end of the week the child has found nine faults, all real, and one surprising virtue, and has become the Lineage's mascot.

choices.text: Greet her with a cup of milk and a gold star, and let her work in peace

effects.log: You greet her. She is delighted, and rules the Audit with a firm hand, and the Lineage passes with distinction.

events.text: An old rival of {b3_house} has died, and the Lineage is invited to the funeral. The blood want to boycott it. The rival's Lineage is a bitter enemy. But the dead god, in the last century, had been quietly gentle with the weakest of your Line. The invitation is correct, formal, and scrawled at the bottom, in a different hand: "please come."

choices.text: Attend in person, with the head's full retinue, and speak

effects.log: You attend. You say a few honest words. The rival's Lineage is silent, and the old enmity is, by a little, broken.

choices.text: Send a wreath and a letter and stay home

effects.log: You send them. The rival's Lineage notes the courtesy, and the enmity stays where it is.

events.text: The Oracle Pool of {b3_house} offers, once a century, to answer one question from the head, whatever it may be. This is the century. The Officers have prepared forty questions. The Steward has prepared one. You have prepared none. The Pool is clear and cold. It waits. The entire Hall is gathered round it, holding its breath.

choices.text: Ask the Pool what the Lineage should fear most

effects.log: The Pool answers. It is something small and domestic, and the Lineage deals with it, and thrives.

choices.text: Ask the Pool what the Lineage has forgotten that it loved

effects.log: The Pool answers with a name, a place, and a song. The Lineage spends a century finding them again, and is warmer.

events.text: A new god has been born into {b3_house}, and the child's domain is a thing nobody has seen before: the smell of rain on hot stone. The Officers are in a stir. The domain is minor, charming and undefined. They need you to rule on whether it counts, formally, as a domain, entitling the child to a pillar, a title and a seat at the table.

choices.text: Declare it a domain, and give the child a pillar

effects.log: You declare it. The child, tiny, is carried to the pillar, and the Lineage is the first in an age to have a new god of a new thing.

choices.text: Rule that it is a sub-domain of Rain, and place the child in Rain's care

effects.log: You place them. The god of Rain, startled, is delighted, and the child grows up beloved and a bit confused.

events.text: The Lineage of {b3_house} is asked by a distant pantheon to send a head to a feast of reconciliation. The invitation is ceremonial and, by the old law, you must go in person, alone, unguarded. The pantheon was your Lineage's enemy for three thousand years. The feast is, the Steward suggests, either a peace or a very elaborate way to remove a head.

choices.text: Go alone, unguarded, as the law requires

effects.log: You go. It is a peace, and a magnificent one, and you return with a pantheon's friendship and a very large cake.

choices.text: Go with an honour guard of the Lineage, and a polite note of regret about the law

effects.log: You go with a guard. The pantheon is slightly insulted, and entirely courteous, and the peace is a more careful one.

events.text: The Lineage of {b3_house} keeps in its cellar a great bell cast in the first age, which must be rung once each century by the head. The ringing takes an hour and a good deal of strength. You are tired, this century, and the rope is heavy. The Officers watch. The bell hangs, enormous and dark, above you in the vault.

choices.text: Ring the bell for the full hour, until your hands blister

effects.log: You ring it. The sound rolls out over the domain, and the faithful below feel it in their bones, and the Lineage is steadied.

choices.text: Ring it for ten minutes, and call the young to take the rope in turns

effects.log: You ring, and then you call them. The young take the rope, one after another, laughing, and the ringing goes on for the hour.

events.text: The faithful of {b3_house} have sent a petition signed by a million mortals, begging that the Lineage not move the date of the Harvest Rite, as the Officers have proposed. The Officers say the date is inconvenient for the Lineage's calendar. The mortals have never been consulted in ten thousand years. The petition is a very long scroll, tied with grass.

choices.text: Keep the date, and reorder the Lineage's calendar to fit

effects.log: You keep it. The Officers sigh, the calendar is rearranged, and the faithful hear of it, and bring more.

choices.text: Move the date, and send a long apology in dreams to every signer

effects.log: You move it. The dreams are received with patience, and the faithful, shrugging, adapt, and the Officers are content.

events.text: One of your oldest friends in {b3_house}, a god of the third rank, has been passed over for a promotion for the fifth time. They are bitter, wry and no longer asking. The post is worth little but honour. The Officers think the god too gentle. You are the head, and could simply give it, over their heads, and risk the blood.

choices.text: Give them the post, and take the consequences from the blood

effects.log: You give it. The blood murmur, and your friend, wordless, takes up the seal, and the old Officers, by degrees, come round.

choices.text: Ask your friend to earn it before the Hall, in a rite of trial

effects.log: You ask. The trial is hard, and your friend wins it, and the blood cannot gainsay it.

events.text: A pestilence of doubt has spread among the young gods of {b3_house}: they have begun to ask what the Lineage is for. The question is put politely, at dinner, over the soup, in rows. The Officers have no answer, and the elders, who do, will not say it. The young look at you, the head, with a bare and terrible hope.

choices.text: Tell them, honestly, what you think the Lineage is for

effects.log: You tell them. It takes an hour, and is a plain and imperfect answer, and the young, listening, nod, and ask for more.

choices.text: Tell them to find the answer themselves, and set them a year-long quest

effects.log: You set it. The year is hard, and the answers they bring back are better than yours.

events.text: A night-watchman of {b3_house} has found the old head, whom you displaced, sitting alone on a parapet at midnight with a flask. The old head is not drunk. The old head is singing, very softly, to the stars. The watchman has come to ask you what to do. It is an old, sad, beautiful song, and the watchman is shaking.

choices.text: Go up and sit with the old head on the parapet

effects.log: You go. You sit. The old head finishes the song, and says, "it is not so bad, being old," and you share the old head's silence, and the flask stays with the old head.

choices.text: Send the watchman up with a cloak and a pot of tea

effects.log: You send them. The old head accepts, and the song resumes, a little warmer, and you are told of it in the morning.

events.text: The Hall of {b3_house} is asked to host the trial of a god accused of a crime against the pantheon: the unauthorised answering of a prayer. The accused is the god of a minor spring, who gave water to a dying man. The Thrones demand a verdict by the end of the week. The accused is composed, and has brought a flask of spring water to share with the jury.

choices.text: Argue before the Thrones that the crime is a virtue

effects.log: You argue. The Thrones are annoyed and impressed, and the verdict is a reprimand and a quiet vow to change the law.

choices.text: Convict, with the lightest sentence, and appeal to the Thrones for a pardon

effects.log: You convict, gently. The pardon comes in a year, and the accused returns to the spring, unrepentant and beloved.

events.text: A very old woman of the mortals has climbed to the gate of {b3_house} and asks to see the head. She says the Lineage once saved her grandmother from a fire, and she would like to say thank you before she dies. The Warden says it was eight hundred years ago. The woman says she knows. The Warden says she cannot be eight hundred. The woman says she is not; her family keeps the thanks.

choices.text: Receive her yourself, in the Hall, with full honours

effects.log: You receive her. She says her thanks, and it takes a minute, and you cry, and the Hall does, and it is the best minute of the decade.

choices.text: Receive her in the gate-house, over tea, without ceremony

effects.log: You receive her so. She says her thanks over a cup, and you say yours, and the Warden sniffs and turns away.

events.text: The Lineage of {b3_house} has a debt of honour to a god it wronged in the second age, and the debt has come due. The creditor sends a polite note: the Lineage must give up a pillar, a name, or an hour. The pillar is the oldest. The name is the founder's. The hour, the note says, is one hour of the head's time, in private. The Officers are appalled by the third.

choices.text: Give the hour, and sit with the creditor in private

effects.log: You give it. The creditor wants to tell you a story, and the story is long and terrible and true, and when it is over, the debt is cancelled.

choices.text: Give the pillar, and carve a new one beside it

effects.log: You give it. The creditor takes it away on a cart, and the Lineage mourns, and the debt is gone.

events.text: A wave of plague among the gods themselves, a sort of weariness, has struck {b3_house}: dozens of the Lineage are unable to rise from bed. The Reader of Omens is baffled. The physician, a god of herbs, says the cause is the Lineage's own grief for something it has never named. She says the cure is to name it.

choices.text: Gather the Lineage in the Hall and ask them to name it together

effects.log: You gather them. The naming is slow and painful, and the Lineage, one by one, rises, and the weariness lifts.

choices.text: Name it yourself, aloud, and say it for them all

effects.log: You name it. The Lineage listens, and the weariness lifts, and you are the one who has said what they could not.

events.text: A messenger comes from a Lineage far below {b3_house} in rank: a petty family of dust-gods who beg to be received as the Lineage's clients. They offer all they have: eleven jars of grey powder and a single small hymn. The Officers wish them away. The dust-gods are tired, gentle and very polite. The hymn, when sung, is the loveliest thing you have heard in a decade.

choices.text: Receive them as clients of the house, and learn the hymn

effects.log: You receive them. The hymn is sung in the Hall, thereafter, once a year, and the dust-gods have a home.

choices.text: Send them on with a letter to a friendlier Lineage

effects.log: You send them. The friendlier Lineage takes them in, and writes you a note of thanks, and the hymn is still sung there.

events.text: The Warden of the Domain Gate of {b3_house} reports that the gate has been opened, by night, three times by someone with a key. No one has seen who. The key is the head's own. You have had it round your neck for years. The Warden, with enormous tact, asks whether you have ever sleepwalked. You haven't. You think.

choices.text: Sit up by the gate three nights, key round your neck, and watch

effects.log: You sit up. On the third night a figure, cloaked, with a duplicate key, opens the gate, and it is your own sleeping shadow, which you catch and talk to.

choices.text: Post two Wardens at the gate and take off the key at night

effects.log: You do. The gate stays shut. Your shadow, you suspect, is hurt.

events.text: The Lineage of {b3_house} has been asked, by a Throne, to lend its Oracle Pool to a council of the Silent Hall for a month. The council will use it to find a lost god. The Pool will be, for a month, unavailable to the Lineage. The Officers resist. The Silent Hall asks only, with infinite politeness, and the Pool has opinions of its own.

choices.text: Lend the Pool, and keep a vigil beside it, to guard it

effects.log: You lend it. The council finds the god, in a distant field, asleep, and the Lineage is credited with the finding.

choices.text: Ask the Pool whether it wishes to go, and respect the answer

effects.log: You ask. The Pool ripples consent, and goes, and returns improved, and slightly snobbish.

events.text: A new faith has risen among the mortals below {b3_house}, which holds that the gods are only the voices of the dead, and the Line only a tradition of remembering. The faith is peaceful, and growing. The Officers want it condemned. The Reader of Omens, pale, says the faith is, in an odd way, true. The leader of the faith has asked, humbly, for an audience.

choices.text: Receive the leader, and ask them to explain their view

effects.log: You receive them. They are gentle, brilliant, and unafraid, and you leave the audience with a new and somewhat humbling thought.

choices.text: Send a dream of friendly disagreement and leave the faith to grow

effects.log: You send the dream. The faith grows, tolerant and odd, and the Line coexists with it for ten thousand years.

events.text: The elders of {b3_house} have come to you, as head, to ask that you take a spouse. It is a matter of the Lineage's continuance. They have a list of candidates, tactfully prepared, with portraits and pedigrees and a short note on each. The Steward holds the list at arm's length, as one holds a fish. Your name is on none of the notes.

choices.text: Read the list aloud, with comments, and let the Hall laugh

effects.log: You read it. The comments are shameless, and the Hall roars, and the matter is shelved with great good humour.

choices.text: Ask the elders what they truly wish, and listen to the answer

effects.log: You ask. They answer with the fear of a Lineage that has seen heads die unmarried, and you listen, and make your own decision.

events.text: It is the thousandth year of your headship of {b3_house}. The Lineage holds a feast in your honour. The Officers have prepared a speech. The blood have prepared a gift. The young have prepared a play. All three are, in the event, terrible. You laugh till you cry. The Steward, in the corner, is also crying. The play includes a puppet of you.

choices.text: Join the play, and take the part of your own puppet

effects.log: You join. The Hall is beside itself, and the play is performed every thousand years thereafter, with you in it.

choices.text: Sit through the whole of it, and thank each in turn, with a joke

effects.log: You thank them. The jokes are good. The Lineage glows, and you go to bed with an aching jaw and a full heart.

events.text: A god of {b3_house} has made a pilgrimage to the sleeping ancestor of another Lineage and brought back a lock of hair. It is a priceless relic and an outrageous theft. The other Lineage is demanding its return. The god says it was a gift. The ancestor, in sleep, is not saying. The hair is silver, and smells faintly of rain.

choices.text: Return the hair, with an apology and a gift of your own

effects.log: You return it. The other Lineage, appeased, sends back a charming note, and the god sulks and is forgiven.

choices.text: Keep it, and send a sworn statement that it was freely given

effects.log: You keep it. The statement is investigated, and, to everyone's surprise, upheld by the ancestor's sleeping hand.

events.text: The Lineage of {b3_house} has a ghost. Not a dead god: a ghost, a fragment of a long-vanished head, who drifts through the Hall in the early morning, correcting small errors in the arrangement of the cups. Today the ghost has rearranged the cups into a pattern. The Steward says it is a message. The pattern, when sketched, is a hand, five fingers, pointing at you.

choices.text: Stand in the Hall at dawn, and wait for the ghost to speak

effects.log: You wait. The ghost drifts to you, tilts a cup, and a drop of wine on the floor reads: "thank you." Then it is gone.

choices.text: Ask the Steward to leave a note for the ghost, on the table

effects.log: You do. The ghost leaves a reply in the morning, in a very old hand, and the correspondence continues.

events.text: A decade of your headship of {b3_house} has passed in peace, and the blood have grown, a little, to like you. At the Feast, an old uncle of the blood proposes a toast: "to the head, who is almost as good as the last." The Hall roars. You raise your cup, and realise that it is the nicest thing anyone has said in ten years.

choices.text: Return the toast, with a salute to the last head

effects.log: You do. The Hall, hearing a head praise a predecessor, is moved, and the old uncle weeps into his cup.

choices.text: Laugh, and tell the uncle that "almost" will do for another thousand years

effects.log: You say so. The Hall roars again, and the uncle, delighted, slaps the table.

events.text: A solemn deputation of the Officers of {b3_house} asks you, as head, to settle the matter of the Feast seating once and for all. There are forty-one seats at the high table and forty-two claimants. The forty-second has brought a cushion, a chair and a petition. The chair is exactly the wrong height. The Steward looks at the ceiling.

choices.text: Add a forty-second seat, lower, and make the lowness an honour

effects.log: You add one. The claimant, elated, spends the Feast looking up at everyone, and calls it the best view in the Hall.

choices.text: Remove the claimant's chair, and offer the seat of the guest of honour

effects.log: You offer it. The claimant is so overcome that the forty-first, moved, offers to swap.

events.text: {npc} arrives from {b3_house} with an aunt, a letter of terms, and a sealed box that has not been opened. The aunt sits very upright and does not drink. {npc} looks at you, then at the aunt, then at you again, with an expression so frank that the aunt coughs. The letter of terms is eleven pages long. The Covenant is, apparently, a serious matter.

choices.text: Open with a question of your own, not a compliment

effects.log: You ask what {npc} would do with a free year. {He} thinks, and answers, and it is a strange and honest answer, and the aunt sets down the cup.

choices.text: Ask the aunt to step out for a stroll in the garden

effects.log: The aunt, after a pause, assents. {npc} releases a long breath, and says, "thank you," and the real talk begins.

events.text: {npc} asks to be shown the oldest thing in your Lineage. You hesitate, then take {him} to the cellar, where a plain clay jar is kept on a shelf, nameless, sealed with wax. {npc} puts a hand on it for a long moment and says, "it is warm." It is not. But {his} hand, when withdrawn, leaves a faint mark on the clay.

choices.text: Say the jar has been warm as long as you can remember

effects.log: {npc} nods, as at a shared secret. The jar, from then on, is a little warmer, or seems so, and the two of you speak of it fondly.

choices.text: Say nothing, and take {his} hand off the jar

effects.log: You take it. {npc} looks at you, startled, and then at the jar, and says, "I am sorry," and you find you are not offended.

events.text: At the first dinner of the Covenant talks, {npc} of {b3_house} eats nothing, and says nothing, and watches you. {He} is not unfriendly; {he} is attentive in the way of those who have been taught to read a host. Near the end, {he} says, quite politely, that your kitchen salts everything the same, and that the Lineage of {b3_house} considers this a character flaw.

choices.text: Admit it, and ask {him} to teach you the Lineage's way

effects.log: {npc} brightens. {He} teaches you, in the kitchen, the next day, with sleeves rolled, and the soup is the best you have had.

choices.text: Defend your kitchen, with a smile, and a counter-charge about their pepper

effects.log: You counter. {npc} laughs, caught, and a long and happy quarrel about seasoning begins, and lasts for decades.

events.text: {npc} has sent you, through an intermediary, a gift before the Covenant is even agreed: a small bell, with no clapper. It is the custom of {b3_house} to send such to a possible spouse. The bell is to be rung by the hand, and its sound is said to tell the Lineage whether the match is good. You ring it. It makes no sound. The messenger looks pained.

choices.text: Ring it again, harder, and listen with your whole body

effects.log: You ring it. Nothing, and then a faint tone, in the bones of your jaw, and you are sure {npc} has felt the same, far away.

choices.text: Send the bell back with a clapper, a small one, and a note

effects.log: You send it. {npc} replies, in a week, with a clapper of {his} own, in the shape of a sparrow, and a note: "now it rings."

events.text: The Warden of the Domain Gate of {b3_house} will not let {npc} leave the Lineage seat alone to meet you. The Lineage insists on an escort of nine. The escort arrives, in full dress, with banners, and stands round the garden in a ring, politely deaf. {npc}, mortified, whispers that this is the third meeting the Lineage has "supervised."

choices.text: Send for nine chairs and nine cups, and make the escort part of the meeting

effects.log: You do. The nine, startled, sit, and by the second cup are telling stories, and {npc} laughs, and the supervision becomes a party.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to walk with you to the far end of the garden, within sight

effects.log: You walk. The escort, with infinite discretion, moves to a slightly greater distance, and you and {npc} speak in privacy.

events.text: {npc} confesses, on the third evening, that {he} does not wish to be a god at all. {He} has been one for six thousand years and has never wanted to be anything but a baker. {He} has not told the Lineage. {He} tells you because {he} says you look like someone who will not repeat it, and because the soup has made {him} bold.

choices.text: Say you will not repeat it, and ask {him} what {he} would bake

effects.log: {npc} lists, with shining eyes, nine loaves. You promise to try them all, and {he} weeps, and the Covenant is, for the first time, a hopeful thing.

choices.text: Say the Lineage might one day let {him} bake, if {he} asked it

effects.log: {npc} stares at you. "It would never," {he} says. "But I could ask." {He} looks, suddenly, much younger.

events.text: On the day of the Covenant talks, a messenger from {b3_house} slips into your hall with a private note from {npc}, written in haste: "my aunt will propose a clause about the offspring. Do not agree. I will explain." The aunt arrives, and takes a seat. The aunt opens with, "a clause about the offspring."

choices.text: Decline the clause politely, and refer to a prior engagement of the heart

effects.log: You decline. The aunt, outplayed, nods slowly, and {npc} across the table closes both eyes in relief.

choices.text: Ask the aunt to explain the clause in full, and listen

effects.log: You listen. The clause is cruel in a dull way, and you refuse it with a long list of reasons, and the aunt is a little impressed.

events.text: {npc} and you find yourselves lost in the long library of {b3_house}, the Lineage having left you alone by ill-concealed design. You wander between the stacks. {npc} points out the oldest shelves with a possessive, shy tenderness. At the end of a row is a chair, a candle and a book left open. {He} says it was {his} mother's.

choices.text: Ask {him} to read you the open page

effects.log: {npc} reads. It is a poem, and a bad one, and {he} loves it, and the two of you stay in the library until the candle is gone.

choices.text: Ask {him} about {his} mother, and listen

effects.log: {npc} tells you. The story is long and tender and has a joke at the end, and you laugh, and {he} cries a little, and neither of you minds.

events.text: The Covenant requires that the two Lineages exchange a hostage of honour for a year. {npc} says {he} will go, if you will keep {his} favourite cat. The cat is vast, old, and disapproving. It sits on your desk and watches you with an air of weighing your suitability. {npc} says it is the best judge of character in the pantheon.

choices.text: Accept the cat, and promise to treat it as {npc}'s own

effects.log: You accept. The cat takes the office chair, and its verdict, a year later, is a slow, deliberate blink.

choices.text: Offer a different hostage: a rare book, with a note

effects.log: You offer the book. {npc} accepts, mock-grave, and the cat, aggrieved, goes to stay with the Warden.

events.text: {npc}'s Lineage, {b3_house}, observes a custom of the first night: that the suitors speak of their worst fear, before the other, in the dark, with no lamp. The aunt has arranged it. The room is bare. {npc} sits across from you. Neither of you can see the other. You hear {him} breathe.

choices.text: Speak the fear aloud, plainly, and let {him} hear it

effects.log: You speak it. A silence, and then {npc}'s voice, low and steady, says {his} own, and the two fears are odd twins.

choices.text: Speak a smaller fear, and keep the real one back

effects.log: You say a lesser one. {npc} hears the lie, kindly, and says, "thank you," and you both know.

events.text: A rival Lineage has sent its own suitor to the same house as {npc}, and the suitor is, by every account, a better match: richer, taller, of greater lineage and kinder to cats. {npc} is shy, brief, plain, and, at the moment, trying to stand up straight. The aunt is delighted by the competition. The rival suitor is charming. {npc} does not look at you.

choices.text: Court {npc} openly, with a gift of your own making

effects.log: You make a gift, a poor one, with your own hands. {npc} sees it, and takes it, and the rival suitor withdraws with grace.

choices.text: Befriend the rival suitor, and let {npc} choose in peace

effects.log: You befriend them. {npc} chooses, in time, and the three of you are friends, whichever it was.

events.text: {npc} arrives for the Covenant talks wearing the ceremonial robes of {b3_house}, which are beautiful, weighty and entirely impractical. {He} cannot sit down in them. {He} spends the first hour standing, politely, while you sit, and the aunt stands behind {him}, equally immobile. Eventually {he} says, in a small voice, that {he} has had cramp since noon.

choices.text: Suggest {he} take the robe off, and offer a plain coat of yours

effects.log: {npc} sheds the robe with an audible sigh, and the aunt, scandalised, hides behind a fan, and the talks resume with a sudden, easy warmth.

choices.text: Stand too, and conduct the whole meeting on your feet

effects.log: You stand. The aunt is moved to sit, and {npc} follows, and the stiff robes rustle and give way.

events.text: At the Covenant garden-party, {npc} introduces you to a dozen gods of {b3_house}, each a cousin, and each, in turn, whispers to you a different secret about {npc}. Some are sweet. Some are scurrilous. One is that {npc} snores. Another that {he} writes bad verse. Another that {he} once, as a child, set fire to the Hall. {npc} watches, from across the lawn, in terror.

choices.text: Collect them all, and confess a secret of your own in turn

effects.log: You collect them. At the end you tell {npc} your own, and {he} laughs till {he} has to sit, and it is a friendship.

choices.text: Ignore them all, and tell {npc} you have heard none

effects.log: You tell {him}. {He} does not believe you, and is grateful all the same.

events.text: On the eve of the Covenant, {npc} comes to your door alone, at night, without the aunt, without the escort, in an old coat with a muddy hem. {He} says, "I walked." {He} has walked from the Lineage seat of {b3_house}, a journey of three weeks. {He} says {he} did not want to arrive in a chariot, to be looked at. {He} wanted to arrive tired.

choices.text: Take {him} in, wash {his} feet, and give {him} a bowl of soup

effects.log: You do. {npc} says nothing, and eats everything, and sleeps for a day, and the Covenant is spoken of afterward as a thing begun in kindness.

choices.text: Send for a chariot to take {him} home refreshed, and meet at the proper hour

effects.log: You send one. {npc} is touched, and accepts, and the Covenant proceeds on an easier footing.

events.text: A letter arrives from the oldest member of {b3_house}, addressed to you, not to {npc}. It is a single page in a trembling hand. It says: "I have known {npc} since the first spring, and I would give a pillar of my own name to see {him} happy. If you are not the one, say so at once, and I will not speak of it. If you are, may the Line forgive me for how little I can offer."

choices.text: Reply that you will try to be the one, and ask nothing in return

effects.log: You reply. The old god reads it, in the Hall, aloud, in a cracked voice, and the Lineage falls silent, and approves.

choices.text: Reply that you do not yet know, and that you will be honest when you do

effects.log: You reply so. The old god nods, saying that honesty is the best gift, and the Lineage waits.

events.text: {npc} has a habit, you notice, of talking to the stars: not praying, just talking. At the Covenant feast {he} slips outside during the dessert, and you follow, and find {him} on the lawn, saying to the sky, "I am nervous." The stars, you could swear, are listening. {He} notices you and smiles a little, caught.

choices.text: Join {him} on the lawn and speak to the stars too

effects.log: You join {him}. You say something small and true to the sky, and {he} laughs, and the stars seem to shift, for a moment, like a room making space.

choices.text: Wait on the porch and let {him} finish

effects.log: You wait. When {he} returns, {he} says, "thank you for not interrupting," and takes your arm.

events.text: A Covenant, by the custom of {b3_house}, must be witnessed by the sleeping ancestor. That means a long climb, a cold cave, and an hour of silence. {npc} is nervous about it, and so is the aunt. At the mouth of the cave, {npc} reaches for your hand, and does not let it go until the end. The ancestor does not wake. Something in the cave breathes in, a little deeper.

choices.text: Keep hold of {his} hand and bow to the sleeper together

effects.log: You bow. The cave seems to warm. {npc} squeezes your hand, once, and the climb down is lighter.

choices.text: Let go, to bow properly, and take it again at the door

effects.log: You do. {npc} smiles, understanding, and the sleeper, you think, approves.

events.text: The terms of the Covenant from {b3_house} include a clause that you must visit the Lineage once a century and sit for a day in the Hall, to be seen. The visits are to be formal, silent and unrecorded. {npc}, sheepish, explains that the clause is a relic, and that no one has enforced it since the second age. {He} says the Lineage would be hurt if you declined.

choices.text: Accept the clause, and propose to visit in disguise, to see the Hall as it is

effects.log: You accept, with the twist. {npc} laughs, and the aunt purses a thin mouth, and the visits become a long, secret game.

choices.text: Accept the clause as written, and sit your day in perfect stillness

effects.log: You sit. The Lineage watches, and is awed, and a little unnerved, and you are admitted to the family.

events.text: {npc} and you are walking in the gardens of {b3_house} when a mortal pilgrim, lost and sunburned, stumbles through a gap in the hedge and falls at your feet, murmuring a prayer. It is a prayer to the Lineage. {npc}, caught off guard, stoops and answers it, quickly, softly, without thinking, with a gentleness that startles you both.

choices.text: Say nothing of it, and walk on, and take {his} hand

effects.log: You walk on. {npc} glances at you, flushing, and says: "I did not mean to be seen doing that," and you say, "I am glad I did."

choices.text: Join {him} in answering, and bless the pilgrim's road together

effects.log: You join. The pilgrim goes on, content, and {npc} looks at you with a new, bright interest.

events.text: It emerges that {npc} is not the intended match at all. The aunt has sent the wrong god. {npc}'s elder sibling, a stately goddess, was the one meant to come, and has been ill. {npc} was sent in a hurry, with the wrong letter. {He} has been silent about it for three days, and has just burst out, in the garden, "I do not think I am who you were expecting!"

choices.text: Laugh, and say you are very glad to have met {him} instead

effects.log: You laugh. {npc} stares, then laughs too, with relief, and the sibling, recovering, is invited to visit, and the Covenant is reshaped.

choices.text: Say the aunt must be told, and the matter set right properly

effects.log: You say so. {npc} nods, miserably, and the aunt is told, and the mistake becomes a comedy in the Lineage for ages.

events.text: The Lineage of {b3_house} invites you and {npc} to a rite of the first walk: you are to walk, side by side, the length of the Hall of Names, past all the pillars, and read aloud the name on each as you pass. There are nine thousand. {npc} says it takes the whole night. The Lineage watches from the galleries, in complete silence.

choices.text: Walk it with {him}, reading half the names each, to the end

effects.log: You walk. It takes the night. At the last name you are hoarse and happy and {npc} is weeping, softly, and it is dawn.

choices.text: Walk it hand in hand, and read the names in a single murmur together

effects.log: You read together. It is a low sound, like a river, and the Lineage listens, and by morning you have, between you, one voice.

events.text: {npc} shows you, at last, the secret of {b3_house}: a small door in the back of the Hall, behind a tapestry, that opens on a room with a single window and a pot of tea. It is where the Lineage's gods go to cry. The room is warm, plain and furnished with a heap of handkerchiefs. {He} says that the Lineage has never shown it to an outsider.

choices.text: Sit down, pour two cups of the tea, and say nothing

effects.log: You sit and pour. The tea is excellent, and {npc} watches you with a bright stare, and then looks at the window and talks.

choices.text: Say it is an honour, and promise to keep the room's secret for ever

effects.log: You promise. {npc} nods, deeply moved, and the room, thereafter, is yours as well.

events.text: {npc} asks, in the formal tone the Lineage of {b3_house} requires, whether you would like to know the full list of the Lineage's expectations of a spouse. It is nine pages. {He} unrolls it. It includes demands about incense, silence at dawn, the correct side of the bed, and a clause forbidding certain jokes. {He} looks at you with desperate hope that you will laugh.

choices.text: Laugh, and write your own list of expectations, nine pages, in reply

effects.log: You write it. The two lists are read aloud together at the Covenant, and the Lineage, on hearing yours, roars.

choices.text: Read it gravely, and ask to be excused only the jokes clause

effects.log: You do. {npc} chokes, and the aunt, hearing, almost smiles, and the clause is struck.

events.text: The Covenant requires one final test from {b3_house}: that the two of you spend a day without any divine power, as mortals, in a village below. You arrive in rough clothes, with no names. {npc}, who has never been mortal, cannot light a fire. You cannot cook. The villagers feed you, bemused, and the day is a disaster, and the best day of your lives.

choices.text: Ask the villagers to teach you both to bake a loaf

effects.log: They teach you. The loaf is flat and sour and you eat it by the stream, and {npc} says it is the best thing {he} has ever tasted.

choices.text: Find a corner of the village green, and sit, and be quiet together

effects.log: You sit. A child brings you a dandelion each, and {npc} wears {his} behind the ear all the way home.

events.text: On the eve of the Covenant, {npc} gives you a gift: a plain wooden box, locked. {He} says the key is in the Lineage seat of {b3_house}, and you must go and get it yourself, from a place {he} will not name. {He} says you will know. {He} says it is a test, and also, quietly, not. The box is light. Something shifts inside.

choices.text: Set out for the Lineage seat, and ask nothing on the way

effects.log: You go. The key is in the cat's collar, and the cat, in the Hall, lets you take it, and inside the box is a lock of {his} hair and a note.

choices.text: Ask {him} for a hint, and trust that {he} will give one

effects.log: {npc} gives one: "ask the cat." You laugh and go, and the key, and the note, are as promised.

events.text: The ceremonial exchange of rings for the Covenant with {b3_house} requires that each give the other a ring they have made themselves. You have made yours; it is not good. {npc} has made {his}; it is a small marvel of interlaced gold. {He} looks at your ring, and says nothing, and holds out {his} hand with a perfectly straight face.

choices.text: Put on the ring {he} made, and offer yours with a laugh

effects.log: You put it on. {npc} takes yours, studies it, and says it is the most honest ring {he} has seen, and wears it all the way home.

choices.text: Offer yours with a little speech about its flaws

effects.log: You give the speech. The Lineage laughs warmly, and {npc} presses your hand, and the ring is kept for ten thousand years.

events.text: {npc}, as a god of {b3_house}, has been formally instructed to give nothing away until the Covenant is signed. {He} has therefore turned into a statue of politeness. {He} answers every question with "the Lineage is honoured." On the sixth day you ask {him} what {he} had for breakfast. {He} opens {his} mouth, and says, "the Lineage is honoured," and then bursts out laughing.

choices.text: Laugh with {him}, and ask again, without the Lineage in the room

effects.log: You ask. {npc} answers, in three sentences, with bacon, and the Covenant has its first honest morning.

choices.text: Say, solemnly, that the Lineage is honoured too

effects.log: You say so. {npc} gives you a look of such comic gratitude that you are friends for ever.

events.text: The Covenant talks with {b3_house} stall on a single point: whose Lineage the child of the match would belong to. The aunt wants the child in the house of {npc}. Your Officers want the child in yours. Neither of you has said a word on the matter. {npc} whispers: "can we perhaps assume, for now, a child that belongs to itself?"

choices.text: Say the child will belong to itself, and put it in the Covenant

effects.log: You say so. The Hall gasps, and the aunt draws up to full height, and then, slowly, nods, and the clause is written.

choices.text: Propose that the child choose at the age of a thousand

effects.log: You propose it. The clause is accepted with surprising ease, and {npc} squeezes your hand under the table.
